issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Marin has no way to mark a test as needing a GPU, a minimum device count, or a specific accelerator. Some accelerator tests skip invisibly in CI as a result, and the two that need real device topology were written outside pytest entirely.

`tests/test_utils.py` provides `skip_if_no_tpu` and nothing equivalent for GPUs or device counts. The root `pyproject.toml` markers are `slow`, `integration`, `data_integration`, `cluster`, `requires_cluster`, `docker`, and `manual`; none describes hardware. `tests/cluster/conftest.py` names two clusters, `MARIN_TPU_CLUSTER` and `MARIN_GPU_CLUSTER = "cw-us-east-02a"`, with no entry for the GB200 cluster `cw-us-east-08a`.

Two tests in `lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py` check the ragged all-to-all MoE backend against a dense reference and run nowhere:

```
uv run python -m pytest lib/levanter/tests/grug/test_grugformer_moe.py -rs -k "ragged or granular or clip"
...
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[ragged_all_to_all]
SKIPPED test_moe_mlp_reports_positive_drop_count_in_ragged_a2a_when_over_capacity
5 passed, 2 skipped
```

They skip on `requires an even number of >=2 devices`, and forcing two CPU devices hits the next guard, `ragged_all_to_all is not implemented on XLA:CPU`. Every job in `.github/workflows/` runs on `ubuntu-latest`. The five that pass cover lowering, offset arithmetic against a NumPy simulation of the collective, and capacity clipping in isolation. None runs the real collective or the SM100 expert kernels.

The root `addopts` does not include `-rs`, so these skips never appear in CI output. A green run with full coverage and a green run with no ragged coverage look identical.

Both files that need real accelerator topology avoided pytest. `lib/iris/tests/e2e/gpu_gang_smoke.py` is a standalone `__main__` script with `--target kind|coreweave` and `--i-understand-the-cost`; it mock-labels kind nodes to simulate an NVLink domain instead of requiring one. `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ragged_ep_check.py` (PR #8549) submits a 4-GPU GB200 job, computes a pass/fail verdict, and raises on failure, but sits under `experiments/` with no scheduled caller.

Two cases need different mechanisms. A test like the levanter one needs N local devices inside the pytest process. A test like `ragged_ep_check` needs no local hardware: it submits a job whose constraint rides in `ResourceConfig.with_gpu("GB200", count=4, ...)`, so what it needs is a cluster fixture and a way to declare that the run is expensive.

#7242 delivered `tests/cluster/`, the `cluster` marker, and `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` for smokes that submit real jobs. It left open which hardware a test needs and what a test that cannot get that hardware should do.

Done when:

- A test can declare a local device requirement and skip with a named reason instead of an ad-hoc in-file guard.
- Skipped tests are visible in CI output.
- A job-submitting test can target the GB200 cluster through a fixture, and its cost is expressible on the test rather than only in the workflow.
- One existing case is ported as the reference: the levanter ragged EP tests, or `ragged_ep_check.py`.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correction to this issue's premise, found while acting on it in #8549.

It says `tests/cluster/` "covers submitting a job to a standing cluster" and that the gap is a GB200 lane and a cost tier on the existing workflow. The workflow no longer exists. #8605 deleted `.github/workflows/marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` on 2026-08-22, and its commit message gives the reason:

> Marin Cluster Smoke had zero successful scheduled runs: all 38 runs from July 17 through August 23 were cancelled around its 100-minute timeout. The workflow and its Grafana lane are deleted. The underlying tests remain directly runnable through the cluster-test runbook.

So nothing runs the `cluster` marker at all now, and this issue covers restoring a runner rather than extending one. The two other gaps it names are unaffected: there is still no way to declare a local device requirement, and `addopts` still carries no `-rs`, so skipped tests stay invisible.

One gap it named is now closed. #8549 moved the 4-GPU ragged transport gate to `tests/cluster/grug/test_ragged_ep_check.py`. That needed only a constant naming the GB200 peer, because `cw-us-east-08a` is already a federation peer of the marin hub and `target_cluster` is a `ResourceConfig` field, so `iris_client` works unchanged. No new fixture was required after all.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correcting my comment above, which was too absolute. "No workflow runs the `cluster` marker" is accurate; "accelerator tests have no automated vehicle" was not.

Scheduled GPU work does run. `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` fires daily at 10:00 UTC against `cw-us-west-04a`, sets `CANARY_ACCELERATOR: gpu`, and runs `python -m experiments.ferries.canary_ferry` on 8x H100 through Iris, with `scripts/ci/validate_canary_metrics.py` asserting the result. That is a real accelerator smoke on a daily cron. It is not pytest and carries no marker.

`iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` looks like a second GPU lane and is not one. It runs `pytest tests/test_integration_test.py -m integration` on PRs touching `lib/iris/**`, and the workflow comment says it submits "against the shared H100" — but the jobs `tests/integration_test.py` submits are `ResourceConfig.with_cpu()` with `require_accelerator=False`. It exercises a CoreWeave-hosted controller, not a GPU.

The deleted `marin-cluster-smoke.yaml` had two jobs, not one. `marin-tpu-smokes` ran on the schedule; `marin-gpu-smokes` was `if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.run_gpu`, so it never ran on a cron at all. The 38 timed-out scheduled runs the deleting commit cites were the TPU job. Standing-cluster GPU tests were therefore never automatic, before or after #8605.

So the gap this issue describes is sharper than "no runner": **no pytest marker anywhere selects GPU work.** The `cluster` marker has no workflow, and the `integration` marker runs only CPU jobs. Every GPU assertion in CI today lives in the canary ferry, outside pytest.

Two facts worth having when someone picks this up. The canary already parameterizes the accelerator (`CANARY_GPU_TYPE`, documented as "H100, GH200, B200", plus `CANARY_GPU_COUNT` and `CANARY_GPU_REPLICAS`), so scheduling GPU work of a given shape from Actions is solved machinery rather than something to build. And `marin-canary-ferry-coreweave.yaml` and `iris-smoke-coreweave.yaml` share the concurrency group `iris-coreweave-ci-shared` because they contend for one host, so any added lane needs a capacity story and not only a config entry.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Background
In #6070, the [PPL circuit-coverage gap dashboard](https://marin.community/analysis/ppl-circuit-coverage-gap/) showed that Marin 32B is much worse than Qwen3 32B at basic "code interpretation" skills: arithmetic, manipulating strings into tokens, exact character/index tracking, and other short deterministic continuations.

We suspect these skills are also important for agentic tasks. Agents need to read observations, preserve exact identifiers, transform text, update state, compare quantities, follow formats, and manipulate tool outputs. Many of these skills are simple in the sense that they are fully algorithmic and should not require a lot of reasoning, but they still need to be reliable.

We want to identify other tasks that seem important for agents and that models may not learn automatically from existing data, mostly web text and code. These tasks are likely to involve textual manipulation, arithmetic, format understanding, span selection, and state tracking, but they can involve other basic algorithmic skills as well.

## Description
Collect short no-code proposals for additional PPL circuit/basic-functionality tasks before implementing them. These tasks do not have to be code-related. The point is to identify small skills an agent should need for reliable tool use, reasoning over observations, formatting, state tracking, and code or data interpretation.

Post one comment per proposed task or small family on this issue using this template:

````markdown
## Proposed task
<short name, e.g. json_path_lookup, loop_counter_trace, calendar_delta, or table_cell_lookup>

## Skill being tested
<the concrete ability: indexing, escaping, stack state, operator precedence, argument binding, table lookup, unit conversion, date arithmetic, format following, etc.>

## Three examples
```text
<compact example 1, including final answer>
<compact example 2, including final answer>
<compact example 3, including final answer>
```

## Failure modes
<what a model might get wrong: off-by-one, byte/char confusion, quote escaping, state update order, unit mismatch, row/column mixup, leakage from task phrasing, etc.>

## Why an agent should need this skill
<how this primitive shows up in tool use, reading observations, updating state, planning, working with user data, or interpreting code/logs/UI text>

## Why ordinary pretraining may not teach it reliably
<why passive pretraining might underrepresent this skill: few explicit inputs paired with outputs, answers hidden in runtime/tool behavior, sparse edge cases, docs explain the rule but do not provide many executed examples, etc.>

## Implementation notes
<optional: useful metadata to store, edge cases to include, or related task family>
````

Example of a fully fleshed-out proposal, based on a task already implemented in `experiments/evals/ppl_circuit_coverage_v2.py`:

````markdown
## Proposed task
string_slicing

## Skill being tested
Python-style string indexing and slicing: start/stop/step handling, omitted characters, Unicode codepoint indexing, and the difference between the prompt prefix and the final answer.

## Three examples
```text
text = "abcdef"; text[1:5:2] -> 'bd'
text = "marin"; text[0:4:1] -> 'mari'
text = "́kder/ejehcp"; text[6:11:1] -> 'ejehc'
```

## Failure modes
Off-by-one start/stop errors, treating the stop index as inclusive, ignoring step, reversing the slice direction, confusing Unicode characters with UTF-8 bytes, copying the entire input string, or including explanatory text instead of only the final Python `repr` answer.

## Why an agent should need this skill
Agents routinely have to extract spans from tool output, logs, file paths, UI text, and user-provided strings. Slicing is a compact proxy for precise span selection: if a model cannot reliably take `text[start:stop:step]`, it will also struggle to copy the right substring from observations, preserve exact identifiers, or reason about offsets in code and data.

## Why ordinary pretraining may not teach it reliably
Pretraining corpora contain many slice expressions, but usually not paired with their executed result. Documentation explains the rule, and tests sometimes include expected outputs, but random slices over arbitrary strings are sparse. Edge cases like non-unit steps, Unicode combining marks, and stop-index exclusivity are especially unlikely to appear as dense input-output practice.

## Implementation notes
Generate short strings with varied punctuation and Unicode, choose valid `start`, `stop`, and `step` values, store those values plus the source text in metadata, and validate the target as `repr(text[start:stop:step])`. The supervised row should put completed few-shot lines in `input`, leave the held-out line ending in `-> `, and put only the quoted slice plus newline in `output`.
````

Good first proposal areas:

- Python/JSON literal lookup and re-emission.
- Regex-lite capture groups and substitutions.
- Small loop/state traces.
- Path, URL, or import-name normalization.
- Date/time arithmetic and formatting.
- CSV/TSV quoting and escaping.
- Boolean/operator precedence.
- Function-call argument binding with defaults.
- Table cell lookup and row/column selection.
- Unit conversion and quantity comparison.
- Checklist/state update after a sequence of actions.

Keep examples compact and avoid telegraphing the task with labels like `Task:` or `Final answer:`. A good proposal should be easy for a human to solve, easy to generate deterministically, and easy to validate from metadata.

### Definition of Done
- At least ten proposal comments are posted on this issue using the template above.
- Each proposal comment includes three compact examples, failure modes, why an agent should need the skill, and why ordinary pretraining may not teach it reliably.
- Accepted proposals are promoted into implementation work on #6236.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Description
Finish the token-native RL rollout data plane for Levanter and vLLM inference contexts. OpenAI compatibility is useful for testing, but the RL path should preserve tokenization identity, policy/version identity, sampled tokens, logprobs, masks, prompt/completion boundaries, finish reasons, and replay metadata without reconstructing token IDs from text.

PR #6186 (`codex/rl-token-rollout-api`, head `c4ba37bda1f429700528a442e2f18e906b96d1b9`) now carries the active implementation slice and has all visible checks green. It includes typed token rollout contracts, vLLM and Levanter token-native context methods, MathEnv and MockEnv token-native adapters, policy/checkpoint identity, tokenizer/chat-template replay identity, structured failure envelopes, stored rollout trace metadata, MoE router/expert replay metadata, OpenAI-shaped identity preservation, and completion-mask preservation through training batch construction.

### PrimeIntellect Decision
Do not block #6186 on converting `PrimeIntellectEnv` to the token-native path. Keep `PrimeIntellectEnv` OpenAI/verifiers-compatible for this PR stack because verifiers stop/tool-routing behavior still needs a concrete tokenized adapter design. This is acceptable for the current slice because #6186 preserves attached `response_token_ids` when present and carries tokenizer/policy replay identity through the shared OpenAI-shaped rollout path.

After #6185/#6186 land, split PrimeIntellect/verifiers work into smaller follow-ups: decide which verifier environments can expose tokenized prompts/results, centralize token-native versus OpenAI-compatible capability selection, add cross-environment roundtrip coverage, and turn missing-token or missing-logprob cases into explicit structured failures or loud errors.

### Definition of Done
- [x] vLLM and Levanter contexts expose the token-native rollout API behind stable types.
- [x] MathEnv and MockEnv can consume token-native outputs when the backend supports them.
- [x] Partial failures have structured envelopes for missing backend generations.
- [x] Integration coverage verifies IDs, boundaries, logprobs, masks, tokenizer identity, and policy metadata survive the round trip for the implemented paths.
- [x] PrimeIntellectEnv has a token-native path, or an explicit design decision documents why it remains OpenAI-compatible while preserving attached token IDs and replay identity.
- [ ] The rollout data plane lands after the serving stack it depends on, or maintainers accept the current stack ordering.

### Current Next Step
#6186 is the main token-native rollout PR and is green. The remaining blocker for this issue is stack acceptance/landing order: #6186 should land after the serving stack it depends on, or maintainers should explicitly accept the current stack ordering. PrimeIntellect-specific token-native work should be a follow-up after #6186 lands, not a blocker for this PR.

### Parent
- #6227

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Fetch issue, parent #6227, and predecessor PR #6186
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no parallel PRs; only #6186 in flight)
- [x] Scope assessment — too large for a single agent PR, blocked on #6186
- [x] Post Research + Proposed Approach for human review
- [ ] Re-engage once #6186 lands and a subtask is carved out

# Research

The token-native rollout API does not exist on `main` yet — it lands with PR #6186 (open, +2517/-24, 21 files), which adds `TokenRolloutRequest`/`TokenRolloutResult` to `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/types.py`, `generate_token_rollouts` on `BaseInferenceContext`, and concrete vLLM + Levanter implementations wired through `MathEnv` and `MockEnv`. This issue is the follow-on hardening pass: extend the typed path to PrimeIntellectEnv (still on OpenAI client + BPE round-trip), define structured partial-failure envelopes, add worker-level backend selection, and write cross-backend integration tests that assert tokenizer/policy identity, prompt/completion boundaries, logprobs, masks, and finish reasons survive the round trip.

The PrimeIntellect path is the largest remaining gap: it still calls `inference_ctx.openai_client()` and reconstructs token IDs via `process_vllm_chat_results` using `tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids()` — exactly the lossy reconstruction the issue calls out. Worker-level selection is also unsettled: `rollout_worker.py` (1098 lines on `main`) does not yet branch on whether a backend supports token-native rollouts.

**Relevant code**
- [`prime_intellect_env.py#L74-L194`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/prime_intellect_env.py#L74-L194) — verifiers path: OpenAI client + token-ID reconstruction
- [`inference_ctx/base.py#L65-L81`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/base.py#L65-L81) — current BPE vocab round-trip the issue wants to replace
- [`inference/types.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/types.py) — where #6186 adds the typed contracts (+309 lines)
- [`rollout_worker.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_worker.py) — where worker-level backend selection would live
- PR #6186 — foundational contracts and MathEnv/MockEnv slice (open)

# Proposed Approach

Hold for #6186 to land, then split into four sequenced PRs against the landed contracts. Doing it in one PR now would conflict with the 21 files #6186 touches and would freeze the contract before review feedback settles.

1. **PrimeIntellectEnv token-native path.** Replace `vf_env.generate(...)` + `process_vllm_chat_results` with a verifiers adapter that calls `inference_ctx.generate_token_rollouts(...)` and constructs `Rollout`s directly from the typed result. Keep the OpenAI client only for environments that don't yet expose tokens. Gate on `inference_ctx.supports_token_rollouts()` (new capability flag on `BaseInferenceContext`) and fall back loudly — `raise`, not silent OpenAI fallback. ~150 LOC + tests.

2. **Structured partial-failure envelopes.** Introduce `TokenRolloutOutcome = Success(TokenRolloutResult) | Failure(reason, request_id, partial_tokens?)` (frozen dataclass union, not booleans). vLLM raises today on per-prompt failures inside a batch; surface them per-request instead so a single OOM/truncation does not drop the whole batch. Wire `rollout_worker` to count `Failure` envelopes into metrics and log structured `finish_reason` for length truncations. ~200 LOC + tests.

3. **Worker-level backend selection.** Add `RolloutWorker._pick_rollout_path(env, inference_ctx) -> RolloutPath` returning `TOKEN_NATIVE` vs `OPENAI_COMPAT`, driven by the env declaring capability and the backend supporting it. Removes the per-env branching that #6186 inlines into `MathEnv`/`MockEnv`. ~80 LOC + tests.

4. **Cross-backend integration coverage.** One parameterized test file `tests/rl/test_token_rollout_roundtrip.py` running the same prompt through (vLLM stub, Levanter, MockEnv) and asserting: tokenizer-id equality, prompt/completion boundary offsets, logprob length == response length, mask shape, finish_reason preserved, policy version + tokenizer name persisted on the result. Reuse fixtures from `tests/rl/test_levanter_token_rollouts.py` and `tests/rl/test_vllm_token_rollouts.py` introduced in #6186. ~250 LOC.

Open questions for the maintainer before implementation:
- Should `PrimeIntellectEnv` keep an OpenAI fallback for verifier envs that need server-side tool routing, or hard-fail on backends without token rollouts?
- Where should the capability flag live — `BaseInferenceContext.supports_token_rollouts: bool` property, or a `Capabilities` dataclass returned by `get_capabilities()`?
- For partial failures, do we want per-request envelopes or a `BatchResult{successes, failures}` shape that keeps batch semantics intact?

Ready to take any one of (1)-(4) as a standalone PR once #6186 merges and these design points are resolved.

## Description
Explain and reduce the v6e prefill-heavy gap for `prefill_b8_i2048_o128_n1`.

Historical comparison row: Levanter `1006.83` decode tok/s and `17116.08` total tok/s versus vLLM `1262.90` decode tok/s and `21469.31` total tok/s, ratio `0.797`. That measured Levanter row had prefill chunks `4096,4096,4096,4096` and one decode iteration with `0.802s` total, `0.623s` device, `0.178s` host, and `0.174s` submit.

The corrected Levanter-only diagnostic completed at `/dlwh/qwen3-v6e8-prefilldiag-drain-prefill-b8-i2048-o128-n1-20260606-1532` from PR #6185 commit `82bb6dbfb`. It validated diagnostic prefill drain and produced `1022` decode iteration tokens for normal, `no_lm_head`, and `lm_head_no_sampling` rows.

Important interpretation correction: production `decode_submit_seconds` was previously measured from the start of the outer iteration before prefill drain, so the `0.174s`/`0.184s` submit field included prefill admission work. PR #6185 commit `dd993c03c` moved the submit timer to immediately before `_run_generation_loop(...)`, commit `6d74fc7ea` added decode iteration/device throughput fields, and commit `f55913d1` now separates prefill drain from the generation loop with `prefill_drain_*`, `generation_*`, and derived `generation_tokens_per_second` benchmark fields.

Corrected backend=both row: `/dlwh/qwen3-v6e8-prefillcorr-20260607-0023` completed successfully from #6185 head `91f6ec06a`. vLLM measured `1212.15` decode tok/s and `20606.54` total tok/s. Levanter measured `898.94` decode tok/s and `15282.00` total tok/s, ratio `0.742`, target fail. The corrected Levanter fields available in that run show prefill chunks `4096,4096,4096,4096`, prefill admission wall times `0.060,0.055,0.055,0.055s`, decode iteration `0.852s` total / `0.677s` device / `0.174s` host / `0.002s` submit / `0.002s` extract, `1022` decode iteration tokens, `1200.223` decode-iteration tok/s, and `1509.350` device tok/s. Because that row predates `f55913d1`, it does not yet include the new generation-only token/time split.


Post-`f55913d1` backend=both row: `/dlwh/qwen3-v6e8-prefillpostsplit-20260607-0419` completed successfully from #6185 head `d63d1edf`. vLLM measured `1264.03` decode tok/s and `21488.50` total tok/s. Levanter measured `957.72` decode tok/s and `16281.24` total tok/s, ratio `0.758`, target fail. The new split shows hot prefill chunks `4096,4096,4096,4096` with prefill wall times `0.060,0.056,0.056,0.056s`, decode iteration `0.800s` total / `0.623s` device / `0.177s` host / `0.002s` submit / `0.002s` extract, `1022` decode iteration tokens, `0.171s` prefill drain for `6` tokens, and `0.629s` generation for `1016` tokens. Derived throughput: `1277.749` decode-iteration tok/s, `1639.896` decode-device tok/s, and `1614.816` generation tok/s.

Follow-up code changes:
- #6185 commit `f7275e5a` stops logging full `InferenceRequest` dataclasses at INFO and instead logs bounded request metadata. In the prefill-heavy measured row, the old path serialized eight 2048-token prompt lists before the first prefill admission; this was a concrete host-side measured-path overhead source. Validation passed with inference-server pytest (`19 passed, 1 skipped`) plus focused pre-commit/Pyrefly on the touched files.
- #6185 commit `f55913d1` adds per-iteration `prefill_drain_seconds_per_iteration`, `prefill_drain_tokens_per_iteration`, `generation_seconds_per_iteration`, `generation_host_seconds_per_iteration`, `generation_tokens_per_iteration`, and `generation_tokens_per_second` to avoid conflating prefill-drain work with generation-loop throughput in future #6229 rows. Validation passed with `test_engine.py` and `test_qwen3_tpu_inference_parity_bench.py` (`63 passed`) plus focused pre-commit/Pyrefly.

Current interpretation: the remaining failure is attributed to end-to-end prefill-heavy wall-clock overhead rather than a proven decode-device regression. The issue remains open as a performance target because the post-`f55913d1` row still fails the end-to-end parity target at `0.758`, even though generation-only throughput is above the vLLM decode row. The remaining question is whether to optimize hot prefill/admission/serving wall-clock for this weak prefill-heavy regime, or deprioritize it relative to the core RL rollout rows.

### Definition of Done
- [x] Rerun one corrected Levanter-only diagnostic on the fixed harness.
- [x] Attribute the original row enough to avoid a false decode-kernel conclusion: the old submit timing was contaminated by prefill-drain work, and new benchmark fields separate prefill-drain, generation-loop, device, host, submit, and extraction timing.
- [x] Collect a post-`f55913d1` row for `prefill_b8_i2048_o128_n1` if this regime remains a priority, so the result includes `generation_*` and `prefill_drain_*` fields after bounded request logging.
- [ ] Decide the next optimization or close/deprioritize this issue based on that post-`f55913d1` row: prefill/host accounting, page/admission settings, or no further work if the row is acceptable for RL rollout priorities.
- [x] Update the epic and handoff with terminal job results from the completed diagnostics/reruns.

### Current Next Step
Do not launch another TPU run automatically. The next step is a decision, not more evidence collection: either optimize the remaining hot prefill/admission/serving wall-clock overhead for this regime, or close/deprioritize it if core RL rollout rows matter more than prefill-heavy parity. The post-split row should be interpreted using `generation_tokens_per_second=1614.816`, `prefill_drain_seconds_per_iteration=0.171`, and `generation_host_seconds_per_iteration=0.006`, not only the end-to-end `decode_tokens_per_second=957.72`.

issues.title: [levanter] Optimize v6e prefill-heavy decode gap

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
🤖 *Follow-up to #6058 (Iris k8s direct-provider gang admission via Kueue). Filed by an agent; do not action before #6058 merges.*

## Summary

The k8s gang-admission work in #6058 surfaced a latent representation problem in how Iris models coscheduling. Two fields encode the same intent — `JobConfig.has_coscheduling` (bool) and `coscheduling_group_by` (str) — and the `group_by` field is **overloaded** to mean two unrelated things across the two scheduling providers. This issue captures the full design for consolidating them. It is a cross-cutting change (proto + `types.py` + a controller SQL-schema migration + ~20 read sites + the scheduler), deliberately scoped **out** of #6058 to avoid entangling a schema migration with a feature launch.

## Problems

### 1. `has_coscheduling` duplicates `group_by != ""` (in intent)

`has_coscheduling` is always derived as `bool(HasField("coscheduling"))` (`transitions.py:1261`), and every real producer sets a non-empty `group_by` (`cli/job.py:467` → `"pool"`, `cli/job.py:491` → `tpu-name`). The bool carries no information that `group_by != ""` doesn't.

It is **not** a one-line removal, though — it is read at three sites that never touch `group_by`:

- **`transitions.py:2987` / `:3024`** — an indexed SQL column predicate (`has_coscheduling == True` / `== False`) that partitions PENDING rows into all-or-none gang promotion vs. flat budget-bounded first-fit.
- **`controller.py:1132`** — `and not task.has_coscheduling` exempts gangs from `max_tasks_per_job_per_cycle`.
- **`controller.py:253`** — maps `group_by` to `None` when not coscheduled but `""` otherwise; `scheduler.py:728` then guards on `is None`. Two inconsistent "no group" sentinels (`None` vs `""`).

### 2. Implementation contradicts the documented source of truth

The proto comments are self-consistent: `job.proto:512` and `:614` both say *non-empty `group_by` ⇒ coscheduled*. The **implementation** derives coscheduled-ness from *message presence* (`HasField`), not from `group_by != ""`. Because `CoschedulingConfig` is unvalidated (`types.py` — bare `group_by: str`, no `__post_init__`), a client can send `CoschedulingConfig(group_by="")` and reach the `has_coscheduling=True, group_by=""` state the proto calls "not coscheduled". That state then gets all-or-none **promotion** (`transitions.py:2987`) but non-Kueue **admission** (`tasks.py:574` gates `kueue_enabled` on `bool(group_by)`) — and on the worker-daemon path it stalls PENDING forever: `workers_by_group("")` returns `{}` (`constraints.py:1086`) while the diagnostic (`scheduler.py:861`) reports "Schedulable". #6058 makes this state reachable.

**Correct single source of truth:** `job.proto:614` — *non-empty `group_by` == coscheduled.*

### 3. `group_by` is overloaded across providers (partial fit with k8s/Kueue)

- **Worker-daemon path:** `group_by` is an *open-domain worker-attribute key* fed to `entities_by_group` — bucket workers by whatever attribute the string names (note `"pool"` isn't even in `WellKnownAttribute`).
- **K8s path:** `group_by` is (a) a truthiness toggle for Kueue admission (`tasks.py:574`) **and** (b) a lookup key into the private `_GROUP_BY_TO_TOPOLOGY` map (`tasks.py:130`) selecting a CoreWeave node label + hard/soft mode. Gang *identity* on k8s is not `group_by` at all — it's `parent-path + attempt_id` via `_pod_group_name`.

Unmapped `group_by` values silently get no topology. That is a *tested, intended* contract (`test_pod_manifest.py:956 test_kueue_unknown_group_by_still_gangs_without_topology`) — the smell is that the degradation is silent (`_GROUP_BY_TO_TOPOLOGY.get → None`), not that it gangs.

## Proposed design

1. **One source of truth for coscheduled-ness:** derive it from `group_by != ""`. Add `CoschedulingConfig.__post_init__` rejecting empty `group_by`, plus a **server-side** boundary check in `transitions.py` (raw-proto clients bypass the dataclass, so server enforcement is mandatory). This makes the broken `True + ""` state unreachable — that is the actual fix, not deleting the bool.

2. **Split the overloaded field:** add a closed `TopologyRequirement` StrEnum (`NONE` / `PREFERRED` / `REQUIRED`) to `CoschedulingConfig`, resolved at the producer where TPU-vs-GPU intent is known. Replace the silent `_GROUP_BY_TO_TOPOLOGY.get → None` with an explicit `NONE`, preserving the gang-without-topology contract.

3. **Keep the CoreWeave label translation in the k8s provider** — a `_REQUIREMENT_TO_LABEL` map next to the existing `_BAND_TO_WPC`. Do **not** hoist `ds.coreweave.com/...` label strings into `cli/job.py`; that is a layering regression (the provider owns its own labels).

4. **Do not introduce a `CoschedulingMode` enum.** Two states carried by empty/non-empty `group_by` is sufficient; a mode enum just re-encodes it and adds an illegal combination to guard (per the repo's "abstract only under real pressure" rule).

### Code sketch

```proto
// job.proto — keep group_by as the gang/attribute key; add a closed topology requirement.
enum TopologyRequirement {
  TOPOLOGY_NONE = 0;       // atomic gang admission only, no placement
  TOPOLOGY_PREFERRED = 1;  // Kueue soft topology, coarser fallback allowed
  TOPOLOGY_REQUIRED = 2;   // Kueue hard topology, must fit one domain
}
message CoschedulingConfig {
  string group_by = 1;               // gang-membership + worker-daemon bucketing key; non-empty when set
  TopologyRequirement topology = 2;  // abstract placement strength; provider maps to its own label
}
```

```python
# types.py — coscheduled-ness == non-empty group_by, validated at the boundary.
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CoschedulingConfig:
    group_by: str
    topology: TopologyRequirement = TopologyRequirement.NONE
    def __post_init__(self):
        if not self.group_by:
            raise ValueError("CoschedulingConfig requires a non-empty group_by")

# transitions.py:1261 — derive from group_by, not HasField (matches job.proto:614):
cosched_group = request.coscheduling.group_by if request.HasField("coscheduling") else ""
has_cosched = bool(cosched_group)

# k8s tasks.py — abstract -> label translation stays IN THE PROVIDER:
_REQUIREMENT_TO_LABEL = {
    TOPOLOGY_REQUIRED: (_KUEUE_REQUIRED_TOPOLOGY, "ds.coreweave.com/nvlink.domain"),
    TOPOLOGY_PREFERRED: (_KUEUE_PREFERRED_TOPOLOGY, "backend.coreweave.cloud/leafgroup"),
}
kueue_enabled = bool(run_req.coscheduling.group_by) and bool(config.local_queue)
if kueue_enabled and run_req.coscheduling.topology != TOPOLOGY_NONE:
    annotate_topology(*_REQUIREMENT_TO_LABEL[run_req.coscheduling.topology])
# DELETE _GROUP_BY_TO_TOPOLOGY; unmapped/"rack" now arrives as topology=NONE -> still gangs (test:956 passes).

# cli/job.py — producer resolves the ABSTRACT requirement only (no CoreWeave label leakage):
CoschedulingConfig(group_by=WellKnownAttribute.TPU_NAME, topology=TopologyRequirement.REQUIRED)  # was :491
CoschedulingConfig(group_by="pool", topology=TopologyRequirement.PREFERRED)                       # was :467
```

### Whole-sweep checklist (not optional — these readers must move together)

- **`transitions.py:2987/3024` SQL predicates** — either keep persisting `has_coscheduling` as a stored bool computed from `group_by != ''` at insert (simplest, preserves the indexed partition), **or** rewrite both predicates to `job_config_table.c.coscheduling_group_by != ''`. Pick one; do not leave the two sides inconsistent.
- **`controller.py:1132`** cap exemption (`not task.has_coscheduling`) must follow the same derived value.
- **`controller.py:253`** — unify the "no group" sentinel on `""` (empty == not coscheduled) so the scheduler guard and the diagnostic agree; confirm no reader depends on the `None` form.
- **`schema.py`** `has_coscheduling` column — migration if the stored-bool option is chosen.

## Open questions

1. **SQL partition migration:** keep a stored boolean column (computed from `group_by != ''` at insert; smaller, index-friendly) or switch both predicates to `coscheduling_group_by != ''`? Team preference needed before writing the migration.
2. **Topology tiers:** are only the current two label families (`nvlink.domain` hard, `leafgroup` soft) ever needed? If more tiers are coming, decide whether the enum encodes strength only (label resolved in-provider) or also tier identity.
3. **External producers:** any non-CLI, non-test RPC client relying on open-domain `group_by` daemon bucketing by a *non-topology* attribute (region/zone)? If so, confirm the split keeps that path working with `topology=NONE`.

## Scope / non-goals

- Boundary validation must be server-side (`transitions.py`); client-side (`client.py:651,667`) is a nicety.
- No backward compatibility: update all call sites in the same PR (repo policy).

---

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Description
Prototype an efficient TPU training attention path for packed THD inputs using `cu_q_lens`/sequence offsets as the packing mechanism. The kernel should exploit the packing metadata to skip inactive attention blocks where possible, instead of treating the packed batch as dense padded BSD.

Reuse ideas from the existing paged-attention forward kernel where applicable, but make the training requirements explicit: either implement forward and backward, or produce a forward-only ceiling with a concrete backward design.

### Definition of Done
- A TPU THD attention API accepts packed q/k/v plus `cu_q_lens` and max sequence length.
- Correctness is checked against a reference attention path on variable-length packed batches.
- Benchmarks show whether block skipping improves over the current BSD/Splash-style path.
- Limitations and fallback behavior are documented for Grug training.

Parent issue: #6071

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue and parent (#6071)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (open PRs/issues for THD attention, cu_q_lens, TPU Pallas)
- [x] Identify the existing Grug TPU attention surface and the closest cu_q_lens kernel in tree
- [x] Decide scope: too large for an agent-authored PR; post research + proposed approach instead
- [x] Hand off to a human for design sign-off before implementation

Status: awaiting human review of the approach below — not opening a PR. Scope (new Pallas fwd + bwd, dispatcher wiring, tests, benches, docs) is well above the 100-line agent-PR cap and requires design choices (THD ABI shape, forward-only ship bar, TPU generation gate).

# Research

Today Grug's TPU attention path is BHSD splash with `SegmentIds` for packing — packed batches are still computed as dense `[B, Hq, Sq, Sk]` tiles, so block skipping for cross-segment zeros is left on the table. The only in-tree TPU kernel that consumes `cu_q_lens` is the inference-side ragged paged kernel; it is forward-only and KV-cache shaped, so it does not give us a training path. There is no existing THD Pallas training kernel and no GPU FA4 analogue for TPU.

**Relevant code**
- [`_core.py#L233-L398`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py#L233-L398) — current Grug `_tpu_splash_attention` (BHSD + `SplashSegmentIds`)
- [`_core.py#L21-L25`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py#L21-L25) — `GrugAttentionImplementation` literal (where a `tpu_thd` option would land)
- [`attention.py#L1995-L2167`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/attention.py#L1995-L2167) — `ragged_paged_attention` + TPU dispatch, the only existing `cu_q_lens` consumer; inference-only
- [`_fa4_cute.py#L130-L160`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L130-L160) — GPU per-token `lower_bounds` packed-segment forward; mirrors the abstraction we need on TPU
- [`_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py) — GPU segmented backward; reference for the dq/dk/dv structure of a TPU backward

# Proposed Approach

Two phases so the forward ceiling is provable before committing to a backward.

1. **THD ABI.** New `tpu_thd_attention(q_thd, k_thd, v_thd, cu_q_lens, max_seq_len, mask)` where `q_thd: [T, Hq, D]`, `k_thd, v_thd: [T, Hkv, D]`, `cu_q_lens: i32[Nseq + 1]` (training case: `cu_q_lens == cu_kv_lens`, no separate `kv_lens`). Same packing convention as `page_table.cu_q_lens` so a future paged-prefill share is straightforward.
2. **Phase 1 — forward-only TPU Pallas kernel.** Q-major outer loop over `block_q` tiles. For each tile derive the owning `seq_id` from `cu_q_lens` via a precomputed `seq_id_of_block: i32[ceil(T/block_q)]` table built in Python and passed to the kernel; iterate KV blocks only within `[cu_q_lens[seq_id], cu_q_lens[seq_id + 1])`, applying per-tile causal + optional sliding-window inside that segment. This is the \"skip inactive blocks\" win the issue is asking about. Borrow tile sizes from the splash path (`block_q=block_kv=512`, multiples of 128) and the running-max/sum recurrence from `default_ragged_paged_attention` ([attention.py#L2245-L2289](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/layers/attention.py#L2245-L2289)).
3. **Phase 1 — wiring + tests + benches.** Add `tpu_thd` to `GrugAttentionImplementation`; dispatch in `attention()` when input is THD (introduce a `PackedTHD` carrier rather than reusing the BSD path with segment_ids — composition not boolean dispatch, per AGENTS.md). Correctness: extend `tests/grug/test_attention.py` to parametrize variable-length packed batches against `reference_attention` (Sq up to 8192, segments `[1, 7, 512, 1023, 4096]`). Benchmarks: a small script reporting kernel time on packed vs dense-equivalent inputs at the Grug-block configs from PR #6059/#6069, with `pack/unpack` cost reported separately per parent issue's DoD.
4. **Phase 2 — backward.** Two-pass dq / dk+dv segmented backward modeled on [`_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py), with the same `seq_id_of_block` skipping. `custom_vjp` on `tpu_thd_attention`. If backward perf does not beat splash + packing overhead we ship the forward ceiling and document the gap rather than land a regression. Limitations to document in either case: `T` padded to multiple of `block_q`, no dense bias, no dropout, segment count bounded by `cu_q_lens` length.

Open questions for a human before implementation:
- Is `PackedTHD` carrier OK, or should the Grug block keep `[B, S, *]` external API and pack inside the dispatch?
- Forward-only ship-or-not bar: what speedup vs splash on the parent issue's d5120/L8 packed batches justifies landing without backward?
- Should we target v4+ only (matching the ragged-paged kernel gate) or also v3?

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Description
Grug full-block GPU performance is now close to the Megatron baseline using FA4 THD attention plus a post-attention reshard, but the remaining overhead appears to come from BSD/TD layout boundaries. Explore making the Grug block's internal residual stream token-major `x_td [T, D]`, with THD metadata (`cu_q_lens`, max sequence length, positions) as the attention ABI and MoE/router/MLP staying TD.

Keep external model/data APIs BSD while measuring explicit pack/unpack and sharding costs. The goal is to align attention and MoE execution layouts without forcing TPU onto the same representation until the TPU kernel story is proven.

### Definition of Done
- A design note identifies the TD block contract and required metadata.
- GPU full-block benchmark compares against PR6059+PR6069 job 54408 (`full_block` 0.01899s).
- Pack/unpack and reshard costs are reported separately from kernel time.
- TPU support is tracked by the linked subissue.

Linked subissue: #6072

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read issue, linked subissue #6072, and related PRs #6059 / #6069
- [x] Map relevant code (attention backend, MoE block, residual layout, reshards)
- [x] Decide scope — exploration/design task, not a self-contained bug fix
- [x] Post research + proposed approach for human review (no PR)

# Research

The current Grug block keeps the residual stream BSD end-to-end. Attention runs FA4 THD by reshaping packed `segment_ids` into per-token `lower_bounds`/`valid` masks ([`_fa4_cute.py#L16-L50`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L16-L50)), so the "THD path" is metadata-only — Q/K/V remain `[B, S, Hq, D]`. The MoE block already flattens to `[T, D]` for routing, runs experts in TD, then `rearrange((b s) d -> b s d)` + `reshard(_batch_spec())` back to `P((\"data\", \"expert\"))` ([`moe/model.py#L408-L417`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L408-L417)). PR #6069 added the post-attention `aligned_v = reshard(..., P((\"data\", \"expert\"), None, \"model\", None))` boundary inside `CausalSelfAttention` ([`moe/model.py#L160`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L160)), which is exactly the BSD↔TD/expert sharding cliff this issue is trying to dissolve.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L420-L460`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L420-L460) — `Block.__call__`, the contract that needs to change
- [`experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L146-L170`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L146-L170) — `CausalSelfAttention`, BSD in/out, internal `aligned_v` reshard
- [`experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L360-L417`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/model.py#L360-L417) — `MoEMLP`, already TD-internal; round-trips through `(b s) d` reshape
- [`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L16-L50`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_cute.py#L16-L50) — packing metadata derived from `segment_ids` (no `cu_q_lens` plumbed end-to-end yet)
- [`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_thd.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_fa4_thd.py) — FA4 THD backend added in PR #6059

# Proposed Approach (for human review — no PR yet)

The change crosses module boundaries (attention ABI, block forward, MoE entry, transformer outer loop, sharding specs, benchmark harness) and requires GPU benchmarking that this agent cannot run, so this stays a design comment.

Sketch of the TD block contract:

1. **External ABI stays BSD.** `Transformer.__call__` packs once at the embedding output and unpacks once before `output_proj`. Pack = `rearrange(\"b s d -> (b s) d\")` + reshard to `P((\"data\",\"expert\"))`; metadata = `cu_q_lens: int32[B+1]`, `max_seqlen: int`, `positions: int32[T]` derived from `segment_ids` at the outer boundary so per-layer cost is zero.
2. **New `Block` contract:** `__call__(x_td: [T, D], meta: ThdMeta) -> ([T, D], stats)`. MoE/MLP/router/GatedNorm/RMSNorm are already shape-polymorphic over leading dims — they need no change. Attention becomes the only consumer of `meta`.
3. **Attention ABI:** `attention(q_thd, k_thd, v_thd, meta, implementation=...)` where `q/k/v` are `[T, Hq, D]`. The FA4 THD backend (PR #6059) is already the right shape; the BSD-padded backends get a wrapper that unpacks `T → (B, S)` with `positions` and re-pads to the largest segment. Drop the internal `aligned_v` reshard in `CausalSelfAttention` — once the residual is `P((\"data\",\"expert\"))` end-to-end the post-attention boundary disappears.
4. **Splitting kernel time from layout time in the benchmark.** The DoD requires pack/unpack and reshard cost reported separately. Concretely, instrument `full_block` with `jax.block_until_ready` checkpoints after: (a) attention QKV proj, (b) FA4 call, (c) attention output proj+reshard, (d) router, (e) expert compute, (f) MoE unshard. Today (c) and (f) are the cliffs; under the TD contract they collapse into (a) and (e). Compare per-segment times against the job 54408 `full_block` 0.01899s baseline; report kernel-only (b)+(e) and layout-only ((a)−proj, (c)−proj, (f)) separately.
5. **TPU stays out of scope.** TPU keeps the BSD path until #6072 lands the THD kernel; the TD contract is a GPU-only execution mode selected by `cfg.attention_implementation`.

**Open questions for the owner before writing a design doc / PR:**
- Should the TD contract be the new default on GPU once #6072 lands, or a parallel `GrugBlockTD` variant gated on `cfg.attention_implementation == \"gpu_fa4_thd\"`?
- Does `_batch_spec() = P((\"data\",\"expert\"))` remain the canonical TD spec, or do we want a distinct `Ttd` axis name so haliax/sharding analysis can tell BSD-flat from TD-packed?
- Where should `ThdMeta` live so iris/zephyr/marin layers don't need to import from `grug` (likely `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_thd_meta.py`)?

Happy to write up the design note and benchmark harness as a follow-up once direction is confirmed.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This eval suite tested whether Marin 32B is unusually sensitive to superficial prompt wrappers by holding task semantics fixed while rendering the same 5-shot examples across 156 prompt-format slices. After a v2 renderer fix for JSON/JSONL continuations and record-extraction targets, the dashboard showed Marin 32B roughly on par with Qwen3 32B and often better, so broad prompt-format sensitivity is not currently a major concern. The remaining hard cases are Python REPL/reasoning examples, which should be split into a separate code-interpretation or small symbolic-execution eval family.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6067#issuecomment-4581650904
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6067#issuecomment-4581900188
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description
Add a prompt-format sensitivity perplexity eval suite that holds task semantics fixed while rendering the same 5-shot support/query examples through many surface templates. The suite should measure format sensitivity, not replace broad task-competence evals.

Initial task families: MCQA, short factual QA, classification, transformation/copy, structured extraction, and code/REPL-style examples. Initial template families: arrow/equals/colon mappings, Q/A, flashcards, problem/solution, key/value blocks, JSON/JSONL/YAML/XML, CSV/TSV/Markdown tables, Python doctest/REPL, shell transcript, and other explicit structured formats where targets remain identical.

### Definition of Done
- Register datasets as `prompt_format_sensitivity/<task>/<template>` for model-perplexity scoring.
- Preserve identical support examples, held-out query, and target text across formats for each task.
- Score only held-out target spans using 5-shot prompts.
- Add tests for rendered examples, target-only spans, 5-shot consistency, and identical targets across templates.
- Launch Marin 32B vs Qwen3 32B scoring and publish local dashboard artifacts/heatmaps when results are available.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS, fix-issue, author-pr
- [x] Actionability check (issue has clear DoD)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no open PRs; #5614 is a sibling synthetic PPL ask, not a dup)
- [x] Map existing perplexity-eval scaffolding
- [x] Post research + proposed approach (analysis only — scope > 100 LOC)
- [ ] Await human go-ahead before implementing

# Research

Actionable. Marin already has the scaffolding to register supervised-target-only PPL slices keyed under \`<area>/<task>\` with cross-template tags; the gap is a generator that (a) holds task semantics + target text fixed, (b) renders the same support+query through many templates, and (c) registers one slice per \`(task, template)\` so per-template PPL is directly comparable. Out-of-scope for a single small PR: HF dataset materialization + 32B scoring launch + dashboard artifacts (per DoD).

**Relevant code**
- [\`experiments/evals/synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L41-L111\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L41-L111) — closest template: slice + registry + supervised_text_dataset
- [\`experiments/evals/synthetic_reasoning_ppl.py#L93-L162\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/synthetic_reasoning_ppl.py#L93-L162) — 5-shot ICL pattern with \`prompt_format:\` / \`icl_shots:\` / \`loss:target_only\` tags
- [\`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L116-L142\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L116-L142) — \`supervised_text_dataset\` scores only the target span
- [\`experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L113-L183\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L113-L183) — bundle registration; marin_32b vs qwen3_32b pair already exists
- [\`tests/evals/test_synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L21-L62\`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/evals/test_synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py#L21-L62) — registry-shape + target-invariant test pattern

# Proposed Approach

Mirror \`synthetic_delimiter_format_ppl.py\`, but factor the generator into two orthogonal axes so target invariance is enforced structurally rather than asserted after the fact:

\`\`\`python
# experiments/evals/prompt_format_sensitivity_ppl.py
class TaskFamily(StrEnum):
    MCQA = \"mcqa\"; SHORT_QA = \"short_qa\"; CLASSIFICATION = \"classification\"
    TRANSFORM = \"transform\"; STRUCTURED_EXTRACTION = \"structured_extraction\"; CODE_REPL = \"code_repl\"

class TemplateFamily(StrEnum):
    ARROW = \"arrow\"; EQUALS = \"equals\"; COLON = \"colon\"
    QA = \"qa\"; FLASHCARD = \"flashcard\"; PROBLEM_SOLUTION = \"problem_solution\"
    KEY_VALUE = \"key_value\"; JSON = \"json\"; JSONL = \"jsonl\"; YAML = \"yaml\"; XML = \"xml\"
    CSV = \"csv\"; TSV = \"tsv\"; MARKDOWN_TABLE = \"markdown_table\"
    PY_DOCTEST = \"py_doctest\"; PY_REPL = \"py_repl\"; SHELL = \"shell\"

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SemanticExample:
    support: tuple[tuple[str, str], ...]   # 5 (input, target) pairs, shared across templates
    query_input: str
    target: str                            # invariant across templates by construction

# task generators return SemanticExample; template renderers turn them into prompt strings.
def render(example: SemanticExample, template: TemplateFamily) -> tuple[str, str]:
    # returns (prompt, target_for_scoring) — target is example.target unchanged
\`\`\`

Registry key: \`prompt_format_sensitivity/{task}/{template}\`. Only task/template combinations where the target text is byte-identical produce a slice (e.g. JSON-target templates only render JSON-target tasks); a single \`COMPATIBILITY\` table gates the cross-product to keep the invariant true.

Tests (mirror existing patterns, not slop):
- registry shape (\`set(datasets) == expected\`, tags include \`prompt_format:<template>\`, \`icl_shots:5\`, \`loss:target_only\`)
- **target invariance**: for each task, \`{row.target for row in renders across templates}\` is a singleton per row index
- **5-shot count**: each rendered prompt contains exactly 5 support examples (count via the renderer's separator, not via free-text matching)
- **target-only span**: \`supervised_text_dataset(input_key=\"input\", target_key=\"target\")\` — target equals the byte-identical \`SemanticExample.target\` and does not appear inside \`input\`

Bundle wiring: add \`prompt_format_sensitivity_bundle()\` in \`perplexity_gap_registry.py\` and include it in \`registered_perplexity_gap_bundles()\`. No new pair needed — \`marin_32b\`/\`qwen3_32b\` already registered.

Suggested split (DoD is too big for one PR):
1. **This PR (~600 LOC)**: generator + renderers + registry + tests. No HF push, no launch.
2. **Follow-up**: \`materialize_*_raw\` StepSpec + HF dataset push + bundle launch on the 32B pair + dashboard heatmap artifact.

Open questions for @dlwh before I start:
1. Confirm task × template compatibility gating (drop incompatible pairs) vs. dummy-quote (e.g. JSON-encoding a free-text target). Gating keeps targets byte-identical; quoting expands coverage but breaks the invariance test.
2. Target HF dataset id — \`marin-community/prompt-format-sensitivity-ppl\`?
3. Examples per (task, template) — match \`EXAMPLES_PER_CONFIG = 1000\`?

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up readout after the v1 dashboard review and the v2 renderer fix:

- Prompt-format sensitivity itself looks basically fine. Across the 156 slices, Marin 32B is roughly on par with Qwen3 32B overall and often better; I do not think this is currently a reason to worry about broad wrapper/template fragility.
- The two issues found in the dashboard were eval-construction issues rather than model evidence: JSON/JSONL needed template-specific scored continuations so the held-out record remains valid JSON, and `record_extraction` should not make every wrapper emit a JSON object. v2 fixes both by scoring the rendered continuation and switching record extraction to compact field-list targets.
- The main remaining signal is not prompt sensitivity: the Python REPL/reasoning examples are consistently hard across formats. That should be tracked as a separate code interpretation / small symbolic execution competency, probably with natural doctest and Python REPL transcript surfaces.

So the current conclusion is: stop worrying about prompt-format sensitivity as a broad failure mode for now; add a separate eval family for code reasoning/interpreter-style continuations.

issues.author: Helw150
issues.body:
## TL;DR

I drove this mix by hand on the **By task results** tab of the explorer, deliberately cranking the benchmark sliders for **humaneval**, **gsm8k**, and (more gently) **mmlu_sl_verb_5shot**. The gradient-based slider mechanism takes a minimum-norm step on the data mix each drag, so the resulting mixture stays close to token-proportional except where it absolutely had to deviate to move those specific benchmarks. That is why the L1 deviation from proportional is only 0.528 — I am not freely optimising, I am taking tiny min-norm steps to satisfy a handful of task-level wishes.

This issue pre-registers, before any actual training, which 300m-swarm benchmarks I expect this mix to win, lose, or move uncertainly on — derived from the DSP regression fit to the 241-run swarm.

## The mix

Live in the explorer (auto-loads with the mix applied):
https://williamheld.com/wandb-analysis/#tab=mixture&w0=0.0059%2C0.0152%2C0.0068%2C0.0209%2C0.0097%2C0.0340%2C0.0156%2C0.0183%2C0.0071%2C0.0578%2C0.0207%2C0.0741%2C0.0354%2C0.0234%2C0.0113%2C0.0305%2C0.0107%2C0.0591%2C0.0247%2C0.0179%2C0.0058%2C0.0113%2C0.0059%2C0.0349%2C0.0080%2C0.0328%2C0.0151%2C0.0073%2C0.0294%2C0.0017%2C0.1789%2C0.0281%2C0.0290%2C0.0011%2C0.0135%2C0.0047%2C0.0106%2C0.0717%2C0.0111&w1=0.0144%2C0.0108%2C0.0108%2C0.0183%2C0.0091%2C0.0273%2C0.0096%2C0.0162%2C0.0021%2C0.0487%2C0.0167%2C0.0627%2C0.0302%2C0.0202%2C0.0090%2C0.0254%2C0.0065%2C0.0495%2C0.0196%2C0.0143%2C0.0091%2C0.0106%2C0.0050%2C0.0281%2C0.0012%2C0.0261%2C0.0119%2C0.0175%2C0.0552%2C0.0044%2C0.1506%2C0.0239%2C0.0537%2C0.0027%2C0.0406%2C0.0101%2C0.0404%2C0.0604%2C0.0270

Notably more concentrated than most swarm runs (largest single phase-0 weight is 17.9% on `dolmino_common_crawl_hq`), so off-swarm behaviour is plausible.

## How the mix was found: gradient-steering sliders

The "By task results" tab is no longer a swarm browser — it is a steering wheel for the demanded data mixture, driven by the same DSP fits used for the predictions below.

- Each task slider's value is the **current DSP-predicted percentile** for that task at the current mix.
- When you drag a slider for task `t` from `cur_pct` to `new_pct`:
  1. **Convert Δpct to Δz** using the local slope of `Φ`: `Δz = (Δpct/100) / φ(z_t)` where `φ` is the standard-normal density. This makes the slider feel linear in the percentile units it displays.
  2. **Compute the analytical gradient** of `predict_t` w.r.t. `(w0, w1)` from the DSP form:
     - `∂predict_t/∂z_d = a_d · ρ_d · exp(-ρ_d z_d) - p_d · 2 · softplus(u_d) · σ(u_d) / (1 + z_d)` (benefit slope minus over-exposure-penalty slope, with `u_d = log(1+z_d) - τ_d`)
     - chain through `∂z_d/∂w0_d = c0_d`, `∂z_d/∂w1_d = γ · c1_d`
  3. **Take the minimum-norm step** that achieves Δz under the local linearisation: `ΔMIX = (Δz / ||g||²) · g`. This is the projection of "I want this much improvement" onto the smallest-magnitude weight change that delivers it.
  4. **Clip** `MIX` to `≥ 0` and **renormalise each phase** back onto the simplex.
  5. **Re-sync every slider**: task sliders re-compute their predicted percentile at the new mix; domain sliders update to show the new weights.

Because each drag is a min-norm step, **the mix drifts away from the starting point only as fast as the slider demands force it to**. If you do not touch a task, the optimiser does not try to improve it. If a task is "cheap" (high gradient, low impact on others), it moves easily; if it requires fighting other tasks, the step is dampened. The result is a mix that satisfies the dragged-up benchmarks while staying close-to-proportional everywhere else by construction.

The actual workflow I used for this issue:

1. Start at token-proportional.
2. On the task tab, drag humaneval and gsm8k as high as they would go without snapping back. Watch the gradient redistribute weight into `dolmino_synth_code`, `dolmino_synth_math`, `dolma3_stack_edu`, `dolmino_stack_edu_fim`.
3. Push mmlu_sl_verb_5shot up moderately. The same domains pick up a bit more.
4. Stop. Read off the final mix and pre-register predictions per the methodology below.

A few practical notes on the slider mechanic:

- The dragged task does not always land exactly at the value you set — only the linearisation does. The slider snaps to the *achievable* percentile after the step.
- Both tabs share the same `MIX` state — you can crank a benchmark on the task tab, switch to the mix tab to see which domains moved, switch back, and the mix is preserved.
- Reset buttons (proportional / David's mix / predicted Pareto improver) overwrite `MIX` directly and trigger a full re-sync.

## Methodology for the pre-registered predictions

1. **Targets.** Per-task swarm outcomes (bpb where the metric is loss-shaped, choice_logprob otherwise, with signs flipped so higher = better) are rank-INT'd per task across the 241 runs so each column is ~N(0, 1) by construction. This makes z-scores comparable across heterogeneous benchmarks and robust to heavy left tails (truthfulqa, piqa, arc).

2. **Predictor.** Per-task fit of Calvin's DSP form (4D + 2 = 158 params per task, D = 39 domains):

   - e_{p,d} = c_{p,d} · w_{p,d}  for phase p in {0, 1}
   - z_d    = e_{0,d} + γ · e_{1,d}
   - y_hat(w) = -b_0 + Σ_d a_d (1 - exp(-ρ_d z_d)) - Σ_d p_d · softplus(log(1+z_d) - τ_d)^2

   Fit by L-BFGS-B on rank-INT'd targets. The over-exposure penalty term lets the form model inverted-U epoching dynamics, so this predictor can in principle invert (unlike a pure rank correlation).

3. **Uncertainty.** For each task t, σ_z(t) is the swarm-residual RMSE of the fit (in rank-INT z units). Range across the 26 tasks: 0.20 (humaneval, tight fit) → 0.83 (winogrande, loose fit). The explorer renders ±1σ as an asymmetric percentile band via Φ(z ± σ).

4. **Confidence ratio.** For each task t, compute Δz(t) = ŷ_t(w_mix) - ŷ_t(w_prop), then rank by Δz / σ_z. Thresholds:
   - |Δz / σ_z| > 2 → confident
   - |Δz / σ_z| ≤ 2 → uncertain (within fit noise)

5. **Baseline.** w_prop is token-proportional sampling: w_d ∝ 1/c_{p,d} normalised, so each domain is weighted by its natural token count.

## Pre-registered predictions

### Confident wins (5)

DSP predicts a large gain well outside its in-sample fit noise.

| task                | Δ_pct | Δz / σ_z |
| ------------------- | ----- | -------- |
| humaneval           | +90   | +16.8    |
| github_python       | +88   | +15.6    |
| github_cpp          | +66   | +13.5    |
| gsm8k               | +85   | +7.1     |
| arxiv_physics       | +24   | +3.0     |

### Borderline wins (2)

Past 2σ but with looser fits, so worth flagging as confident-ish.

| task                  | Δ_pct | Δz / σ_z |
| --------------------- | ----- | -------- |
| csqa                  | +21   | +2.6     |
| mmlu_sl_verb_5shot    | +52   | +2.3     |

### Confident losses (2)

DSP predicts a notable loss exceeding fit noise.

| task                            | Δ_pct | Δz / σ_z |
| ------------------------------- | ----- | -------- |
| uncheatable/bbc_news            | -6    | -3.8     |
| uncheatable/ao3_english         | -2    | -3.2     |

### Uncertain (17)

|Δz / σ_z| < 2. The predicted move is within fit noise — any observed change here should be regarded as uncalibrated by this method.

- *Lean better*: boolq (+44, +1.9), arxiv_cs (+9, +1.7)
- *No signal*: wsc273, winogrande, paloma_macro, arc_easy, truthfulqa, medmcqa, openbookqa, sciq
- *Lean worse*: hellaswag_5shot (-0.6, -2.0), hellaswag_0shot (-0.4, -1.6), copa (-35, -1.5), piqa (-10, -1.5), arc_challenge (-2, -1.4), wikipedia_english (-11, -1.2), socialiqa (-8, -1.1)

## Reservations and known limits

1. **Copa is the loudest false-confidence trap.** Predicted -35 pct sounds dramatic, but σ_z = 0.79 (one of the loosest fits) means a ±1σ band already covers ~30 percentile points around the prediction.
2. **σ_z is in-sample noise.** The confident-win list is more credible than the confident-loss list because the win Δz's (3.4-3.6) are an order of magnitude larger than σ_z, so even a doubled out-of-distribution σ wouldn't flip the sign. The confident losses (Δz of -0.7 to -0.9 vs σ ≈ 0.24) are at the edge of that buffer.
3. **Two wins (mmlu, csqa) are right at the 2σ threshold.** A stricter cutoff demotes them to "lean better."
4. **Tasks already near the ceiling at proportional don't have much room.** Piqa is at the 96th percentile under proportional; a -10 pct prediction collapses to whatever room exists between 86 and the floor of what's measurable.
5. **The 'no signal' bucket should be the post-hoc bucket too.** If a benchmark there moves substantially, that's evidence against the DSP model (or against the iid noise assumption around it), not validation of any in-bucket lean.

## Source

- Explorer: https://williamheld.com/wandb-analysis/
- Source + build script: https://github.com/marin-community/wandb-analysis

issues.author: RohithKuditipudi
issues.body:
## Goal 

Prior work has shown in principle that we can predict the pass@k profile of a larger model from the profiles of smaller models within a model family/scaling ladder. However, in practice this may require an infeasible amount of sampling from the smaller models. Also, the predictions can still be quite noisy.

Motivated by the above, we have two goals:
1. We would like to design smooth proxies that let us predict the pass@k performance for extremely large k (e.g., k > 100k) without actually having to sample k times from a model.
2. We would like to validate that we can predict the pass@k profile of the largest model in a scaling ladder based on the profiles of smaller models in the ladder.

## Approach

For (1), our main idea is to design scaffolds with tunable knobs that make the target task considerably easier. One example of such a scaffold is doing variations of guided decoding with a larger model (in this case, the amount of guidance is the knob). We would then like to predict pass@k for large k on the original task based on pass@k for smaller k on the easier task.

For (2), we will evaluate whether we can predict pass@k on individual task instances (e.g., individual MATH questions) for the largest models in the Marin isoflops/Delphi ladders based on the smaller models, both with and without the scaffolds from (1). We will also train the ladder models on the recipes in #4547 to obtain a few different ladders and see if we can predict which recipe is the best for the largest base model in each ladder (#4551)

issues.title: Predicting pass@k

issues.author: suraj-ranganath
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested whether NAMO's apparent advantage in Marin came from its adaptive matrix weight-decay behavior rather than optimizer dynamics alone. A 16-run, 50k-step GPT2-small-equivalent Marin sweep compared NAMO/NAMO-D variants with adaptive versus AdamW-style matrix decay, plus Muon standard and reduced-decay variants. The reported endpoint result was the opposite of the initial concern: NAMO/NAMO-D with AdamW-style matrix decay finished better than the adaptive-decay counterparts, while Muon with 0.2x reduced decay did not diverge but finished slightly worse than standard Muon. A requested larger 480k batch-token reproduction remains blocked on hardware access, since the original experimenter only had A5000s rather than the requested A100-scale setup.

### Helpful links
- Experiment submission PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/3104
- NAMO implementation PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/2966
- 16-run W&B report and result summary: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/3037#issuecomment-3974642939
- Larger-batch rerun request and hardware blocker: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/3037#issuecomment-4004518214
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

A recent claim in https://github.com/minxin-zhg/namo/issues/1 suggests the [NAMO optimizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17080)'s gains may be partly due to a weight-decay implementation difference rather than optimizer dynamics alone. In NAMO-style updates, matrix weight decay is scaled by an adaptive learning-rate term, while AdamW/Muon typically apply decoupled decay using base LR. I want to run a controlled Marin experiment to test this directly at meaningful scale (50k steps), using GPT2-small-equivalent training setup on pretokenized fineweb-edu-10B and evaluating on Paloma C4 (`eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb`, `loss`). This was suggested by @alxmrs on https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/2966#discussion_r2854439864.

Planned variants (same model/data/schedule family, differing only in optimizer/decay behavior):
1. NAMO (current adaptive matrix decay behavior)
2. NAMO with AdamW-style matrix decay ablation
3. Muon with standard decay
4. Muon with reduced decay (0.2x), as discussed in the report

This issue tracks the experiment PR, runs, and analysis.

## Hypothesis

Goal: Determine whether NAMO's observed advantage in Marin is robust when matrix weight decay is matched to AdamW-style decay.

Hypothesis:
- If decay mismatch is a major contributor, NAMO (adaptive decay) should outperform NAMO (AdamW-style decay) by a noticeable margin.
- Muon with reduced decay may improve early convergence but can show weaker late stability.

### Links

* Marin PR to implement NAMO/NAMO-D: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/2966
* NAMO/NAMO-D Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17080
* NAMO/NAMO-D Original Implementation: https://github.com/minxin-zhg/namo

## Results

50k-step endpoint results are summarized in the managed block above. A larger 480k batch-token reproduction was requested but is blocked on suitable GPU access.

Levanter's inference stack is designed to serve the following use cases:

- single turn batch evaluation during training and after training (mostly via lm-eval-harness)
- RL training, initially single turn but eventually multi-turn.
- potentially data rewriting workloads

It is not designed for low-latency serving of production traffic, although it may be possible to adapt it for that use case in the future. I don't think it will ever be a goal of the project to serve production traffic.

Requirements:

- Fast weight swap
- log probs
- Tensor Parallel
- Good throughput
- not embarrassing latency
- Eventually:
  - Data Parallel (for evaluation during training)
  - Multi-turn (for RL training)



## Tasks

### Bugs

- [x] See what is going wrong with RPA marin-community/levanter#1181 
- [ ] Don't let generation loop run out of pages marin-community/marin#1899 

### Generation Params

- [ ] top_p
- [ ] top_k?
- [ ] others?

### Core Speed

- [x] marin-community/marin#1897
- [x] marin-community/marin#1896
- [ ] look into dispatch overhead
- [x] marin-community/marin#1888
- [ ] Avoid computing full logit matrix during prefill (unless we want logprobs for prefill tokens)
- [ ] figure out why the profiler isn't giving me anything useful

### Prefix Cache

[This one is hash based and might be better/informative](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax-llm-examples/pull/22/files#diff-7db975ef2cdc92a3e44bb2ad5d10c049405c8cd365645981308cdc48eacc1b1dR191)

- [x] marin-community/marin#1894
- [ ] Use radix tree draft to actually drive scheduling
- [ ] Enable automatic prefix caching
- [ ] When returning from JIT scheduler, insert allocated pages into the radix cache. careful to handle the case where there were the sampled tokens already happen to exist.
- [ ] Radix cache must return freed pages when a sequence is released
- [ ] Manage list of free pages outside the radix cache
- [ ] Double check radix LRU evict


### Concurrency

Manage multiple requests inside of Engine with a worker thread and async or callbacks to handle finished/streaming

- [x] marin-community/marin#1893
- [ ] async or callback to handle finished/streaming


### Quality of Life
- [x] marin-community/levanter#1200

### Data Parallel

Basic idea: single controller on worker 0, which shards batches across DP axis.
Each worker has its own Engine instance with its own model replica.
Controller packs batches, device_puts and shards them to each worker.

Workers have to run the loop if any sequences are active unless we're very careful...

- [ ] create batched TokenQueues doing some kind of sequence packing thing
- [ ] shard batches across DP axis
- [ ] Workers run the loop if any sequences are active. Periodically check in with controller for new work when not active
