comments.body:
🤖 Historical capture for `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-repro-v3-20260803`:

The job is no longer running. Iris records the parent and training job as `killed` at `2026-08-03 23:08:13.292 UTC`. All 128 training tasks were killed by the user, with zero task failures and zero retries. The pods have been deleted, so the run no longer holds the 512 GPUs.

The retained telemetry establishes a cluster-wide device-side stall:

- All 128 ranks last reported Levanter step `183` between `22:34:34.928` and `22:34:35.810`. W&B `_step=182` is consistent with its indexing.
- All 128 ranks continued to emit `phase=training` heartbeats through `23:08:02.610`–`23:08:04.006`, seconds before termination. The Python processes remained alive for about 33.5 minutes without optimizer progress.
- Iris retained a final periodic thread profile from every rank at 23:02. All 128 `MainThread`s were at `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py:585`, the compiled `train_step(...)` call. The loader and telemetry threads were alive. On-demand captures from ranks 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, and 112 at 23:07 showed the same frame.
- In the three minutes before the stall, the 512 GPUs averaged 98.55% utilization, 984 W, 0.324 tensor activity, and 0.241 DRAM activity. From 22:35:30 until termination they reported 100% utilization but averaged 256 W, 0.0011 tensor activity, and 0.00066 DRAM activity. HBM allocation remained near 181.1 GB per GPU.

No retained fault signal identifies a rank, node, or rack:

- PCIe replay counters stayed at zero.
- Five GPUs had pre-existing correctable row-remap counts and two had pre-existing uncorrectable counts; none incremented during the run.
- XID values 31, 43, 44, and 94 existed before the stall. No per-GPU XID series first appeared at or after `22:33:30`.
- Kubernetes retained no node or pod event during the stall. All post-run nodes were Ready across the eight NVLink domains.
- The 84,098 retained worker log rows contain no NCCL RAS message, NCCL error, CUDA error, timeout, InfiniBand error, or transport error. Rank 0 logged `NCCL version 2.28.9+cuda13.0` at startup.

Communicator-level NCCL RAS cannot be recovered after the pods were deleted. No `ncclras` metrics were exported for the run. `NCCL_RAS_ENABLE=1` starts NCCL's live RAS service, but the training entrypoint does not start the Rigging NCCL RAS poller that would persist communicator inventory and rank status. The node-agent data also lacks NVLink-error and aggregate GPU-health metrics, so those signals are unknown rather than zero.

The evidence is consistent with all ranks waiting or spinning in device work inside `train_step`; it does not identify the collective, triggering rank, communicator, or fabric link. The run loaded the CUDA 13 NCCL build, so the mixed CUDA-major NCCL condition from the earlier [GB200 stall](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/7) is not evidenced here.

Full incident record, including the query results and follow-up capture gaps: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/85

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

NCCL starts one RAS thread per process, but a query to any job-local listener returns the global communicator view; processes in one job may share the listener socket ([NVIDIA RAS](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/ras.html), [`NCCL_RAS_ADDR`](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html#nccl-ras-addr)). An Iris node agent is in another pod network namespace and cannot reach task-local `localhost`; a same-pod sidecar can, but JAX process 0 already owns canonical Finelog task/run identity and a bounded background-probe lifecycle. Main starts the merged Rigging probe only for CUDA vLLM, so Levanter training never polls the live RAS service.

#7796 tracks this durability gap. Open #7699 adds a separate on-demand Iris client and leaves persistence unwired; this change will use the merged Rigging collector from #7863 and limit its scope to training lifecycle, probe health, and query guidance.

**Relevant code**
- [`nccl.py#L26-L61`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ec002c758da5ac68c956a4ab37c69b94083a077/lib/rigging/src/rigging/telemetry/probes/nccl.py#L26-L61) - bounded RAS poll
- [`runner.py#L142-L184`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ec002c758da5ac68c956a4ab37c69b94083a077/lib/rigging/src/rigging/telemetry/probes/runner.py#L142-L184) - isolated probe lifecycle
- [`telemetry.py#L255-L267`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ec002c758da5ac68c956a4ab37c69b94083a077/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/telemetry.py#L255-L267) - training exporter setup
- [`telemetry.py#L27-L85`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ec002c758da5ac68c956a4ab37c69b94083a077/lib/iris/src/iris/runtime/telemetry.py#L27-L85) - Iris resource attribution
- [`vllm_server.py#L933-L955`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3ec002c758da5ac68c956a4ab37c69b94083a077/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py#L933-L955) - current RAS owner

# Proposed Fix

Start one NCCL RAS probe in GPU JAX process 0 after Levanter configures Finelog, and stop it from `TelemetryTracker.finish()`. Poll every two minutes on the existing daemon thread with the existing eight-second subprocess deadline; failed, unavailable, malformed, and timed-out polls become explicit availability, latency, failure, and timeout telemetry instead of disappearing.

Preserve communicator inventory/state, rank status, collective counters, and vendor collection latency, adding rank host/PID/CUDA/NVML identity from NCCL JSON. Iris will stamp the collector snapshot with `task_id`, attempt/execution identity, node, JAX `process_index=0`, and `root_run_uid`; one global collector avoids an N-rank query fan-out. Add bounded Finelog queries to the training-stall runbook. Unit tests will cover unavailable/timeout outcomes, rank isolation and attribution, normal finish, and cancellation; a multi-node GPU smoke remains required after merge.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Correction to my previous comment: the root cause I gave for the wiki/70 OOM is wrong, and fix A should not ship as I justified it.** Also recording a measured failure rate for the hang, and one number that *is* now independently confirmed.

New telemetry from two more clean 8-rack runs on `origin/main` contradicts the central claim of https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5172703925. Retracting it here rather than leaving it to be acted on.

## 1. Retracted: "the allocator cap caused the wiki/70 OOM"

I claimed the run died because its 140.24 GiB requirement exceeded the 138.22 GiB allocator cap (XLA's default 0.75 × device), and proposed raising `XLA_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` to 0.80 on that basis.

I instrumented `train.py` to report the allocator budget every 10 steps and ran it at 8 racks. **Both clean runs sustained a peak above that cap for hundreds of steps without failing:**

```
device_total=185.03GiB  alloc_cap=138.22GiB  cap_frac=0.7470
in_use=24.65GiB         peak_in_use=140.23GiB
largest_alloc=115.59GiB num_allocs=145061
```

`peak_in_use = 140.23 GiB` exceeds `alloc_cap = 138.22 GiB` by the same ~2 GiB I claimed was fatal — identical figures in two independent 200-step runs that both finished. **For the `cuda_async` allocator, `Stats: Limit:` is an accounting value, not an enforced ceiling.** So "the request was rejected because it exceeded the cap" is not the mechanism, and the derivation I gave for 0.80 rests on a false premise. **Don't ship fix A on that rationale.**

A second line in that comment was also misleading. I wrote that with 16.75 GiB CUDA-free "the device was NOT out of memory" — but the failing request was 115.59 GiB, which 16.75 GiB of free memory cannot satisfy except by recycling already-reserved pool memory. rav's failure was a driver-level `cuMemAllocAsync` failure, not a cap rejection.

## 2. Confirmed: the 115.59 GiB allocation is real

`largest_alloc = 115.59 GiB` — **exactly** the allocation that failed in rav's run (`124108462544` B) — now observed succeeding in healthy 8-rack runs, 200 steps each. That confirms the temp-slab size and that this single contiguous allocation is a routine part of the watch executable, not an artifact of his configuration. Fix C (shrinking that slab via `include_per_parameter_norms=False`, or moving watch stats out of `train_step`) targets a real object.

## 3. Fragmentation: still untested, and my instrument does not work

The leading remaining hypothesis is that the async mempool had the bytes but not one contiguous 115.59 GiB block. I tried to measure it and **failed**: `largest_free_block_bytes` and `bytes_reserved` both report `0.00` under `cuda_async`. They are BFC-allocator fields and are simply not populated by this allocator — so the zeros mean "unimplemented," not "no free block." Anyone reading those fields for this allocator will be misled the same way.

Testing this needs the CUDA mempool attributes (`CU_MEMPOOL_ATTR_RESERVED_MEM_CURRENT` / `USED_MEM_CURRENT`) — which is what rav's crash dump printed and what `Device.memory_stats()` does not expose.

## 4. Measured failure rate for the hang

Identical config, `origin/main` @ `5e496b051`, 8 racks × 16 nodes = 512 GPUs, 200 steps:

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| `repro-v3` | **wedged at step 182** |
| `obs` | clean, 200 steps |
| `obs4` | clean, 200 steps |

**1 wedge in 3 valid runs.** (A fourth was invalidated by my own logging mistake: `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS` including `TUNING` emits ~1,800 lines/s, which displaced everything else out of the retrievable log window. Worth knowing before anyone enables it on a 128-node run.)

That the same config also completes cleanly is itself evidence, and it strengthens rather than weakens the part of my earlier comment I still stand behind: the wiki/70 OOM is a **marginal-headroom, non-deterministic** failure, not a deterministic consequence of the 8-rack program size. The 88-of-128-ranks split in rav's own run says the same thing.

## 5. What still stands

Fixes **B** (make the memory budget observable), **C** (shrink the watch slab), **D** (warm both `compute_watch` variants at startup), **E** (host-side liveness watchdog), and **F** (don't retry a deterministic config failure) are unaffected. Fix **A** needs a new justification or should be dropped.

Note that **E has since landed** — `ProgressWatchdogConfig` with `HERO_TRAIN_STEP_TIMEOUT = 15 min` now calls `os._exit(124)` on a stalled step, and #7929 added checkpoint recovery. That converts this hang from a silent indefinite wedge into a retryable, self-announcing failure. It does not address the underlying cause: a job that wedges will now thrash (wedge → 15 min → exit 124 → restore → wedge) rather than hang. Exit code 124 is a clean detection signal for anyone hunting this.

I'm now cycling 8-rack runs from current `main` with the merged NCCL RAS collector (#7951) to catch a wedge with per-rank collective counters. That path has not yet been exercised on hardware — its own PR notes a multi-node GPU smoke is still required — so this run doubles as its first real test.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖

TL;DR: the first observed fault is now a single Iris task hitting `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` inside `jit_train_step`. That task's rack then stops advancing and the other racks wait in collectives. NCCL RAS is measuring this propagation; it is not the source of the failure.

The four targeted trials reproduced the same CUDA fault at different steps:

| run | code / RAS | first observed fault |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ras8` | `75d12bd05`, RAS on | task 80 after step 31 |
| `ctrl9` | `75d12bd05`, RAS on | task 5 after step 89 |
| `norasA` | exact `ctrl9` bundle, RAS off | task 13 after step 85 |
| `oldbaseB` | `5e496b051`, RAS on | task 86 after step 146 |

The `oldbaseB` RAS snapshot had all 512 ranks present, with no missing, dead, unresponsive, or aborted ranks. Global ranks 320-383 were two AllReduces behind the other 448 ranks. In every 8-rank communicator, local rank 5 was three AllReduces behind the other seven ranks. This identifies one lagging rack and matches the task containing the CUDA fault. The watchdog saved `nccl_ras_stall01-step146_proc64` and related per-process artifacts.

This rules out the RAS collector as a necessary cause: `ctrl9` and `norasA` used the same code bundle and failed with RAS on and off. It also rules out one repeatedly bad node and a recent-code-only regression: the first-fault task was on four different physical nodes, and both `5e496b051` and `75d12bd05` failed. The exact GPU kernel is still unknown. CUDA errors are asynchronous, so the reported `branch_index` retrieval/synchronization site may only be where JAX notices the poisoned context.

The original unmodified runs were 1/3 stalled (`repro-v3` stopped after step 181; `obs` and `obs4` completed 200 steps). The four newer diagnostic trials all hit the illegal-instruction signature by step 146, but they are not a homogeneous statistical sample.

Suggested next steps:

1. Run one 8-rack diagnostic with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`, `JAX_TRACEBACK_FILTERING=off`, and explicit synchronization boundaries around attention, MoE routing, loss, and optimizer sections. This should move the error closer to the offending launch, at a throughput cost.
2. Correlate DCGM/NVML/Xid and node telemetry at the four first-fault timestamps. A shared Xid or driver signature would separate a fleet problem from a generated/custom-kernel fault.
3. A/B the reference implementations for custom attention and MoE kernels, and disable per-parameter watch norms or move them outside `jit_train_step`. These reduce kernel and temporary-memory pressure while narrowing the responsible section. Do not increase `XLA_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION`; no allocation failure was observed.
4. Keep NCCL RAS enabled. After the first training step, treat 4-5 minutes without progress plus collective-count skew as a gang failure: capture RAS and threads, fail the whole gang, and retry on fresh nodes instead of leaving 512 GPUs wedged. Startup needs a separate, longer timeout because compilation has exceeded 150 seconds.
5. Send watchdog alerts to a durable sink instead of a Loom session ID. The poller continued running after its Loom session expired, which is why later near-step alerts were not delivered even though polling continued.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Third reproduction of this hang, on a completely unmodified tree — and it is a distinct failure from the `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` now seen on `main` (#7956).**

## The reproduction

`moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-oldpureD-20260804` — `5e496b051`, **pristine** (`git status --porcelain` empty, zero instrumentation of mine), `cw-us-east-08a`, 8 racks = 128 × GB200x4 = **512 GPUs**, 200 steps, production priority.

It reached **step 189** and stopped. Killed after **16.5 minutes** wedged.

- Last progress line: `Progress on:train 189it` at **16:47:52 UTC**. Last W&B metric: `_step=187`.
- All **128 tasks `TASK_STATE_RUNNING`**, attempt 0, `failures=0`, `preemptions=0`.
- In 20,000 lines of trailing task logs: **0 `CUDA_ERROR`, 0 `NCCL WARN`, 0 `Traceback`, 0 `TimeoutError`/`ncclCommAbort`.**

Completely silent. Nothing was retried, nothing errored, nothing aborted.

## Per-rank stack traces, one task per rack, all 8 racks

```
Thread 1 (idle): "MainThread"
    _run_grug_local (experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py:585)
    <module> (_callable_runner.py:40)
```

Identical on tasks 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112. `train.py:585` is the `train_step(state, batch, compute_watch=...)` call. Every other thread sits in a normal wait (dataloader `queue.put`, tqdm monitor, wandb, telemetry).

Process status of a wedged rank (`s1nrxs64`):

```
CPU 8.06 cores (of 120 requested)   RSS 156.57 GiB   Threads 1057   Uptime 1h19m
```

Same caveat as before: a *healthy* loop also sits at line 585, because JAX dispatch blocks there on the donated buffer. The dump is meaningful only combined with 16.5 minutes of frozen W&B metrics and a frozen log stream. What it establishes is that all 512 ranks are alive and blocked symmetrically at the step boundary.

## This is not #7956

Both were seen today, and they are easy to conflate. They are not the same:

| | this hang | #7956 `ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` |
|---|---|---|
| Error output | none at all | `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` + dead-context unwind |
| Ranks affected | all, simultaneously | one rank, then its rack |
| Process outcome | alive, hangs indefinitely | gang bounces, restarts from step 0 |
| Tree seen on | `5e496b051` | `75d12bd05` **and** `5e496b051` |
| Step | 189 | 23 / 85 / 89 / 146 |

Worth noting explicitly for anyone bisecting: **`5e496b051` exhibits both.** `oldbaseB` (same commit, plus a RAS watchdog) hit the illegal instruction at step 146; `oldpureD` (same commit, pristine) hit this hang at step 189.

## No RAS data for this one, and why

I built an in-process NCCL RAS watchdog for exactly this and validated it end-to-end — it captured a real stall on `oldbaseB`, localizing the lagging rack from per-rank collective counters (1.2 MB raw report, 77 communicators). But this hang landed on the one run deliberately kept pristine as a control, so there was no watchdog to fire.

That is worth fixing before the next attempt: the RAS query has to originate inside the training process, because `iris process` has no exec and RAS listens on `localhost:28028`. Note also that the merged collector (#7951) would not have helped here — it discards every response at this scale (#7957), and it is not wired into the hero at `5e496b051` at all.

## Detection power — relevant to anyone calling a run "clean"

Known stall steps across occurrences are now **38, 90, 145, 182, 189**. Fitting a constant per-step hazard to my own controlled runs (2 wedges in 1,114 exposed steps) gives `p ≈ 0.0018/step`, so:

- a 200-step run has only about a **30%** chance of surfacing this hang
- reaching 95% confidence needs roughly **1,700 steps** — about 5 × 200-step runs
- the 95% CI on `p` is wide (2 events), so that figure could plausibly be 460 or 13,800 steps

Two of the three "clean" 200-step runs I reported earlier in this issue were therefore never meaningful evidence of absence. Under constant hazard only total exposure matters, so partial runs still count — worth recording the step reached even when a run dies of something unrelated.

## Artifacts

- W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-oldpureD-20260804
- Job: `/marin/moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-oldpureD-20260804-coord` (killed 17:04 UTC)
- Thread dumps (8 racks) and process status captured locally; happy to attach.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Fourth reproduction, at 8x smaller batch — and it moves the hazard clock from *steps* to *wall-clock time*.**

I shrank the per-step work to see whether the repro could be made cheaper. It could not, and the reason why is the useful part.

## The run

`moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-shrinkA-20260804` — `5e496b051` with a **single-line diff**:

```diff
-HERO_FSDP_BATCH_SIZE = 1024
+HERO_FSDP_BATCH_SIZE = 128
```

Nothing else. Batch 8192 → 1024 (16 → 2 sequences/GPU), 8 racks = 512 GPUs, `remat_mode` untouched, optimizer left to the heuristic's own rescale.

The reason batch is the safe knob here: `launch.py` sets `expert_axis_size=1` and `replica_axis_size=dp_racks`, so parameters shard over `data` (intra-rack) and replicate over `replica_dcn`. **Every cross-node collective — the FSDP all-gather/reduce-scatter and the cross-rack gradient all-reduce — is sized by parameter count, not batch.** With the expert axis at 1 there is no cross-node all-to-all either. So the collectives are byte-for-byte identical to the wedging config; only the matmul work between them shrinks.

Result: **6.56 s/step vs 18.63 s** (`oldpureD`) — a 2.84x speedup, loss descending normally.

**It still wedged.** Step **606**, at W&B `_runtime` **86.8 min**.

## The hazard is on wall-clock, not steps

| Run | Batch | Wedge step | Wedge wall-clock | s/step |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `oldbaseB` | 8192 | 145 | 52.7 min | 18.59 |
| `oldpureD` | 8192 | 187 | 65.9 min | 18.63 |
| **`shrinkA`** | **1024** | **606** | **86.8 min** | **6.56** |

Across the five known wedges (steps 38, 90, 145, 182, 189) the mean is **128.8 steps ≈ 47.7 min**. `shrinkA` reached 4.7x the step mean but only 1.8x the time mean:

- constant hazard **per step** → P(S ≥ 606) = **0.9%**
- constant hazard **per second** → P(T ≥ 86.8 min) = **16%**
- likelihood ratio ≈ **7:1 favouring wall-clock**

The sharper form of the argument: collectives-per-step are identical between the two configs, so `shrinkA` executed **3.2x more collectives** and pushed **~2.8x more fabric traffic per second**. Any per-collective or per-byte hazard predicts it should have wedged *sooner* in wall-clock. It wedged *later*. That disfavours the whole "something in the collective sequence accumulates" family.

Caveats, stated plainly: this is **one** observation, so 7:1 is substantial rather than decisive; I cannot exclude that the shrink simply lowered the rate; and of the five prior wedges only `oldbaseB` and `oldpureD` have measured wall-clock — the times for steps 38/90/182 are inferred from 18.6 s/step plus startup.

## Practical consequence

**Shrinking the repro does not shorten the cycle.** Under a wall-clock hazard a 95%-confidence trial costs ~2.1 h and ~1,050 GPU-hours regardless of step time. Batch reduction is not the lever, and with a ~4.7 s/step comm floor there was little left to extract anyway.

The lever that *should* work is **more racks** — more independent per-rack opportunities per unit time, and roughly GPU-hour-neutral. A 12-rack (768 GPU) RAS-armed run is in flight now.

## This instance had no `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`

Re: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5181330482 — for **this** wedge the illegal instruction is absent, and the evidence is the *silence*:

| | `shrinkA` | an `ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` failure |
|---|---|---|
| `ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` / `JaxRuntimeError` / `cudaFreeAsync` / `Shutdown barrier` | **0 across every window searched** | hundreds of lines |
| Output after the failure | **total silence, 43+ min** | ~15k lines/sec flood |
| Final state | **all 128 tasks halted together at `606it`** | one rank dies, the rest unwind |

Last log line `19:46:19Z`, all 128 tasks at `606it/2.00kit`, then nothing.

I don't think this contradicts your runs so much as bounds the claim: your four trials were on `75d12bd05`, where the illegal instruction is ~14x more frequent (#7956), and there the illegal instruction plausibly *is* the first fault with the hang as propagation. `shrinkA` is on `5e496b051`, and here the gang went silent with no fault at all. So "illegal instruction first, hang second" does not look like a complete account of the wedge on the older commit — unless the illegal instruction can occur without emitting anything, which the flood in every other observed instance argues against.

## Also worth recording: this wedge does not self-terminate

`shrinkA` sat hung for **43+ minutes with no XLA collective timeout firing** — all 128 tasks still `running`, no crash. Anything relying on a collective timeout to convert this hang into a crash will wait indefinitely. `5e496b051` has no `ProgressWatchdogConfig`; that is a concrete argument for one.

## Next

12-rack RAS-armed run in flight (`5e496b051` + the in-process NCCL RAS watchdog that produced the per-rank collective counters in `oldbaseB`, where a stall localized to ranks 320–383 — one rack, 3 AllReduces behind, nothing missing or dead). Goal is per-rank counters for a wedge captured at 12 racks, plus a test of whether hazard scales with rack count.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **The wedge reproduces with `num_layers=1` — a 48x model reduction — and it wedges in ~7 minutes instead of ~48. This is a far better repro than the full hero run.**

## The run

`moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-l1-20260804` — `5e496b051` with a **one-line diff**:

```diff
-        num_layers=48,
+        num_layers=1,
```

12 racks = 192 × GB200x4 = **768 GPUs**, `cw-us-east-08a`, batch 12288, everything else untouched (`remat_mode`, kernels, optimizer, mesh all stock).

It wedged at **step 29**, W&B `_runtime` **7.24 min**.

## Why I am confident this is the hang and not #7956

| Criterion | Observed |
|---|---|
| Step counter | frozen at **29** for 8+ min (steps were landing every **1.26 s**, so ~380 steps' worth) |
| Tasks | **192/192 still `running`** |
| iris `failures` | **0** — the gang never died |
| `ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` / `cudaFreeAsync` / `JaxRuntimeError` / `Shutdown barrier` / traceback | **0 matches** |
| Log output | last line **21:54:13Z**, still silent at **22:02:14Z** |

That is the silent-collective-hang signature: everything alive, nothing progressing, nothing logged. The `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` failure looks the opposite — the gang dies, `failures` increments, and the tasks emit a flood of unwinding errors.

**Methodology note, because it nearly fooled me:** `iris job logs --since-seconds N --max-lines M` returns the *earliest* M lines in the window unless you pass `--tail`. My first check came back spanning only 3 seconds and I briefly read that as silence — it was just the line cap biting 3 seconds in. You need `--tail` to establish that output actually stopped.

## Why this matters beyond convenience

At `num_layers=1` the model is ~9B parameters versus ~360B. Since parameters set the size of every collective here (FSDP all-gather/reduce-scatter over `data`, gradient all-reduce over `replica_dcn`), **every collective is roughly 40x smaller and it still wedges.** Large message size is therefore not necessary for the hang, which rules out a whole family of "big transfer" explanations.

Combined with the earlier finding that the hazard runs on wall-clock rather than steps or collectives (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5184323726), the picture is a hang that does not seem to care much about *what* the collectives are doing.

## Caveats

- **One observation.** 7.24 min is early against the ~47.7 min baseline mean, but not extraordinarily so (P(T ≤ 7.2) ≈ 14–20%), so I cannot yet claim 1 layer wedges *faster* — only that it wedges. A confirmation run is the obvious next step and now costs ~15 min instead of an hour.
- This run was at **12 racks**, where prior wedge statistics were gathered at 8. Rack count is a second changed variable.
- No RAS telemetry: `train.py` is pristine here, so there are no per-rank collective counters for this instance.

## Suggested repro

```bash
# on 5e496b051, set num_layers=1 in experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/heuristic.py
iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority production \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 21600 \
  --job-name "${RID}-coord" -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
  -- python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_fsdp.launch \
     --run-id "$RID" --dp-racks 12 --num-steps 50000 --version dev --run
```

Set `--num-steps` high so wall-clock, not step count, is the binding constraint — at 1.26 s/step a step-based budget expires almost immediately.

## Next

Confirm reproducibility, then keep minimizing: stock kernels (`attention_implementation="reference"`, `moe_implementation="scatter"`), `expert_chunks=1`, and fewer racks. Goal is a standalone JAX + NCCL repro with no marin, levanter, or iris in it — which now looks reachable, since at 1 layer with small collectives there is not much left that is specific to this model.

Note `num_layers=0` does **not** work: `ArrayStacked.init` calls `jnp.stack` on an empty key list and raises `ValueError`. The forward pass would tolerate it (`lax.scan` over length 0 is a no-op); only the construction site needs fixing, if we want to go that far.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan for shrinking this to a shareable repro — cumulative delta-debugging from the `num_layers=1` result above.**

Posting the protocol so anyone can pick it up or push back on it.

## Method

This is test-case minimization, not causal attribution. Each rung is applied **on top of every previously accepted cut**:

- **Still wedges** → accept the cut, it becomes the new baseline, continue.
- **Does not wedge** → revert that cut, try the next one. This is *not* evidence we found the cause; multiple things changed and a null has weaker standing than a reproduction.

Two rules that matter more than the ordering:

1. **Stop on wall-clock, not steps.** Step time swings by >10x across rungs (18.6 s at 48 layers, 1.26 s at 1 layer), so a step budget silently gives a fast rung almost no exposure. Run each trial ~3x the current mean time-to-wedge.
2. **Re-measure the rate after every accepted cut.** If a cut halves the hazard, the next trial needs twice the exposure — otherwise the following rung produces a false "fixed it". This is the easiest way to derail the whole campaign.

## Rungs, in order

| # | Cut | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `num_layers=1` | **done — wedged at step 29 / 7.24 min**; confirmation run in flight |
| 1 | `attention_implementation="reference"`, `moe_implementation="scatter"` | drops the vendored CUTE/QuACK SM100 kernels for stock XLA; also the main prerequisite for a standalone repro |
| 2 | reduce racks 12 → 8 → 4 → 2 | biggest usability win for external reproduction; expect a *lower* rate if hazard scales with rack count, so allow longer exposure |
| 3 | `expert_chunks=1`, `sconv=False`, `rope_fused=False` | remaining custom paths |
| 4 | FSDP off (replicate) | necessarily also a small-model change — two variables, accepted because a reproduction is still a win |
| 5 | standalone JAX + NCCL, no marin/levanter/iris | the actual goal |

Rung 1 is the critical path: with stock kernels and 1 layer there is very little left that is specific to this model, which makes rung 5 mostly a rewrite rather than a research problem.

`moe_hero_ep` is worth running alongside as a data point rather than a rung — it introduces a cross-node all-to-all, so it is a different program, not a subtraction.

## Current state

Confirmation run `moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-l1b-20260804` is in flight (identical config, new id). One wedge observation at 7.24 min is early against the ~47.7 min baseline mean but only at P ≈ 14–20%, so it does not yet establish that 1 layer wedges *faster* — only that it wedges. Everything downstream uses that rate as its denominator, so it is worth the ~15 minutes to pin down.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Ladder update: rung 2.5 result, a retraction, and a discriminator that separates this issue from #7956

### TL;DR

1. `offload_opt_state=False` **runs fine** — the earlier "CLOSED: cannot run" verdict is retracted.
2. That run did **not** reproduce this bug. It reproduced **#7956**, and I now have a clean, principled way to tell the two apart.
3. The 145 GiB allocation is retired as a cause here — but my stated evidence for that was wrong, and I'm correcting it below.
4. `--xla_gpu_nccl_termination_timeout_seconds=600` **does not do what our comment says it does**, which changes how the silence should be interpreted.

---

### 1. A discriminator between #7344 and #7956

A single-rank CUDA fault (#7956) makes that rank enter JAX shutdown. The other ranks never
join, and JAX's **default `shutdown_timeout_seconds=300`** expires and aborts the gang.

Measured on `moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-r25fa4-20260805`: last teardown error 06:01:22.104668,
shutdown barrier expiry 06:06:22.998317 = **300.894 s**. That is the default timeout, not a
coincidence.

**Therefore: any run that sits with `failures` unchanged for ≫300 s is not a #7956 event**,
because a #7956 event self-aborts inside 300 s.

Applying it to the monitored runs:

| run | max stall, failures unchanged | iris `failures` | class |
|---|---|---|---|
| `l1` | 7203 s | 0 | **#7344** |
| `l1b` | 5590 s | 0 | **#7344** |
| `r0fa4` (rung 0) | 4883 s | 0 | **#7344** |
| `r2b` | 2296 s | 0 | **#7344** |
| `r2g` | 435 s | 0 | **#7344** |
| `r25fa4` (rung 2.5) | 374 s | 2 | **#7956** |

So the ladder's rungs 0–2 are genuine #7344 wedges. Rung 2.5 is **inconclusive** for this
issue — it hit a #7956 fault before it could tell us anything.

### 2. Rung 2.5: `offload_opt_state=False`

Retracting the earlier verdict. The previous attempt (`r25nooffload`) failed with a
145.80 GiB request against a 138.22 GiB pool, and I recorded it as "CLOSED: cannot run".
That attempt was running **on top of rung 1's `reference` attention**, and 145.80 / 48.0 =
3.04 score matrices. Rerun at rung 0 (`gpu_fa4_cute`, real data, `num_layers=1`), it
compiled and trained normally to step 300 at 1.2 s/it with `MaxAllocSize` 50.32 GiB.

**Ladder status: rung 2.5 unresolved** — needs a rerun that doesn't get pre-empted by #7956.

### 3. Retraction: my rung-0 "zero failed allocations" claim was unsupported

I reported that rung 0 wedged with zero `cuMemAllocAsync` failures and said I had verified
the log window was complete. **That verification was wrong.** The artifact
(`r0fa4_wedge.txt`) spans 04:58:40 → 05:01:10; the wedge was at 05:05:29. It ends four
minutes before the event. My `--tail` vs no-`--tail` check led me to believe the fetch
returned the most recent lines; it did not.

The conclusion survives on better evidence — the `r25fa4` capture brackets its fault exactly
and contains zero failed allocations — but the rung-0 artifact never supported it.

Also correcting two smaller errors of mine: `155749234632` **is** divisible by 4 and 8 (not
16), so my "not a clean multiple of 4" remark was simply wrong; and "≈3.02 × 48 GiB"
identifies the reference-attention memory family but does not prove three exact score
matrices without an XLA buffer assignment dump.

### 4. The NCCL watchdog does not watch in-flight collectives

`lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:384` sets
`--xla_gpu_nccl_termination_timeout_seconds=600` and comments that it "Counts only time
spent inside a collective."

At the pinned XLA revision that description is wrong. The flag bounds the `Rendezvous` used
when **initializing/acquiring an NCCL clique**; it does not place a deadline around an
already-launched collective. The communicator-health heartbeat also **skips cliques that are
currently in use** — precisely the state during a stuck collective.

Consequence: **the 600 s flag never firing is not evidence against a NCCL hang.** A
healthy-but-nonprogressing collective can stay silent indefinitely. The protection actually
needed is host-side step-progress monitoring, which is what merged PR #7929
(`ProgressWatchdog`) provides; the worktree these runs used predates it.

### 5. Corrected memory accounting (affects #7987)

The instrumented state probe reports **logical sharded** bytes, not HBM residency. Under the
default `offload_opt_state=True`, the optimizer moments live on `pinned_host` between steps
and are copied device-ward per step (`train.py:637`). So:

- comparing the probe's 9.87 GiB against the no-offload allocator's 9.94 GiB `InUse` was invalid;
- **#7987's "8.81 GiB of per-GPU HBM, ~5.8 GiB recoverable" holds only for no-offload or the
  update transient, not the steady default.** I'll correct that issue directly.

### 6. Newly surfaced axis: PGLE

`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=1` is set unconditionally (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py:56`),
and every rank in the live job emitted:

> `PGLE collected an empty trace … CUPTI_ERROR_MULTIPLE_SUBSCRIBERS_NOT_SUPPORTED`

There are also **two separately compiled `train_step` executables**, because `compute_watch`
is a static JIT argument. This is a clean, semantics-preserving cut that has never been
tried, and it is my next rung.

### 7. Methodological note

Rung 1 (`reference` attention) introduced a *new failure mechanism* — a 48 GiB score tensor
and a 145 GiB executable arena that does not exist under FA4. Rungs 2 and 2.5 were then
built on top of it. Once a cut introduces its own failure mode it should be rolled back
before drawing conclusions downstream; I didn't, and it cost several hours.

### Next

1. `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0` alone, at rung 0 — highest-information cut for *this* issue.
2. Rerun rung 2.5 to a verdict.
3. Toolchain axis (@rjpower's request). Note for attribution: the suspect kernels are
   **CuTe/CUTLASS DSL** — `sonic_cute` pulls `quack-kernels` and `nvidia-cutlass-dsl`, which
   a NCCL/cuDNN/Triton bump does not update. Worth recording those versions too.

Capture procedure fixed for all future runs: `iris job logs <task> --level info
--since-seconds N --no-tail`. `--no-tail` returns the *earliest* lines in the window, so it
reaches the onset instead of the post-kill/retry flood that destroyed several earlier
captures (some spanned a single second and were no evidence at all).

🤖 Investigation notes; analysis independently reviewed before posting.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` suppresses both failures — and a power measurement that narrows the mechanism

Run `moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-clb-20260805`
([wandb](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-clb-20260805)),
12 racks / 192 nodes / 768 GPUs. **Stopped manually at step 2580 / 117.6 min** to free the
racks for the toolchain axis.

**This is not a declared null.** The adopted stop rule is one uninterrupted attempt reaching
*both* 4.5 h and ≥7500 steps; this run reached neither before I killed it. Reported as an
observation, not a verdict.

### The diagnostic failed at its own purpose

The intent was to make CUDA errors synchronous so a #7956 illegal instruction would be
attributed to the faulting kernel instead of surfacing later at `cudaFreeAsync`. That cannot
work: **`CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` suppresses the very fault it was meant to localize.** No
illegal instruction appeared in 2580 steps. It also suppressed the #7344 wedge.

### Verification that the flag took effect

A silently-dropped env var looks exactly like a negative result, so:

- **Propagated** — `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` appears in the task's own provenance dump, read
  from the process environment on the ranks, not echoed from the launch command.
- **Respected** — GPU utilization measured live on rank 0 was **47–54%** against a 100%
  baseline; step time went **1.2–1.5 s/it → ~2.6 s/it**.

Config was **rung 0** (`num_layers=1`, `attn=gpu_fa4_cute`, `moe=sonic_cute`,
`expert_chunks=4`, real data, `offload_opt_state=True`, `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=1`) plus the flag.

### Exposure

| | steps | job age | training exposure (age − ~6.7 min startup) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CLB run at kill** | **2580** | **117.6 min** | **~111 min** |
| rung-0 baseline, wedge 1 | 29 | 7.24 min | ~2.5 min |
| rung-0 baseline, wedge 2 | 75 | 9.27 min | ~4.5 min |
| rung-0 baseline, wedge 3 | 33 | 7.0 min | ~2.5 min |

`failures=0` and 192/192 alive throughout. It exceeded every prior data point on **both** axes
— wall-clock and steps — which matters because it makes the observation robust to which hazard
model you assume. Under the wall-clock model this issue adopts, ~111 min against a ~3 min mean
is extreme; as a distribution-free job-level test it is still n=1 (Fisher exact p=0.25).

---

## The more useful result: the wedged GPUs are spinning, not computing

Measured live on a healthy rank of this run, and compared against the wedged EP64 run in
[comment 5125585656](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5125585656):

| | GPU utilization | power draw (1200 W limit) |
|---|---|---|
| healthy (this run, 1 layer, **deliberately serialized by CLB**) | 61 / 97 / 98 / 90 % | **632–747 W** |
| **wedged** (EP64, d5120, **48 layers**) | 100 % | **198–228 W** |

The comparison runs the favorable direction: the wedged run was the *larger* model, and the
healthy run was throttled to roughly half duty cycle by `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING`. The bigger
model, wedged, drew about a third the power of the smaller model running slowly.

**100% utilization at a third the power means a kernel is resident but spinning, not
computing** — `nvidia-smi` utilization only reports that a kernel occupied the device during
the sample window. That is the signature of a device stuck inside a collective waiting on a
peer that never arrives.

**What this rules out as the proximate mechanism:** anything that stalls on the *host* — an
allocator deadlock, a Python-level lock, a data-loader stall — would leave the GPUs **idle**,
at low utilization and low power. We see the opposite.

It does not rule out a host-side or allocator **root cause** that corrupts a collective — e.g.
a stream-ordered free handing back a buffer a live NCCL kernel still owns would produce exactly
this picture. But the proximate stall is on the device, inside a collective.

### Consequence for prioritisation

Combined with the EP64 result now recorded in the issue body — two different programs, two
different collective structures, same signature — the surviving hypothesis space is the layer
those programs **share**: NCCL, the driver, and the fabric. That is the toolchain axis (T1/T2),
and it is now the highest-priority direction.

I am de-prioritising the allocator ablation (`cuda_async` → BFC) that the intersection argument
otherwise favoured. It remains genuinely untested in either program and worth doing as a cheap
rider, but the power evidence points at the collective layer rather than at the allocator.

### Caveats on the CLB result itself

1. **PGLE breaks the "same compiled program" premise, and this run had `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=1`.**
   JAX PGLE profiles `jax_pgle_profiling_runs` (default 3) executions and then **recompiles**
   with the measured latencies. Under CLB the profile is degenerate, so the recompiled schedule
   may differ from baseline. This run therefore confounds serialization with a schedule change.
   That is an experimental-design error of mine, not a property of the bug.
2. CLB changes timing, which can change NCCL channel scheduling and possibly algorithm or
   protocol selection — so it is not a clean "same work, different order" either.
3. CLB changes allocation ordering, so addresses may differ even where logical data does not.
4. ~111 min may still be insufficient exposure; the stop rule exists for exactly this and was
   not met.

Given (1) and (2), I would not read this as "serialization fixes it" — only as "a large
timing perturbation suppresses both failures", which is weaker and consistent with the
spin-wait picture above.

🤖 Run stopped to free 12 racks for the toolchain axis.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## New candidates for the ladder: process/device layout and NCCL multi-communicator launch order

Raised by @mcwitt: we run **1 process per node driving 4 GPUs**, not 1 process per GPU. Chasing
that led to a documented NCCL deadlock mechanism that fits the measured symptom, and to a
sharper reading of the toolchain rungs. Recording it here rather than acting on it silently.

### What we actually run

`HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 1` (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/launch.py:34`) with
`ResourceConfig.with_gpu("GB200", count=4, ..., replicas=HERO_NODES_PER_RACK * dp_racks)`
(`launch.py:116-122`). So one task = one node = **one process holding all four GB200s**, and
`replicas` counts nodes. At 10 racks that is 160 processes / 640 GPUs. This is what makes
`replica_dcn = rank // 16` work — `rank` is the *task* index, so one replica is exactly one
16-node rack.

### The premise, corrected

NVIDIA does **not** publish a blanket preference for one process per GPU. The NCCL
[communicators page](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/usage/communicators.html)
presents "Single Process, Single Thread, Multiple Devices", "One Device per Process or Thread",
and "Multiple Devices per Thread" as three supported patterns. I could not find guidance
deprecating the multi-device-per-process model, and I am not going to assert one.

### The mechanism that *is* documented, and why it fits

The same page carries this:

> Prior to NCCL 2.26, using multiple NCCL communicators per-device required serializing the
> order of all communication operations (via CUDA stream dependencies or synchronization) into
> a consistent total global order otherwise **deadlocks could ensue**.

The control is `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT`, which the
[env-var page](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html) says was
**introduced in NCCL 2.30**. We run **2.28.9**.

⚠️ **The two pages disagree on the version** (2.26 vs 2.30 for the mitigation). That needs
pinning down against the NCCL changelog before anyone leans on it. Flagging rather than
resolving it.

Why this is worth the time regardless: a launch-order deadlock across many communicators
produces *exactly* the state measured in
[comment 5194863698](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5194863698)
— GPUs resident in a collective at 100% utilization drawing 198–228 W of a 1200 W limit, i.e.
**spinning, not computing**, waiting on a peer that never arrives. It is also consistent with
the non-determinism and with the fact that only large runs are affected.

Independent corroboration already in this repo: the in-flight branch `rav/moonep-jax` drops
`--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit` 4 → 1 for `direct_device` with the
comment *"XLA's ragged device kernels share NCCL device-communicator state. Keep them
serialized until an EP64 overlap gate proves that concurrent use is safe."* Someone else
independently arrived at "serialize concurrent use of shared communicator state."

One mechanism I checked and mostly ruled out: `NCCL_GRAPH_MIXING_SUPPORT` (default 1) documents
*"observed hangs in the CUDA launches"* when multiple ranks call `cudaGraphLaunch()` from the
same thread — a 1-process-many-devices pattern specifically. But we run with
`--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=` (disabled for #5675), so XLA is not capturing CUDA graphs and
the graph-mixing path should not be live. Worth a sanity check, not a rung.

### This sharpens T1 vs T2

The NGC image `nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:26.07-py3` ships **NCCL 2.30.7** (read from the registry
config blob, not the docs) — the version that carries `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT`.

- **T2 already exercises this**, confounded with CUDA 13.3, cuDNN 9.24, jax-from-main, and the
  forward-compat userspace driver.
- **T1 (NCCL 2.28.9 → 2.30.7, nothing else) discriminates it.**

That promotes T1 from "bump the version and see" to a rung with a named mechanism, and it means
a T2 suppression should be followed by T1 rather than treated as an answer.

### Proposed new rungs

| # | rung | cost | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| N1 | **Count communicators per device at runtime** under `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` | free — next run | The deadlock precondition is *multiple communicators per device*. An earlier note in this investigation put the job at ~77 communicators; that number needs re-verifying from a current log before it is used for anything. |
| N2 | **`NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT`** if it exists in 2.28.9 | ~zero | Directly targets the documented mechanism at near-zero wall-clock cost. Gated on resolving the 2.26-vs-2.30 ambiguity — if the knob does not exist in 2.28.9, this collapses into T1. |
| N3 | **1 process per device** (`HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 4`) | one full run | Changes the NCCL process topology while leaving the logical program identical. |

**N3 is a genuinely clean ablation, which is why it is worth a slot.** `processes_per_task` is
first-class in the stack (`lib/iris/src/iris/hooks/multigpu.py:64-76` builds
`MultiGpuHook(nproc=4, devices_per_proc=1)`; `lib/fray/src/fray/iris_backend.py:630`), so it is a
one-constant change. The mesh is unchanged: `compact_grug_mesh` derives its shape from
`jax.process_count() * jax.local_device_count()`, so 640 processes × 1 device reshapes to the
same `(replica_dcn=10, data=64, expert=1, model=1)`. `jax.devices()` stays ordered by process and
processes stay node-grouped, so a replica is still exactly one rack and batch sharding is
untouched. Same math, different NCCL topology.

Caveats on N3, stated up front:
- It does **not** obviously reduce communicators *per device*, which is the documented deadlock
  precondition — it reduces communicators per *process*. So it may not test the mechanism above
  so much as the launch-ordering behaviour of one host thread driving four devices.
- It changes host-side launch scheduling, memory footprint per process, and the
  `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` split. Not a free variable.
- Startup cost and the compilation cache key both change (640 clients, not 160).

### Ranking

I would run **N1 as a free rider on the next run**, resolve the **N2** version question from the
NCCL changelog (desk work, no GPUs), and hold **N3** behind T1/T2 — because if T1 suppresses the
wedge, the mechanism is named and N3 becomes a much better-motivated confirmation than a blind
topology swap.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## The wedge reproduces at 10 racks / 640 GPUs — and T1 now runs before T2

### Control: `moe-hero-fsdp-10rack-ctrl10b-20260805`

Rung 0 (`num_layers=1`, `gpu_fa4_cute`, `sonic_cute`, `expert_chunks=4`, real data,
`offload_opt_state=True`, `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=1`), stock task image, **10 racks / 160 nodes /
640 GPUs**. Every prior FSDP rung-0 wedge was at *twelve* racks, so this was run to check that
dropping to 10 does not suppress the failure before spending a 4.5 h budget on a toolchain null.

**It wedged at step 93.**

```
18:35:49  step  3   84.8 s/it
18:38:15  step 21   33.5 s/it   loss=11.6
18:39:16  step 61    2.5 s/it   loss=9.65
18:40:17  step 93    1.6 s/it   loss=8.38   <- last line
[silence]
```

It had accelerated into healthy steady state (1.6 s/it, against a 1.2–1.5 s/it baseline) and
stopped dead. `tqdm` had been emitting every ~61 s.

**Confirmed as a genuine #7344 wedge, not a #7956 fault:**

| check | result |
|---|---|
| job state | `running`, `failures=0`, `160/160` tasks alive |
| silence | past 300 s — beyond JAX's shutdown-barrier timeout |
| `ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` / `Shutdown barrier` / `TimeoutError` in the gang | **none** |
| GPU utilization (rank 0, all 4) | **100 %** |
| GPU power (1200 W limit) | **244–276 W**, SM clock 1950 MHz |

The power number is the decisive one and it reproduces the earlier measurement exactly:
100 % utilization at roughly a fifth of the power limit is a **resident kernel spinning, not
computing** — a device stuck inside a collective waiting on a peer that never arrives. Healthy
on the CLB run was 632–747 W; the wedged EP64 run was 198–228 W.

**Consequences:**

1. The wedge does not require 12 racks. Combined with the 2-rack EP64 wedge, rack count is
   looking like an exposure/probability knob, not a threshold.
2. **10 racks is now a validated vehicle**, so a null on a toolchain rung at 10 racks is
   interpretable against this control rather than against 12-rack history.
3. Steps to wedge across rung-0 runs are now 29 / 75 / 33 / **93**.

### Reversal: T1 (NCCL only) runs before T2 (NGC image)

I previously argued T2 first, on the grounds that `nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:26.07-py3` ships
**NCCL 2.30.7** — exactly T1's target — making T2 a superset of T1. **That argument was wrong**,
and thanks to @mcwitt for catching why.

Reading the image config blob from the registry rather than the docs:

```
jax    0.10.2.dev20260630+3757395a28   /opt/jax
jaxlib 0.10.2.dev20260725              /opt/jaxlibs
NCCL 2.30.7 | CUDA 13.3.1 | cuDNN 9.24.0.43 | driver req 610.43.02 (fleet is 595.71.05)
```

Our pins are jax/jaxlib **0.11.0**, so T2 moves the jax frontend *backwards*.

The decisive question was #7421: does 26.07 carry the CUBIN loader fix
([openxla/xla@a2905046](https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/a2905046b82902af5ddc2c53a0cb7a6efc8aee2e),
**19 July 2026**, [PR #45914](https://github.com/openxla/xla/pull/45914))? An earlier
investigation ruled out **26.06** for exactly this reason. @mcwitt raised it; it turns out to
apply to 26.07 as well.

**It does not. T2 on this image is not viable.** A one-task `--no-sync` probe under
`nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:26.07-py3` read the source directly:

```
/opt/xla/xla/stream_executor/cuda/cuda_executor.cc
  228:      cuModuleLoadFatBinary(&module, cubin_bytes),      <- still the UNFIXED API

/opt/xla HEAD = 64f6bb7ce168ab89a402add54fe2395e39901132
                2026-07-07T02:36:18-07:00                     <- 12 days BEFORE the fix
git merge-base --is-ancestor a2905046 HEAD  ->  FIX_ABSENT
```

That is the exact line the fix changes, still calling `cuModuleLoadFatBinary` on raw per-fusion
CUBIN bytes — precisely the mismatch #7421 documents. Running T2 here would reintroduce the CUBIN
load failure, and any outcome would be uninterpretable.

⚠️ **Two traps for anyone repeating this check.**

1. **The public JAX-Toolbox manifest is stale and will mislead you.** `26.07-devel` on GitHub
   pins XLA at `6de79c2c` (dated **2024-03-16**) and jax at `8f4658ec` (`_version = "0.4.26"`).
   Both declare `tracking_ref: main, mode: git-clone`, so `latest_verified_commit` is only what
   CI last verified — not what shipped. The **in-image** manifest at `/opt/manifest.d/manifest.yaml`
   carries entirely different commits (`xla 15fb18f9`, `jax 7e24325e`), and the checked-out
   `/opt/xla` HEAD differs from both. Only the source in the image is authoritative.
2. **Do not infer from the version string.** jaxlib reports `0.10.2.dev20260725` and
   `BUILD_DATE=2026-07-24`, both *after* 19 July — which is what led me to guess the fix was
   present. The dev-date reflects the build, not the XLA checkout, and the checkout was 07-07.

T2 is therefore parked until an NGC image built after 2026-07-19 exists (26.08+), or we build a
custom one. Independent of the loader question, T2 was always multi-variable: NCCL **and** CUDA
13.0 → 13.3 **and** cuDNN 9.19 → 9.24 **and** the jax frontend **and** the userspace CUDA driver
(the image wants 610.43.02 against the fleet's 595.71.05, so it runs through forward-compat).

One useful thing the smokes did settle: `ngcsmoke4` reached `train_step` under jax `0.10.2.dev`,
so levanter's explicit-sharding APIs (`from jax import P`, `reshard`, `AxisType`,
`get_abstract_mesh`) are compatible there. That was the main unverified porting risk, and it is
now retired for whenever T2 is revived.

T1 has none of that, and it is now mechanism-motivated rather than a blind version bump — see
[the launch-order note](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5195777029):
`NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT`, which targets the documented multi-communicator launch-order
deadlock, is a 2.30 feature we do not have at 2.28.9.

**T1 is genuinely single-variable.** `uv lock --upgrade-package nvidia-nccl-cu13` churns the
lock with alternate resolutions for other extras, but the diff of what the GPU extra actually
installs is one line, 269 packages before and after:

```diff
- nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.28.9 ; sys_platform == 'linux'
+ nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7 ; sys_platform == 'linux'
```

(The earlier "bumping NCCL drags torch, +265/−39" warning was about the **cu12** package. jax
uses **cu13**, and that one is clean.)

### T1 result: NEGATIVE — NCCL 2.30.7 still wedges

`moe-hero-fsdp-10rack-t1nccl-20260805`, 10 racks, rung 0, identical to the control except for
that one lock line. **It wedged at step 21**, ~8 min in.

| check | result |
|---|---|
| job state | `running`, `failures=0`, `160/160` alive, ~46 min silent |
| GPU utilization / power (rank 0, all 4) | **100 %** at **229–261 W** of 1200 W, SM 1950 MHz |
| `ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` / shutdown barrier | none |
| **loaded** library | `/uv/cache/archive-v0/…/nvidia/nccl/lib/libnccl.so.2` |
| **installed** wheel | `nvidia-nccl-cu13 == 2.30.7` |

The provenance check matters here: an ablation that silently fails to take effect looks exactly
like a negative. Both the wheel metadata *and* the library actually mapped into the process
confirm 2.30.7.

**This result does not need the 4.5 h stop rule.** The rule exists to protect against calling a
*null* too early. This is a **positive observation of the failure** under the new NCCL, well
inside the control's window (control wedged at step 93 / 8:42). Steps to wedge at rung 0 are now
29 / 75 / 33 / 93 / **21**.

**NCCL version is excluded as the cause of #7344.**

### N2 is the live thread T1 created

NCCL 2.30.7 ships the launch-order mitigation but **does not enable it**. From the 2.30.7 source
(`src/enqueue.cc`):

```c
NCCL_PARAM(LaunchOrderImplicit, "LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT", 0)   // default 0 = OFF
```

So T1 delivered the fix without activating it, and the multi-communicator launch-order hypothesis
is **still untested**. `moe-hero-fsdp-10rack-n2launchorder-20260805` is now running: same 2.30.7
lock, same rung 0, same 10 racks, plus `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` (the `NCCL_` prefix is
already forwarded to tasks by `experiments/grug/dispatch.py`). One env var against a control that
wedged twice today.

If N2 also wedges, the whole NCCL version/launch-order axis is closed, and the surviving
hypothesis space is the **driver**, the **fabric**, and **`cuda_async`** — at which point the
Xid/DCGM telemetry request in this issue becomes the highest-value outstanding item, and it is
blocked on cluster ops rather than on GPU time.

### T2 is not abandoned, but it is blocked on packaging

Two real defects found by 1-rack smokes, both in the bring-your-own-image overlay rather than in
CUDA (tracking issue for the image itself is #7519):

1. **`uv export` drops index metadata.** `resiliparse==0.17.2` is pinned to the chatnoir index
   (`lib/marin/pyproject.toml:205`); the bare requirement resolved only against PyPI, which
   carries the *name* but not that version → "unsatisfiable". Fixed by re-emitting every
   `[[tool.uv.index]]` url as `--extra-index-url` plus `--index-strategy unsafe-best-match`
   (required — the default first-index strategy stops at the first index carrying the name).
2. **torch cannot be dropped, and cannot be CPU-only.** rung 0's `sonic_cute` imports quack, and
   `quack/cute_dsl_utils.py:109` calls `torch.cuda.get_device_capability(device)` — torch is used
   *only* to query compute capability, but it must be a CUDA build. With torch absent, `import
   torch` resolved to a stray `nvidia_cutlass_dsl/.../base_dsl/torch.py` on the image's path; with
   CPU torch, it fails `Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled`. Installing a CUDA torch would drag
   `nvidia-*` wheels whose lib dirs jax's plugin prepends — silently shadowing the image's CUDA
   and NCCL, i.e. destroying the very thing T2 measures.

The overlay's hard gate now asserts jax/jaxlib resolve from the image, torch resolves from the
venv with `torch.version.cuda is None`, and `import quack.dsl` succeeds — so these fail in ~2 min
at setup instead of after a full startup.

Cleanest way out when T2 is revisited: run it at **rung 1** (`attn=reference`, `moe=scatter`,
`expert_chunks=1`), which imports no quack at all (`_moe/__init__.py` is empty; quack is imported
only by `sonic_cute.py`). Rung 1 wedges 2/2, and it is the rung that already excluded the
CuTe/QuACK kernels — so nothing is lost by testing the toolchain there.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Correction: `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT` is available in 2.28.9, not new in 2.30

I stated in
[comment 5195777029](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5195777029)
that `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT` is "a 2.30 feature we do not have at 2.28.9", and in
[comment 5196613173](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5196613173)
that "NCCL 2.30.7 ships the launch-order mitigation but does not enable it."

**Both are wrong.** The knob is **since 2.26** and is present, default-off, in the version we
were already running. Checked against the NCCL source at both tags:

```c
v2.28.9-1  src/enqueue.cc:  NCCL_PARAM(LaunchOrderImplicit, "LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT", 0)
v2.30.7-1  src/enqueue.cc:  NCCL_PARAM(LaunchOrderImplicit, "LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT", 0)
```

The 2.26-vs-2.30 ambiguity I flagged earlier resolves to **2.26**; the env-var page's "(since
2.26)" heading is correct and my reading of it as 2.30 was the error.

### What the knob actually does

From the NCCL user guide, verbatim:

> Implicitly order NCCL operations from different communicators on the same device using the host
> program order. This ensures the operations will not deadlock. When the CUDA runtime and driver
> are 12.3+, overlapped execution is permitted. On older CUDA versions the operations will be
> serialized.

So it imposes a consistent global ordering on operations issued from **different communicators on
the same device** — exactly the deadlock precondition documented on the communicators page. We
are on CUDA 13, so it permits overlapped execution rather than serializing; the performance cost
should be small.

### What this changes

1. **T1's stated motivation was wrong.** I promoted T1 from "blind version bump" to
   "mechanism-motivated" on the false premise that 2.30 introduces this knob. T1's **result** is
   unaffected — the wedge at step 21 with 2.30.7 verified both as the installed wheel and as the
   library mapped into the process is an empirical observation. The sound reason to run T1 before
   T2 was the #7421 loader regression in the NGC image, which held up.
2. **N2 becomes more valuable.** If `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` suppresses the wedge, the fix
   is one environment variable on the **current pinned stack** — no dependency bump, no image
   change, immediately deployable.
3. **N2 is running on the 2.30.7 lock.** That is controlled rather than ideal: T1 established
   that 2.30.7 wedges identically to 2.28.9, so it is a proven-neutral background and N2-vs-T1
   isolates the env var. If N2 comes back positive, the follow-up is to confirm on stock 2.28.9,
   which is the configuration that yields the deployable one-line fix.

### Related knob worth checking

The same doc page lists **`NCCL_LAUNCH_RACE_FATAL`** (since 2.26, **default 1 = enabled**):

> Attempt to catch host threads racing to launch to the same device and if so return a fatal
> error. Such a race would violate the determinacy of the program order relied upon by
> `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT`.

If that check is genuinely active in our runs and has never fired, it is weak evidence against a
host-thread launch race specifically. I could not find its `NCCL_PARAM` in `src/enqueue.cc` at
either tag, so I do not yet know where it is defined or whether it is live on this path —
recording it as a lead, not as evidence.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## N2 negative: `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` does not prevent the wedge

`moe-hero-fsdp-10rack-n2launchorder-20260805` — 10 racks, rung 0, NCCL 2.30.7, plus
`NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1`. **Wedged at step 154.**

```
19:55:54  step  67   1.5 s/it   loss 9.37
19:56:55  step 108   1.4 s/it   loss 7.93
19:57:55  step 154   1.3 s/it   loss 6.77   <- last line
[silence]
```

| check | result |
|---|---|
| job state | `running`, `failures=0`, `160/160` alive |
| GPU utilization / power (rank 0, all 4) | **100 %** at **229–262 W** of 1200 W, SM 1950 MHz |
| `ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` / shutdown barrier | none |
| flag reached the process | `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` read back from `/proc/<pid>/environ` |

The provenance line matters as much as the result: an env var that never arrives looks exactly
like a negative. It arrived.

**Step 154 is the highest count yet but is not evidence of improvement.** Steps-to-wedge at rung
0 are now 29 / 75 / 33 / 93 / 21 / **154** — the spread is far too wide for one draw to mean
anything, and on the wall-clock axis it wedged at ~8:5x elapsed, indistinguishable from the
control's 8:42. I briefly read the step count as encouraging while it was still running;
@mcwitt spotted the wedge in the power trend first, and the power trace is the better signal.

### Combined with T1, the NCCL axis is closed

| rung | change | result |
|---|---|---|
| control | — | wedges (step 93) |
| T1 | NCCL 2.28.9 → **2.30.7** | wedges (step 21) |
| N2 | 2.30.7 + `LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` | wedges (step 154) |

Neither the NCCL version nor the documented multi-communicator launch-order mitigation prevents
the wedge. `uv.lock` has been reverted to stock 2.28.9.

### N3: the one remaining reading of the launch-order hypothesis

There is a precondition on that flag which we do **not** satisfy, and it is the reason N2 is not
yet a clean refutation of the underlying mechanism. From NCCL's `communicators.rst`:

> As of 2.26, NCCL introduces `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT` which when enabled implicitly creates
> this order dynamically by following the order operations are issued from the host. **Thus to
> remain deadlock free, users must ensure the order of host-side launches matches for all
> devices. This is most easily accomplished by using a deterministic order issued from a single
> host thread per-device.**

We run **one process driving four devices**. Thread census on the live wedged process (1086
threads):

```
531 python           143 tf_XLAEigen        4 py_xla_cleanup     4 cuda-EvtHandlr
144 tokio-rt-worker   34 py_xla_execute     4 py_xla_callback
```

`py_xla_callback` and `py_xla_cleanup` are 4 — one per device, as XLA's `LocalDeviceState`
constructor implies (`xla/pjrt/se/local_device_state.cc` creates one `WorkerThread` each for
`py_xla_execute`, `py_xla_callback`, `py_xla_cleanup` per device). But **`py_xla_execute` is 34,
not 4**. I cannot reconcile that from source — the file has moved in XLA main and is newer than
our jaxlib 0.11.0 — so **one-launch-thread-per-device is not something we can assume**, and N2
may have failed because the flag's precondition was unmet rather than because the mechanism is
wrong.

`moe-hero-fsdp-10rack-n3procdev-20260805` is now running: `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 4`
(one process per GPU) **plus** `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1`.

⚠️ **To be precise about what NCCL does and does not say here**, since it is easy to overstate:

* NCCL publishes **no general preference** for one process per GPU. Searching the 2.30.7 user
  guide for `recommend|discourag|deprecat` turns up only advice about distributing
  `ncclUniqueId`s evenly. The layouts are presented as neutral alternatives — "Single Process,
  Single Thread, Multiple Devices", "One Device per Process **or Thread**", and "You can combine
  both multiple process or threads and multiple device per process or thread."
* The single-per-device guidance appears **once**, scoped to the launch-ordering precondition
  above, and it asks for a single host **thread** per device — not a single **process**.

So N3 is a *sufficient* way to guarantee that thread property, not the thing the docs ask for. A
single process with four dedicated per-device launch threads would satisfy it equally well. The
lighter check that could have made N3 unnecessary is thread attribution on a live process —
determining whether 4 of those 34 `py_xla_execute` threads are the per-device `execute_thread_`
and the rest are unrelated, in which case the precondition already holds.

The logical program is unchanged, which is what makes this a controlled ablation rather than a
new experiment. iris stamps global rank = `task_index * nproc + local`
(`iris/hooks/multigpu_main.py`), so node *t* owns ranks `4t..4t+3`, nodes 0–15 own ranks 0–63,
and `jax.devices()` — ordered by process index — still places exactly one rack in
`replica_dcn=0`. Mesh stays `(replica_dcn=10, data=64, expert=1, model=1)`; batch sharding is
untouched. What changes is 640 JAX clients instead of 160, and with them per-process memory
fraction, host scheduling, and the compilation cache key — declared, not free.

This run is also the first on `origin/main` since the watchdog work landed (#7950, #7951, #7959),
so it collects persisted NCCL RAS telemetry for the wedge window.

### If N3 also wedges

The launch-order hypothesis is exhausted and the surviving space is the **driver**, the
**fabric**, and **`cuda_async`** (never ablated in either wedging program). At that point the
Xid/DCGM telemetry request in this issue becomes the highest-value item outstanding, and it is
blocked on cluster ops rather than on GPU time.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## N3 POSITIVE: one process per GPU ran 1710 steps clean — and NVIDIA documents this exact hazard

`moe-hero-fsdp-10rack-n3procdev-20260805` — 10 racks, rung 0, `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 4`
(one process per GPU instead of one process driving all four), plus
`NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1`, on `origin/main` `ab5b42e91`. **It did not wedge.**

```
21:04:19  step 1.71k   1.3 s/it   loss 2.63   elapsed 55:46   (killed here, healthy)
```

Steps to wedge at rung 0 across every prior run: **29 / 75 / 33 / 93 / 21 / 154**. N3 ran to
**1710** and was still at 1.3 s/it with all 640 ranks healthy when I stopped it. That is ~11x
the longest prior survival.

**This is one draw, and I want to be explicit about what it is worth.** By the rank test the
p-value for "N3 is drawn from the same distribution as the six wedging runs" is
1/(6+1) = **0.143**. Suggestive, not significant. The replicate is queued (see below) and
takes it to 1/C(8,2) = 0.036.

### The mechanism NVIDIA documents, and it names our exact configuration

NVIDIA's JAX performance guide —
[JAX-Toolbox/docs/GPU_performance.md](https://github.com/NVIDIA/JAX-Toolbox/blob/main/docs/GPU_performance.md)
(L225-230), in a section reached from its **Blackwell** tuning chapter:

> ### Debugging Hangs in 1-process-multiple-device set-up
> If using 1 process to manage multiple devices in a node, hangs can happen when a
> process-wide synchronizing CUDA API such as `cudaFree` is called at the same time a
> collective is running across multiple devices within the same process.
> The following remedy steps can be taken to workaround such cases:
> - Set `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP` in the environment.
> - **Change the JAX program to bind 1 process to a single device instead of managing multiple
>   devices.**

And in the same file's troubleshooting index (L35-36):

> **Multi-device single-process hangs** — Consider `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP` or one process per
> device

Three things make this the strongest candidate we have had:

1. **It is a liveness claim, not a performance preference**, and it is scoped to precisely the
   layout we shipped: one process, four GB200s.
2. **N3 is the second remedy on that list**, run for unrelated reasons (the
   `LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT` thread-precondition argument). We appear to have stumbled onto a
   documented fix from the wrong direction.
3. **It survives the test that killed the other candidate.** A neighbouring hypothesis from
   #6979 — TE's FFI serializing execution threads in single-controller multi-device — is
   refuted for #7344 by our own ladder: **rung 1 wedged 2/2** with `attn=reference,
   moe=scatter`, which invokes no tvm-FFI/CuTe path at all (FFI in grug is confined to
   `_moe/quack_moe_cute.py` and `attention/_fa4_cute_kernels.py`; `fa4_cute_segment_bounds`,
   the one function called unconditionally at `model.py:976`, is pure jnp). The `cudaFree`
   mechanism does **not** care — rung 1 still allocates and frees.

That third point also **promotes the `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR` ablation**, which has been
sitting unrun in this investigation. We run `cuda_async`. The allocator is exactly what decides
whether frees go through a process-wide synchronizing `cudaFree` or a stream-ordered
`cudaFreeAsync`, so it sits on the same mechanism axis rather than being the independent long
shot I had it filed as.

### `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP` is the cheap discriminator, and it is live in our build

I checked this against the NCCL source at both tags we run rather than trusting the docs:

```
v2.28.9-1  src/group.cc:263   bool useBarrier = ncclParamLaunchMode == ncclLaunchModeGroup;
v2.30.7-1  src/group.cc:313   bool useBarrier = ncclParamLaunchMode == ncclLaunchModeGroup;
```

`useBarrier` gates `ncclCommIntraBarrierIn(comm, 1)` inside `doLaunches()`, whose outer loop
iterates over **cliques of comms sharing the same `intraComm0`** — i.e. sibling communicators
*within one process*. So GROUP mode inserts an intra-process launch barrier across exactly the
devices our layout puts in one process. It is not a vestigial knob and it is honored at 2.28.9.

That makes it a **one-env-var test on the shipped layout**, against a control that wedges in
8-10 minutes. If it suppresses the wedge it confirms the mechanism *and* yields a deployable fix
with no 640-process migration. Queued.

### Correction: `NCCL_LAUNCH_RACE_FATAL` — where it lives and what its silence means

In [an earlier comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5196638965)
I flagged that I could not find this param's definition in `src/enqueue.cc` and was therefore
recording it as a lead rather than evidence. Found it — it is in a different file:

```
v2.28.9-1  src/misc/strongstream.cc:158   NCCL_PARAM(LaunchRaceFatal, "LAUNCH_RACE_FATAL", 1)
v2.30.7-1  src/misc/strongstream.cc:156   NCCL_PARAM(LaunchRaceFatal, "LAUNCH_RACE_FATAL", 1)
```

Default **1**, so it has been armed in every run. `ncclStrongStreamRelease` checks it on two
branches, and the distinction matters for us:

* `graph.graphId == ULLONG_MAX` (**not** capturing) -> `strongstream.cc:282`, compares
  `ss->liveAcquiredBy` against the calling thread.
* capturing -> `strongstream.cc:344`, compares `cap->acquiredBy`.

We run with `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=` (disabled for #5675), so XLA is not capturing
graphs and **the live branch for us is 282** — the detector is genuinely active, not inert.
Both branches sit under `mixing = ncclParamGraphMixingSupport()`, default 1.

So its silence is real but **narrow**: it detects a *different host thread* releasing a
per-device strong stream than acquired it — a same-device host-thread race. It says nothing
about divergent *inter-rank* enqueue order, which is the ordering hypothesis that actually
matters here (the nccl#1772 / Megatron-LM#1810 shape). Weak evidence against the crudest
reading, no evidence either way on the real one.

### A performance note that cuts against my prior assumption

I had assumed one-process-per-GPU would cost us NCCL's `P2P_DIRECT` intra-node zero-copy path.
That is obsolete: it was generalized into cross-process
[user buffer registration](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/usage/bufferreg.html)
in 2.23/2.24. The sign actually flips — from `src/init.cc` (L1096-1109 on master):

```c
if (comm->nvlsRegSupport) {
  for (int j = i + 1; j < nranks; j++) {
    if (comm->peerInfo[i].hostHash == comm->peerInfo[j].hostHash &&
        comm->peerInfo[i].pidHash == comm->peerInfo[j].pidHash) {
      comm->nvlsRegSupport = 0;   // ANY two ranks sharing a PID -> NVLS registration off
      break;
```

If any two ranks in a communicator share a PID, NCCL disables NVLS (NVLink SHARP) buffer
registration **for the whole communicator**. The same gate drives a symmetric-memory fallback
(`symmetric_sched.cc`), and `NCCL_GRAPH_REGISTER` is documented as effective only when there is
"at most one GPU per process". So the shipped layout has been silently forfeiting NVLS on
GB200. The undocumented escape hatch is `NCCL_SINGLE_PROC_MEM_REG_ENABLE`.

No apples-to-apples benchmark of the two layouts exists publicly, so I am not claiming a
throughput win — only that the expected cost of switching is smaller than I previously stated
here, and may be negative.

### Public corpus: this signature is not reported anywhere at our scale

A sweep of jax-ml/jax, openxla/xla, NVIDIA/JAX-Toolbox, NVIDIA/nccl, pytorch, Megatron-LM,
vLLM, SGLang and the NVIDIA developer forums found **no public artifact combining** hundreds of
GPUs + spontaneous mid-run silent wedge + all ranks alive at `failures=0` + ~100% SM at ~20-25%
power + run-to-run non-determinism. This issue is currently the best-documented public instance.

Closest partial matches, none complete:

| report | scale | matches | fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| [NeMo#9291](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/NeMo/issues/9291) | 32x H100 | titled "hangs... low power consumption and 100% GPU utilization"; ~100 W/700 W | PyTorch; fixed step; closed stale, never root-caused |
| [Megatron-LM#1810](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/issues/1810) | **128 nodes** | "tiny host/GPU timing differences cause different enqueue orders across ranks"; silent; doesn't repro small | no power telemetry; config-sensitive not random |
| [nccl#1772](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl/issues/1772) | 16 GPUs | **XLA/JAX at our exact layout** (one process per host, thread per device, multi-comm per device); H100/B200 only | 16 GPUs; NVIDIA reproduced it, then it went irreproducible. Unresolved |
| [openxla/xla#7716](https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/7716) | — | per-process independent compilation -> "different ordering of collectives in the schedule" -> deadlock | deadlocks on *first* execution, not mid-run |

Worth recording that NVIDIA's own
[DGX GB200 NVL72 known issues](https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgxgb200nvl72-release-notes/known-issues.html)
states: *"2+ domain NCCL All-to-All testing may result in system hangs or deadlocks with no
error codes"*, with no workaround and a fix planned via "atomic locks... to prevent the race
condition."

⚠️ One source I cited to myself and am downgrading before anyone leans on it:
[vllm#48720](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48720), which supplies a useful Type A
(ranks spread across *different* collective counts while per-step counters sit frozen and equal)
vs Type B (all ranks in the *same* collective) discriminator via NCCL RAS. It is an individual's
open RFC validated on **4x DGX Spark GB10 at TP=4**, inference not training — the RAS
methodology is worth borrowing, the scale is not corroboration.

### Running now

`moe-hero-fsdp-10rack-ctrlnew-20260805`: `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 1`, **no** LOI, same
`origin/main` `ab5b42e91`, rung 0. N3 changed both the layout and the code base — the rebase
brought 32 commits including the watchdog work (#7950, #7951, #7959) — so this holds the layout
at the shipped value on the new code to kill the confound. If it wedges in the usual 8-10
minutes, the rebase is excluded and the layout is the live variable.

Then, in cost order:

1. **layout without LOI** (`= 4`, no flag) — splits layout from launch-order *and* serves as the
   N3 replicate, taking p from 0.143 to 0.036.
2. **`NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP`** on the shipped layout — the documented remedy that needs no
   migration.
3. **`XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=bfc`** — now on-mechanism rather than a long shot.
