comments.body:
### Correction to the comment above: `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP` is deprecated

I described GROUP as yielding "a deployable fix with no 640-process migration." **Withdraw the
"deployable" half.** Reading NCCL's own env docs rather than only the JAX-Toolbox guide:

```
v2.30.7-1  docs/userguide/source/env.rst:964
  NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE  (since 2.1.0)
  ...
  Setting is to GROUP will use cooperative groups (CUDA 9.0 and later) for processes
  managing more than one GPU.
  This is deprecated in 2.9 and may be removed in future versions.
```

So NVIDIA's JAX performance guide is recommending a knob NVIDIA's NCCL documentation deprecated
at 2.9. Both statements are current; they are simply inconsistent. The code path *is* still live
at both our tags (`src/group.cc:263` / `:313`, verified above), so the experiment is valid — but
it should not be shipped.

This does not change the plan, only the labels on it:

* **GROUP stays queued as a mechanism probe, not a candidate fix.** It is the sharper of the two
  tests: one env var on the shipped layout, isolating the `cudaFree`-vs-in-flight-collective
  race specifically, where process-per-GPU changes launch scheduling, communicator topology,
  memory fraction and the compile cache key simultaneously. A GROUP positive tells us *why* N3
  worked; a GROUP negative says N3's mechanism is something other than the documented one, which
  matters for predicting whether it holds at 12+ racks.
* **Process-per-GPU is the fix to ship** if the discrimination sequence holds it up — it is
  what JAX recommends, what every NVIDIA SLURM recipe in JAX-Toolbox uses, what the JAX-Toolbox
  container asserts (`assert(len(jax.local_devices()) == 1)`), and it removes the precondition
  rather than synchronizing around it. GROUP buys ordering with a barrier
  (`useBarrier` -> `ncclCommIntraBarrierIn` in `doLaunches()`), so it costs throughput by
  construction; the layout change instead *recovers* NVLS registration per the `src/init.cc`
  PID gate quoted above.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## The control wedges: 48 layers on current `main`, shipped layout, zero diff — plus four corrections

`moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-ctrl48b-20260806` ([wandb](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-ctrl48b-20260806)) — commit `ae5c93e70`, **byte-identical to stock `main`**, 48 layers, 8 racks / 128 nodes / 512 GPUs, `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 1` (the shipped layout). No ablation, no flags, nothing removed.

**It wedged twice.**

```
attempt 1   step 9 @ 01:31:39 -> step 33 @ 01:38:58    then silent; gang restarted ~02:02
attempt 2   step 1 @ 02:04:55 -> step 17 @ 02:11:43    then silent 36+ min -> wedge captured
```

(The job restarted itself in place because `experiments/grug/dispatch.py` sets `max_retries_failure=3`. That resets the step counter to 1 under the same job ID and run name — worth knowing, because it makes a wedge look like a slow run in wandb. The `Step 1 is less than the current step 34. Cowardly refusing to log metrics.` warning is the fingerprint.)

### Power: wedge signature on four racks

Tasks 0 / 16 / 64 / 112 — four different racks — at 02:47:40–47:

```
task0    100 %  262.88 / 244.55 / 240.09 / 261.16 W   all 1950 MHz
task16   100 %  243.95 / 232.34 / 241.05 / 268.84 W   all 1950 MHz
task64   100 %  276.81 / 252.41 / 251.59 / 280.27 W   all 1950 MHz
task112  100 %  262.64 / 235.22 / 245.43 / 269.83 W   all 1950 MHz
```

Re-sampling task0 63 s later gives 262.80 / 244.41 / 240.62 / 261.24 W — **sub-watt drift, power frozen, clocks pinned**. Healthy compute on this same run 55 minutes earlier was 900–1110 W with clocks swinging 1297–1950 MHz. ~20 % of working power with the clock pinned is a resident kernel spinning, not computing. No task at 0 % util, so this is not PGLE straggler skew.

### GPU health at wedge time: clean

```
ecc.errors.uncorrected.volatile.total    0
ecc.errors.uncorrected.aggregate.total   0
remapped_rows.pending / .failure         No / No
clocks_event_reasons.hw_slowdown         Not Active
```

No ECC events, no row remapping, no thermal or power throttle. Nothing NVML can see is wrong. (Separate comment follows with the Xid/DCGM request to cluster ops — NVML never exposes Xid, and `dmesg` is blocked in the container.)

### RAS: the same structured one-rack desync, on a new rack

```
Group  Comms  Nodes  Ranks/node  Ranks/comm  Status   Errors
    0      1    128           4         512   RUNNING  MISMATCH
    1      4    128           1         128   RUNNING  OK
    2      8     16           4          64   RUNNING  OK
    3     64      8           1           8   RUNNING  MISMATCH

#0-0 MISMATCH  Communicator ranks have different AllReduce operation counts
  448 ranks have launched up to operation 3068
   64 ranks have launched up to operation 3066
  lagging = ranks 384-447 = replica_dcn 6 = RACK 6, subnet 10.186.211.x
```

64 ranks is exactly one rack. Group 3 (replica comms) also mismatched; group 2 (data axis) OK — the desync is **across** racks, not within. Structurally identical to the per-GPU capture, on the opposite process layout.

### The lagging rack varies — the rank-0-role hypothesis is dead

| run | layout | lagging rack | subnet |
|---|---|---|---|
| `oldbaseB` | shipped | rack 5 | `10.186.210.0/24` |
| `procgpu2` | per-GPU | rack 0 | `10.186.213.x` |
| `ctrl48b` | shipped | **rack 6** | `10.186.211.x` |

Three trials, three different racks. It is not about rank 0's wandb/tqdm/checkpoint duties. This matches #7956's four different faulting nodes.

Note also the failure is **host-side**: the lagging rack stopped *launching* operations. It did not fail inside a collective — it stopped issuing them while every rank stayed alive.

---

## Corrections

**1. Per-GPU layout does NOT fix the wedge.** [Comment 5197407315](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5197407315) reported N3 as "POSITIVE: one process per GPU ran 1710 steps clean." That result was at **rung 0 (`num_layers=1`)** and does not carry to the real model. At 48 layers, `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-procgpu2-20260805` with `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 4` **wedged at ~step 152**, with the same RAS structure shown above. Both layouts wedge. Layout is not the trigger.

**2. 48 layers on current `main` was never shown to be clean.** An earlier control (`ctrl48`) reached step 75 and I stopped it to free racks. That was **my premature kill, not a clean result** — and step 75 is far below the historical failure window for this config (steps 182 and 189 on `5e496b051`). It was never evidence of health, and should not be read as any. `ctrl48b` above then wedged at steps 33 and 17.

**2b. NVIDIA's documented multi-device-single-process hang is ruled out as our mechanism.** The [JAX-Toolbox GPU performance guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/jax-toolbox/performance-profiling/gpu-performance) describes exactly the hazard we had been chasing — *"hangs can happen when a process-wide synchronizing CUDA API such as cudaFree is called at the same time a collective is running across multiple devices"* — and prescribes two remedies: `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP`, **or one process per device**. We have now run the second remedy at 48 layers (`procgpu2`) and it wedged anyway. A documented hazard whose documented fix does not fix it is not the hazard we have. This is independent of the deprecation argument against `NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=GROUP`.

**3. The multi-communicator mechanism proposed in comment 5197407315 is undercut by its own census.** That comment offered NCCL multi-communicator launch ordering as the leading candidate, on the basis that the shipped layout creates 4 communicators per device against per-GPU's 3. But `procgpu2` wedged in an earlier run at step 3 when only **one** communicator existed. A mechanism requiring multiple concurrent communicators cannot explain a single-communicator wedge.

**4. `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` → BFC (candidate #19) is not on-mechanism.** I described it as testing NVIDIA's documented stream-ordered-allocator hazard. It does not: neither allocator calls `cudaFree` on the hot path, so the ablation does not exercise that hazard. It remains a legitimate toolchain variation, but it should not be ranked as mechanism-directed.

**5. Retracting a wedge call.** I called a step-3 stop on `8rack-layoutonly` a wedge from a single node's power reading, then killed it ~10 minutes in. `procgpu2` later ran past step 3 to 152 on that same config, so step 3 was not reproducible. That event is unclassified and should not be counted.

---

## An accidental NVLS ablation we already have

NCCL disables NVLS registration for a whole communicator if any two ranks share a PID (`src/init.cc` L1096-1109). So the two layouts we have been running differ in NVLS state for free:

| layout | ranks sharing a PID | NVLS | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| shipped (`processes_per_task=1`, 4 GPUs/proc) | yes | **off** | wedges |
| per-GPU (`processes_per_task=4`, 1 GPU/proc) | no | **on** | wedges |

Both wedge, so **NVLS is neither necessary nor sufficient**. No run needed to establish this; `NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE` can come off the candidate list.

## Next ablation running

`moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-affin1-20260806` — identical to the control above plus `NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY=1`.

Motivation, measured on the wedged control at 02:52 (lagging node task 96 / rack 6 vs healthy task 0 / rack 0):

```
34 NUMA nodes: node0 (cpus 0-71), node1 (cpus 72-143), + 32 CPU-less HBM nodes
Mems_allowed_list (pid 1):  0-1        -- cannot allocate onto HBM nodes at all
per-thread Cpus_allowed_list:
  task96 (lagging)   979 @ 0-143    24 @ 0-71    18 @ 72-143
  task0  (healthy)   995 @ 0-143    13 @ 0-71    29 @ 72-143
pinned threads are ALL XLA: py_xla_execute (34), py_xla_cleanup (4), py_xla_callback (4)
```

XLA NUMA-pins its own execute threads per Grace socket; NCCL's proxy threads are among the ~480 unpinned `python` threads spanning both sockets. NCCL's default (`NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY=0`) intersects the GPU-local CPU set with the process mask, and since that mask is all of `0-143` the intersection yields no effective pinning. Setting the flag to `1` makes NCCL pin to the GPU's NUMA node outright — despite the name.

This is a **host-side** ablation, chosen because RAS says the failure is host-side: the lagging rack stopped *launching* operations rather than failing inside one. Thanks to @ben.feuer for pointing at NUMA affinity on GH200/GB200. Note his specific mechanism — non-HBM-aware pinning placing host buffers in HBM — is ruled out here by `Mems_allowed_list: 0-1`.

ECC/row-remap/throttle are all clean at wedge time and NVML never exposes Xid, so this does not replace the Xid pull; see the following comment.

## What this changes

Wedges are landing **much earlier than assumed** — steps 17 and 33 here, against 152 / 182 / 189 previously. Any repro budget that assumed ~200 steps to failure was too conservative, and the full 48-layer hero is now a *cheap* reproduction vehicle rather than an expensive one. The rung-0 ladder was built to make the repro affordable; that premise is weaker than it was, and rung-0 results have now twice failed to predict 48-layer behaviour (N3 being the clearest case).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Request to cluster ops: Xid / DCGM data for the wedged racks on `cw-us-east-08a`

This is the one diagnostic we cannot self-serve from inside the job, and it is now the highest-value missing evidence. Details of the wedge itself are in the comment above.

### Why we can't get it ourselves

Verified from inside a running task on `cw-us-east-08a` (2026-08-06):

| source | result |
|---|---|
| `dmesg` | `Operation not permitted` — needs `CAP_SYSLOG` |
| `/dev/kmsg` | absent from the container |
| `dcgmi` | not installed in the task image |
| `nvidia-smi -q` | **no Xid section at all** — NVML does not expose Xid, by design |

What NVML *does* expose, we already sample at wedge time, and it is **clean**: `ecc.errors.uncorrected.volatile.total = 0`, `ecc.errors.uncorrected.aggregate.total = 0`, `remapped_rows.pending = No`, `remapped_rows.failure = No`, `clocks_event_reasons.hw_slowdown = Not Active`. So the failure is invisible to everything inside the container, which is precisely why the host-side log matters.

### The ask

For each window below, from the **host** (not the container):

1. **Xid errors** from the host kernel log for the listed nodes — `dmesg -T | grep -i xid`, or the equivalent from your log aggregation. Xid 13/31/43/45 (app faults), 48 (DBE), 62/63/64 (row remap), 74/79 (NVLink/GPU fallen off bus), and 119/120 (GSP RPC timeout) are all of interest; we would rather see the raw lines than a filtered set.
2. **DCGM health** for the same nodes/windows — `dcgmi health -g <group> -c`, plus NVLink error counters and any `DCGM_FI_DEV_*` retired-page or throttle fields.
3. **NVLink / NVSwitch fabric events** on those racks — link down/retrain, IMEX or fabric-manager errors, NVLink CRC/replay counters.
4. Anything the fabric manager or IMEX daemon logged in the window.

### Windows and nodes

**Wedge 1 — `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-ctrl48b-20260806`, rack 6.** Last forward progress `2026-08-06 02:11:43 UTC`; wedge confirmed still frozen at `02:47`–`02:53`; job killed `03:05`. The lagging rack was all 64 ranks on these 16 nodes (subnet `10.186.211.x`):

```
10.186.211.127  10.186.211.129  10.186.211.133  10.186.211.135
10.186.211.137  10.186.211.139  10.186.211.141  10.186.211.143
10.186.211.145  10.186.211.147  10.186.211.149  10.186.211.151
10.186.211.153  10.186.211.155  10.186.211.157  10.186.211.161
```

One hostname confirmed on that rack: `s44txs64` (`10.186.211.x`, task 96). For contrast, a *healthy* node in the same job at the same instant: `s2rsxs64` (task 0, rack 0).

**Wedge 2 — `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-procgpu2-20260805`, rack 0.** Wedge began ~`2026-08-06 00:50 UTC`, RAS captured `00:59`, job torn down `01:17`. Lagging rack on subnet `10.186.213.x`.

**Wedge 3 — `oldbaseB`, rack 5**, subnet `10.186.210.0/24`.

### Why this is worth the effort

The lagging rack is **different every time** — rack 5, rack 0, rack 6 across three trials — which rules out a role-specific software cause (it is not rank 0's logging/checkpoint duties) and matches the four different faulting nodes recorded in #7956. Every rank stays alive with `failures=0`; one rack simply stops launching collectives while the other seven spin. If there is a hardware or driver event behind this, it will be in the host log and nowhere else we can reach.

If it is easier to grant the capability than to pull the logs, `CAP_SYSLOG` on the task container (or shipping `dcgmi` in the image) would let us collect this ourselves at the moment of the next wedge, which is strictly better than a post-hoc pull — we currently have a reproduction that wedges within 20–40 minutes.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
### Amendment to correction 1 above: `procgpu2` refutes per-GPU *alone*, not the N3 pair

In [the previous comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5199932737) I wrote that the N3 result does not carry to the real model, citing `procgpu2` wedging at 48 layers with `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 4`. That is too strong, and @mcwitt caught it.

**N3 was two changes, not one.** [Comment 5197407315](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5197407315) records the config as `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 4` **plus `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1`**. `procgpu2` had only the first — its launch command carries no `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT`, and it ran NCCL 2.28.9.

So the state of the matrix at 48 layers on current `main` is:

| | no LOI | `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` |
|---|---|---|
| shipped layout | `ctrl48b` — **wedged** (steps 33, 17) | not run |
| per-GPU | `procgpu2` — **wedged** (~step 152) | **NOT RUN** ← this is N3's config |

And at rung 0 (`num_layers=1`, 10 racks):

| | no LOI | `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` |
|---|---|---|
| shipped layout | baseline — wedged | `N2` — **wedged** |
| per-GPU | `layoutonly` attempts — inconclusive | `N3` — **1710 steps clean** |

Both single ablations are independently falsified: LOI alone wedges (N2), and per-GPU alone wedges at 48 layers (`procgpu2`). So if N3's survival is real, it is an **interaction between the two**, and neither single-knob ablation could ever have detected it. My correction implied the pair had been tested. It has not.

What stands from the original correction: the claim that a rung-0 result predicts 48-layer behaviour is still unsupported, and **no configuration has been shown clean at 48 layers**. What I withdraw is the specific inference that `procgpu2` falsifies N3.

The caveat from the N3 comment also still stands and is worth repeating: it is **one draw**, rank-test p = 1/7 ≈ 0.143, and the replicate that would have taken it to 0.036 was never run. It may be a fluke. But it is the only configuration in this investigation that has ever survived a long run, and it has never been tried on the real model — so it is now queued at 48 layers / 8 racks.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## NUMA/CPU-affinity ablation: two trials, both censored by #7956 — plus a step-number coincidence worth flagging

Both attempts of `NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY=1` (otherwise identical to the `ctrl48b` control: stock `main` `ae5c93e70`, 48 layers, 8 racks, shipped layout) failed to reach a verdict. Reporting them as **no verdict**, not as evidence about the flag.

```
affin1  03:07 launch -> step 5
        03:17:14  task 98 dies: cudaFreeAsync failed to free ...
                  CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION   (InUse 65 MiB of a 138 GiB limit,
                  Free/Total 0/0 -- context already poisoned, the free is the messenger)
        03:17:15  reaches the JAX Shutdown barrier alone, 1/128
        03:22:15  barrier DEADLINE_EXCEEDED after 5 min -> all 128 aborted

affin2  05:06 launch -> step 5 @ 05:18:20, step 17 @ 05:19:26, then SILENT
        05:30:11  gang aborted on a shutdown barrier (so a rank exited ~05:25),
                  well before the watchdog's 1 h grace expired. Capture ran too
                  late -- tasks were already dead, so no power and no RAS.
```

### The one thing worth flagging

`affin2` went silent at **step 17** — the same step `ctrl48b` attempt 2 stopped at. Steps-to-wedge at 48 layers now read 33, 17, ~152, and (weakly) 17.

If step 17 recurs, that argues for a **deterministic trigger** — a PGLE recompile boundary, or a hook firing at a fixed step — rather than the random hazard model the wall-clock analysis in [comment 5184323726](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5184323726) supported. I am not claiming that yet on two occurrences, but it is now something to watch for explicitly rather than notice in hindsight.

### What the affinity data itself showed

Measured on the wedged `ctrl48b` control, comparing the RAS-identified lagging node against a healthy one:

```
34 NUMA nodes: node0 (cpus 0-71), node1 (cpus 72-143), + 32 CPU-LESS HBM nodes
Mems_allowed_list (pid 1):  0-1        -- cannot allocate onto HBM nodes at all
per-thread Cpus_allowed_list:
  lagging node   979 @ 0-143    24 @ 0-71    18 @ 72-143
  healthy node   995 @ 0-143    13 @ 0-71    29 @ 72-143
pinned threads are ALL XLA: py_xla_execute (34), py_xla_cleanup (4), py_xla_callback (4)
no NCCL-named threads exist; NCCL proxies sit among the ~480 unpinned "python" threads
```

**The originally-suggested mechanism is ruled out.** `Mems_allowed_list: 0-1` makes it structurally impossible for host allocations to land on the 32 HBM NUMA nodes, so "default pinning is not HBM aware" cannot be placing buffers there. Placement is balanced (N0 ~1.31M pages, N1 ~1.34M) and the lagging node is indistinguishable from the healthy one.

What the data *does* show is a split responsibility: XLA NUMA-pins its own execute threads per Grace socket, while NCCL's proxy threads run unpinned across all 144 CPUs and both sockets. NCCL's default intersects the GPU-local CPU set with the process mask, and since that mask is all of `0-143`, the intersection yields no effective pinning — which is why `NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY=1` (not `0`) is the knob that would actually pin them.

Thanks to Ben Feuer for the GH200/GB200 NUMA pointer that prompted this.

*Not a finding:* the pinned-thread split differs between the two nodes (24/18 vs 13/29). With n=1 per condition and no baseline for normal variation, that is noise.

### Correction to my own earlier reading

An earlier version of this measurement reported "no CPU affinity is applied at all." That was wrong — the per-thread aggregation had a parse bug returning an empty field for every thread, collapsing all masks into one bucket. XLA pinning was present the whole time.

The ablation is re-queued rather than retired; two censorings are bad luck, not a fundamental blocker.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Tooling: we can dump a wedged rank's Python stack on demand — `py-spy` is already in every task

This unblocks the diagnostic this investigation has been missing. RAS tells us the wedge is **host-side** (the lagging rack stops *launching* collectives while every rank stays alive), but we have never seen where that rank's main thread is actually stuck.

**`$IRIS_VENV/bin/py-spy` is installed in every task** by the iris runtime setup script — it has been there the whole time, mentioned only in passing as "the profiler's py-spy probe". So there is no need to keep a wedged job alive for an hour waiting for the progress watchdog's diagnostic thread (which cannot fire before `training_start + 1 h`, because of the startup grace added in #8006).

```bash
iris --cluster=marin task exec "$TRAIN/$TASK" --timeout 300 -- bash -c '
  PYSPY="$IRIS_VENV/bin/py-spy"
  for d in /proc/[0-9]*; do
    tr "\0" " " < "$d/cmdline" 2>/dev/null | grep -q "_callable_runner.py" && echo "${d#/proc/}"
  done | while read p; do echo "== pid $p =="; "$PYSPY" dump --pid "$p"; done'
```

Layout note: with `processes_per_task=4`, pid 1 is `iris.hooks.multigpu_main` and the trainers are its children, so scan `/proc` for `_callable_runner.py` rather than dumping pid 1. With `processes_per_task=1`, pid 1 *is* the trainer.

Verified against a healthy run:

```
Process 815: python -u /app/_callable_runner.py
Thread 815 (active): "MainThread"
    _run_grug_local (experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py:593)
    <module> (_callable_runner.py:40)
```

Main thread **active** inside the `train_step` dispatch. At a wedge, run this on a task in the RAS-identified lagging rack *and* on a healthy rack for contrast. Whether the lagging main thread sits inside a collective or is blocked materialising a device value distinguishes **"stuck in NCCL"** from **"the host never issued the next op"** — different root causes, and we currently cannot tell them apart.

## Measurement: the `compute_watch` step costs ~90 s, once

`WatchConfig(interval=20)` makes step 20 the first iteration with `compute_watch=True`. That is a **second executable** (its own compilation, and its own PGLE profiling target) which computes per-parameter norms over grads and params for a 359B model with `split_scan_layers`.

In-log rate series from a healthy 8-rack run:

```
05:52:54  step 17   19.2 s/it
05:55:47  step 21   48.4 s/it   <- 173 s for 4 steps vs ~77 s steady
05:56:47  step 24   29.6
05:59:23  step 32   20.1
06:01:59  step 40   19.4        <- no spike
06:08:18  step 60   18.6        <- no spike
06:13:21  step 75   22.3
```

So step 20 costs roughly **+90 s over the steady rate, exactly once**. Steps 40 and 60 are ordinary. That makes it a one-time compile/profile of the watch executable, not a recurring watch computation.

### A hypothesis I raised and then falsified — recording it so nobody re-runs it

I noticed that the last *logged* step before each known wedge sits just below a multiple of 20 (`ctrl48b` attempt 2 → 17, attempt 1 → 33, `procgpu2` → 152) and hypothesised that wedges cluster on `compute_watch` steps. `tqdm_loggable` emits on a ~75-80 s timer — about every 4 steps at this rate — so a stall just after a multiple of 20 would present exactly like that.

**The rate series above kills it.** Since only step 20 is special and 40/160 are ordinary steps, `ctrl48b` attempt 1 (~40) and `procgpu2` (~160) cannot be watch events. Only attempt 2 (~20) could be, and one point is nothing.

Two methodological notes that cost me time and may save someone else's:

- **`tqdm` step numbers are timer-sampled, not per-step.** "Wedged at step 17" only means 17 was the last line emitted before silence; the true stall is somewhere in ~17-21. Do not build step-number arguments on logged values without checking the emit cadence.
- **Log silence is not evidence of a wedge.** `iris job logs` on a 128-task gang lags by minutes. A run can look silent for 5+ minutes while computing normally. Confirm with power every time: healthy compute is 700-1150 W with clocks *varying*; the wedge signature is 237-280 W with clocks pinned at 1950 and power frozen to sub-watt between samples. That check has caught three false alarms of mine tonight.

comments.body:
## N3 pair at 48 layers: censored by #7956 at step 76 — and #7956 is now the binding constraint

`moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-n3full-20260806` — the first test of the **N3 pair** (`HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 4` **plus** `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1`) on the real 48-layer model, 8 racks, `ae5c93e70`. This is the cell identified in [comment 5200665476](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5200665476) as untested: both knobs are independently falsified (LOI alone wedged as N2; per-GPU alone wedged as `procgpu2`), so only the pair was unexplored.

**Both knobs verified before trusting anything** — the discipline that the affinity flag taught us, where an env var arrived and changed nothing:

```
NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1          read back from /proc/1/environ
RAS: 128 nodes / 4 processes per node / 1 GPU per process / 512 / 512
     3 communicator groups (vs the shipped layout's 4)
```

**Result: no verdict.** It ran cleanly to step 76 — past `ctrl48b`'s two wedge points — at a steady 18.6-19.5 s/it, then died of #7956:

```
06:14:42  task 9 (global rank 36, rack 0)
          cudaFreeAsync failed to free 0xc663e3400: INTERNAL: CUDA error:
          CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION: an illegal instruction was encountered   (x48)
06:14:42  reaches the JAX Shutdown barrier alone -- "1/512 ... first task at the barrier: 36"
06:20:23  barrier DEADLINE_EXCEEDED -> all 512 ranks aborted
```

**Step 76 is not evidence the pair works.** `procgpu2` wedged at ~160, so 76 sits comfortably inside the window where the control can still look healthy. It is equally not evidence against. The cell remains open and is re-queued.

## The thing that actually changed tonight: #7956 is censoring almost everything

| run | reached | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `affin1` | step 5 | #7956, task 98 |
| `affin2` | step 17 | #7956, task 104 |
| `n3full` | step 76 | #7956, task 9 |

Three consecutive runs killed before any wedge verdict. Earlier in the same session `ctrl48b` and `procgpu2` both reached wedge verdicts, so the censorship rate appears to have **risen during the night**. Faulting racks were 6, 6, 0 — so it is not one node, but it is also not uniformly spread.

This matters for planning as much as for diagnosis: every 48-layer trial is a multi-hour exposure window, and at the current rate most of them will be censored before they can answer anything. Two consequences we are acting on:

1. **Prefer short repro vehicles while this persists.** A rung-1 run wedges in ~7 minutes and is far less exposed than a multi-hour 48-layer run.
2. **This strengthens the Xid/DCGM request** in [comment 5199937610](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5199937610). Three fresh `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` events with timestamps and task identities are exactly what a host-log pull should be correlated against. Adding them here for whoever picks that up:

```
2026-08-06 03:17:14 UTC   affin1  task 98   (tasks 96-111 = rack 6)
2026-08-06 05:2x    UTC   affin2  task 104  (rack 6)
2026-08-06 06:14:42 UTC   n3full  task 9    (rack 0), global rank 36
```

All three show the same shape: a failed **free** (`cudaFreeAsync`) reporting `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` with no memory pressure (`InUse` 65 MiB against a 138 GiB limit on `affin1`, `Free/Total 0/0` = context already poisoned). The free is the messenger, not the cause — consistent with what the issue body already records.

comments.body:
Btw the CW Grafana may be worth glancing over. For `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-ctrl48b-20260806` I think we see a/the wedge at ~2:13:
During that period (2026-08-06 02:03:00 - 2026-08-06 02:13:00) we also see some alerts (from `s7vpxs64`, which participated in the job): * GPUXID43ApplicationResetChannelError * GPUXID13UserApplicationFault The timeline lines up, the nodes participated in the job, could that be related?
GPUXID43ApplicationResetChannelError

From https://modal.com/docs/guide/gpu-health on GPUXID43ApplicationResetChannelError: Marked as non-critical, indicates GPU stopped processing, due to a user application encountering a software induced fault. Restart applications and check whether the same Xid is returned. And report if the issue persists. (...)

GPUXID13UserApplicationFault

From https://modal.com/docs/guide/gpu-health on GPUXID13UserApplicationFault: Marked as non-critical, this error indicates GPU memory anomalies affecting code and data segments, arrays being out of their declared ranges, applications having illegal memory access issues, or instruction errors. Restart applications and check whether the same Xid is returned. To debug, refer to [cuda-memcheck](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-memcheck) or [CUDA-GDB](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-gdb/index.html). In rare cases it can be caused by the hardware degradation. Please contact Modal support if the issue persists. (...)

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## We can run on the NVIDIA JAX image after all — and the dependency-shadowing risk is now proven closed

This matters because a reproduction inside NVIDIA's own container is what makes this actionable for NVIDIA support.

### The earlier "not viable" verdict was too strong

[Comment 5196613173](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5196613173) parked this work because `nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:26.07-py3` pins `/opt/xla` at `64f6bb7c` (2026-07-07), twelve days before the #7421 loader fix (`openxla/xla@a2905046`, 2026-07-19), and concluded 26.07 "would reintroduce the #7421 CUBIN load failure".

Re-reading #7421: that failure is **intermittent** for large JAX programs generally, and becomes **deterministic only "in the CuTe MXFP8 producer path"**. Identical configurations pass on retry. It also fires at *first execution* and raises a `JaxRuntimeError`, which is trivially distinguishable from a silent wedge.

**Rung 1 (`attention_implementation="reference"`, `moe_implementation="scatter"`) never touches the CuTe path.** So the deterministic mode does not apply, and the worst case is a startup failure cleared by relaunching. Confirmed empirically below: the smoke trained with no CUBIN failure at all.

Also checked, so nobody repeats it: **26.07 is still the newest NVIDIA JAX image** (no 26.08 yet), and `ghcr.io/nvidia/jax` is **abandoned** — its `:main` tag is from 2023-04-17 with CUDA 12.1 and NCCL 2.17.1. It is not a nightly channel.

### The shadowing trap, and proof that it is closed

Iris prepends `/app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages`, so **the task image's Python stack is normally invisible — swapping the image alone is a no-op.** `experiments/grug/byo_image_setup.py` makes `$IRIS_VENV` a thin overlay instead (`uv venv --python <image python> --system-site-packages`, then the locked closure minus every image-owned package).

Two fixes were needed to its hard gate:

1. It ended with `import quack.dsl`, which is **unsatisfiable at rung 1** — quack calls `torch.cuda.get_device_capability`, while the same gate requires a CPU-only torch (a CUDA torch drags `nvidia-*` wheels whose lib dirs jax's plugin prepends, shadowing the image's CUDA and NCCL and destroying exactly what this measures). Rung 1 is the configuration that dissolves that contradiction, so the check was removed.
2. Absence of wheels is necessary but not sufficient, so I added a **positive** provenance check on the resolved shared objects, failing hard if any resolves under `/uv/cache` or `site-packages`.

Gate output from the 1-rack smoke:

```
[byo-image] jax     0.10.2.dev20260630+3757395a28  /opt/jax/jax/__init__.py
[byo-image] jaxlib  0.10.2.dev20260725             /opt/jaxlibs/jaxlib/jaxlib/__init__.py
[byo-image] jax-cuda13-plugin 0.10.2.dev20260725
[byo-image] jax-cuda13-pjrt   0.10.2.dev20260725
[byo-image] nvidia-nccl-cu13  absent (expected: NGC ships these as system libs, not wheels)
[byo-image] nvidia-cudnn-cu13 absent (expected)
[byo-image] torch   2.11.0+cpu  /app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/torch/__init__.py
[byo-image] libnccl.so.2:    /lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libnccl.so.2
[byo-image] libcudart.so.13: /usr/local/cuda/targets/sbsa-linux/lib/libcudart.so.13
[byo-image] libcuda.so.1:    /lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so.1
[byo-image] provenance gate passed
```

jax and jaxlib resolve from `/opt` in the image; NCCL, CUDA runtime and the driver stub all resolve to image paths; torch is the CPU build from our venv and drags no CUDA. **No shadowing.**

Then it trained: step 1 at 71.5 s/it, step 7 at 8.2 s/it, no `Failed to load in-memory CUBIN` anywhere.

One caution worth repeating from the earlier writeup, because I nearly fell for it again: **do not infer the XLA checkout from version strings.** `jaxlib` reports `0.10.2.dev20260725` and `BUILD_DATE=2026-07-24`, both *after* the #7421 fix, while `/opt/xla` is a 2026-07-07 checkout. The image is pinned to `JAX_TOOLBOX_REF=26.07-devel`. Only the source in the image is authoritative.

Note also that 26.07 ships **NCCL 2.30.7 and CUDA 13.3.1**, against our 2.28.9 / CUDA 13.0. NCCL 2.30.7 alone was already tested (T1) and wedged, so a wedge on this image is not attributable to the NCCL version.

### What this run is and is not

The 1-rack smoke **cannot reproduce the wedge** and must not be read as evidence about it: a single rack has no cross-rack collective at all, and the desync we are chasing is cross-rack (RAS reports the intra-rack communicator OK while every rack-spanning group is MISMATCH). It is a validation of the image swap only. The 8-rack rung-1 run is what can reproduce, and is next.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## The wedge REPRODUCES on NVIDIA's own JAX container — with a verified provenance chain

`moe-hero-fsdp-ngc-8rack-20260806` — 8 racks / 128 nodes / 512 GPUs, rung 1, running entirely on **`nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:26.07-py3`**. Wedged at **~step 115-120, about 10 minutes in**.

This is the artifact that makes the issue actionable for NVIDIA: the failure occurs on their image, with their jax, jaxlib, XLA, CUDA and NCCL, and we can prove none of ours leaked in.

### Provenance — verified, not assumed

The failure mode we had to rule out is that iris prepends `/app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages`, so **swapping the image alone is a no-op**. The overlay venv plus a hard gate closes that:

```
[byo-image] jax     0.10.2.dev20260630+3757395a28  /opt/jax/jax/__init__.py
[byo-image] jaxlib  0.10.2.dev20260725             /opt/jaxlibs/jaxlib/jaxlib/__init__.py
[byo-image] nvidia-nccl-cu13 / nvidia-cudnn-cu13   absent
[byo-image] torch   2.11.0+cpu  /app/.venv/...     (CPU build, drags no CUDA)
[byo-image] libnccl.so.2    => /lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libnccl.so.2
[byo-image] libcudart.so.13 => /usr/local/cuda/targets/sbsa-linux/lib/libcudart.so.13
[byo-image] libcuda.so.1    => /lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libcuda.so.1
[byo-image] provenance gate passed
NCCL version 2.30.7+cuda13.3      (ours is 2.28.9 / CUDA 13.0)
```

The gate hard-fails if `jax`/`jaxlib` resolve from the venv, if torch carries CUDA, or if any of those shared objects resolve under `/uv/cache` or `site-packages`.

### Wedge signature: confirmed by frozen power

```
             pass A (06:59:55)                    pass B (07:00:03)
task0    282.52 / 208.40 / 210.86 / 235.77 W   226.62 / 206.38 / 207.09 / 232.10 W
task16   223.32 / 202.93 / 199.49 / 217.42 W   223.25 / 206.37 / 198.08 / 220.79 W
task64   219.94 / 205.00 / 203.31 / 231.59 W   219.85 / 202.90 / 203.12 / 229.38 W
task112  223.00 / 210.20 / 207.03 / 229.85 W   223.00 / 210.21 / 207.03 / 231.87 W
```

All 100% util, every clock pinned at 1950 MHz. `task112` GPU0 reads **223.00 W in both passes** and GPU2 **207.03 W in both**. Re-sampled four minutes later, `task112` GPU1 was still **210.21 W** and GPU3 still **231.87 W** — identical to two decimals. Last progress was step 115 at 06:56:01; still frozen at 07:03:47.

ECC, row-remapping and throttle state: **clean** on both a lagging and a healthy node.

### The desync structure is DIFFERENT from every previous wedge

```
#0-0 MISMATCH  Communicator ranks have different AllReduce operation counts
  504 ranks have launched up to operation 1208
    8 ranks have launched up to operation 1206
  Rank 332-335 -> node 10.186.210.89
  Rank 388-391 -> node 10.186.210.205
```

**Eight ranks — two individual nodes, in two different racks.** Every prior capture (`ctrl48b`, `procgpu2`, `oldbaseB`) showed exactly one rack, 64 ranks, lagging. Group 2 (the intra-rack communicator) also now reports an **AllGather** mismatch, where it previously read `OK`.

I am flagging this rather than smoothing it over: this may be a second failure mode, or rung-1 wedges may simply differ structurally from 48-layer wedges. It shares the frozen-power signature, all-ranks-alive, and an operation-count desync — but "one rack lags" does not hold here.

### A correction: this is NOT a "host-side" stall

I have been describing the wedge as host-side, on the grounds that RAS says the lagging rack stops *launching* operations. **The stacks refute that reading.** Using py-spy on the lagging node and a non-lagging node:

```
LAGGING  rank 332, task 83, s6htxs64      NON-LAGGING  task 19, s4btxs64
Thread 1 (idle): "MainThread"             Thread 1 (idle): "MainThread"
    _run_grug_local (train.py:593)            _run_grug_local (train.py:593)
```

**Identical.** Both blocked at the same line, which is the `train_step(...)` dispatch. With native frames:

```
Thread 1 (idle): "MainThread"
    0xfc0017f097a4 (libc.so.6)
    absl::...::synchronization_internal::FutexWaiter::WaitUntil (xla_cuda13/xla_cuda_plugin.so)
    _run_grug_local (experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py:593)
```

So every rank's host thread is parked in an absl futex inside the XLA CUDA plugin, waiting for the PJRT async-execution queue to drain — exactly what you expect when the device is stuck. **The divergence is below Python, in the XLA/PJRT/NCCL layer, not in host scheduling.** RAS's "launched up to operation N" counts NCCL operations enqueued on the device, not Python-level progress, and I conflated the two.

Consequence: ablations motivated by host-side blocking are weakened. In particular the plan to remove the per-step `int(state.step)` device→host sync was motivated by the EP64 faulthandler stacks pointing at `__int__`; those stacks were taken on arbitrary tasks, and here the main thread is not in `__int__` at all.

py-spy cannot see NCCL's proxy threads — the process has **1222 OS threads** but py-spy reports only the 8 registered with the interpreter, and NCCL's proxies are unnamed among 486 `python` threads. Getting inside NCCL needs gdb or an interposer.

### What this does and does not establish

- **Establishes:** the wedge is not caused by our jax/jaxlib/XLA/CUDA/NCCL build. It reproduces on NVIDIA's, with NCCL 2.30.7 + CUDA 13.3.1 rather than our 2.28.9 + CUDA 13.0.
- **Consistent with** the earlier T1 result, where bumping only NCCL to 2.30.7 on our stack also wedged.
- **Does not establish** anything about 48 layers. This is rung 1, and rung-0/1 results have twice failed to predict 48-layer behaviour. Running 48 layers on the image is blocked by a real tension: it needs `sonic_cute` → `quack` → `torch.cuda`, and a CUDA torch drags `nvidia-*` wheels whose lib dirs jax's plugin prepends — reintroducing exactly the shadowing this setup exists to prevent.

comments.body:
## Re: the CW Grafana Xid alerts — this may unify #7344 and #7956, and here is the data to test it

@ravwojdyla — this is a significant lead, and it also **supersedes part of my escalation request** in [comment 5199937610](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5199937610). I concluded Xid data was unavailable because `dmesg` is blocked in the container (needs `CAP_SYSLOG`), `/dev/kmsg` is absent, `dcgmi` is not in the image, and NVML never exposes Xid. I did not check whether CW surfaces it in Grafana. It does, and that is a much better path than a manual host-log pull.

### Why the specific Xids matter

- **Xid 13** — user application fault: illegal memory access, out-of-range arrays, or **instruction errors**.
- **Xid 43** — GPU stopped processing after a software-induced fault; channel reset.

**Xid 13 is the plausible host-side counterpart of `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`**, which is exactly #7956. And Xid 43 says *the GPU stopped processing*.

That suggests a mechanism I had not been considering — one underlying fault with two presentations:

- the runtime notices and the rank dies → **#7956** (shutdown barrier, gang abort)
- the channel is reset but the process stays alive, and that GPU simply stops advancing its NCCL work → **#7344** (silent wedge; that rank's operation count stops climbing, everyone else spins waiting)

If that holds, #7344 and #7956 are the same event seen from two sides, which would explain why they have been so hard to separate — and why the "discriminator" we adopted (does a rank die?) tracks the *reporting path* rather than the *fault*.

I want to be explicit that this is a hypothesis on one correlated timestamp. What would confirm or kill it is checking the Xid stream against the wedges I captured overnight, all of which have precise timestamps and hostnames.

### Correlation set from last night — three wedges

All confirmed by frozen power (100% util, clocks pinned 1950, sub-watt drift between passes) with ECC/row-remap/throttle clean.

| run | last progress (UTC) | wedge confirmed | RAS-identified lagging unit | hosts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-ctrl48b-20260806` | 02:11:43 | 02:47–02:53 | **one rack** — ranks 384-447, 16 nodes `10.186.211.127`–`.161` | lagging `s44txs64`; healthy `s2rsxs64` |
| `moe-hero-fsdp-ngc-8rack-20260806` | 06:56:01 | 06:59–07:04 | **two nodes, two racks** — ranks 332-335 on `10.186.210.89`, ranks 388-391 on `10.186.210.205` | lagging `s6htxs64`; healthy `s4btxs64` |
| `moe-hero-ep-8rack-20260806` | 12:25:38 | 12:36–12:51 | **one rank** — rank 173 (task 43, GPU 1) | lagging `sdktxs64`; healthy `s1mwxs64` |

Your `ctrl48b` wedge time of ~02:13 lines up with my last progress line at 02:11:43. Worth noting `s7vpxs64` is not one of the two hosts I sampled on that run — I only sampled a lagging-rack node and a healthy one, so it may well be in the lagging rack (ranks 384-447) without my having touched it.

### And three #7956 faults from the same night, for the other direction

| run | fault time (UTC) | task | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-affin1-20260806` | 03:17:14 | 98 | `cudaFreeAsync failed ... CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`, ×48 |
| `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-affin2-20260806` | ~05:25 | 104 | same shape; gang aborted 05:30:11 |
| `moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-n3full-20260806` | 06:14:42 | 9 (rank 36) | same shape; gang aborted 06:20:23 |

**The decisive check:** do the wedge rows show Xid 13/43 on a node *inside the RAS-identified lagging unit*, and do the #7956 rows show Xid 13 on the faulting task's node? If both, the two issues collapse into one. If wedges show Xid 43 without 13 while #7956 shows 13, that separates the reporting paths cleanly.

The EP row is the sharpest test: its lagging unit is a **single GPU** (rank 173 = task 43 GPU 1 on `sdktxs64`), so a matching Xid should name one specific GPU rather than a whole node.

I do not have Grafana access from here (`grafana.oa.dev` is IAP-gated and the CW read token is a deployment secret), so I cannot run this correlation myself — but every timestamp and hostname above is exact, and the underlying capture files are on disk if more detail is useful.

### One correction this prompts to my own earlier writeup

In [comment 5201483589](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5201483589) I reported that py-spy stacks are **identical** on lagging and non-lagging ranks — both parked in `absl::...FutexWaiter::WaitUntil` inside `xla_cuda_plugin.so` — and concluded the divergence is below Python, in XLA/PJRT/NCCL rather than host scheduling. An Xid-43 channel reset on one GPU fits that observation well: the host thread would look identical everywhere, because every rank is simply waiting on a device that is not going to finish.

## EP at 8 racks wedges too — and the "one rack lags" structure does not hold

Two more results, plus a structural finding that undercuts something I asserted earlier in this thread.

### EP64 at 8 racks: wedged at ~step 1290

`moe-hero-ep-8rack-20260806` — `moe_hero_ep` on current `origin/main` (`f8a0c7cba`, which includes #7981 "Run the FSDP hero shape on the EP64 mesh"), scaled to **8 racks**: 128 nodes / 512 GPUs, `expert_axis_size=64` (intra-rack), `replica_axis_size=8` (cross-rack), batch 8192, 48 layers / 128 experts top-4, `moe_implementation=fixed_all_to_all`.

The shipped launcher is hardcoded to `HERO_EP_NODES = 16` — **one rack**. That had to change, and the reason matters: our desync lives on the cross-rack axis, so a 1-rack EP job has no cross-rack collective at all and could not exhibit the failure. A clean result there would have been a null by construction. I added `--dp-racks` mirroring the FSDP launcher.

It ran clean for **5.3 hours / ~1290 steps**, then wedged. Frozen power confirms it (`task16` GPU0 241.17 W in both passes, clocks pinned 1950, sub-watt drift throughout; ECC/remap/throttle clean).

**So collective structure is not the discriminator.** FSDP and EP both wedge at the same infrastructure scale, with completely different dominant collectives. But EP was *far* more robust — ~1290 steps against FSDP's 17-160.

### `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0`: wedged (probable negative)

`moe-hero-fsdp-8rack-mnnvl0-20260806` — the control config plus `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0`, to force cross-domain traffic off multi-node NVLink onto IB/RoCE. Motivation was that MNNVL is the transport distinctive to GB200 and our desync is cross-rack.

Wedged at **~step 24**. Frozen power (`task16` GPU2 226.05 W and GPU3 246.67 W identical across passes; `task64` GPU2 241.06 W identical).

**Caveat, stated because it weakens the result:** I verified `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0` reached the trainer (`/proc/1/environ`), and the run showed a steady **25.8 s/it against the control's 19.2 s/it** — a ~35% slowdown consistent with the transport actually changing. But `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` in these runs, so NCCL emits no INFO-level transport lines and I could **not** directly confirm MNNVL was disabled. The throughput drop is suggestive, not proof; node-placement variance could produce something similar. Treat this as a probable negative. A definitive version needs `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, at the cost of very large log volume on 512 ranks.

### The lagging unit is NOT always one rack

Earlier in this thread I described the signature as "exactly one rack, 64 ranks, lagging" and built the rank-0-role and rack-identity arguments on it. **That does not survive more captures:**

| run | lagging unit | detail |
|---|---|---|
| `ctrl48b`, `procgpu2`, `oldbaseB` | **one rack** (64 ranks) | e.g. ranks 384-447 |
| `ngc-8rack` (rung 1, NVIDIA image) | **two nodes, two racks** (8 ranks) | `10.186.210.89` + `10.186.210.205` |
| `ep-8rack` | **one rank** | rank 173 = task 43, GPU 1 |
| `mnnvl0` | **one rank** | rank 193 = task 48, GPU 1 |

RAS in the two single-rank cases:

```
Group 0 (global, 512):   511 ranks at op N      ->  1 lagging
Group 2 (intra-rack, 64): 63 ranks at op M      ->  1 lagging
Group 4 (8 ranks):         7 ranks at op K      ->  1 lagging
```

So the lagging unit ranges from a single GPU to a whole rack. "One rack lags" was an artifact of the first three captures, not a property of the bug. What is invariant is: *some* subset stops advancing its operation count while every rank stays alive and every GPU spins at 100% util on frozen power.

Small observation, offered as weak: both single-rank cases lagged on **local GPU index 1** (rank 173 = 43×4+1, rank 193 = 48×4+1). n=2, so this is a thing to watch rather than a finding.

### Running tally of ablations that do NOT prevent the wedge

| ablation | result |
|---|---|
| NCCL 2.28.9 → 2.30.7 (T1) | wedges |
| `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` (N2) | wedges |
| per-GPU process layout (`procgpu2`) | wedges |
| `NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY=1` | censored ×2, weak negative |
| NVIDIA JAX container (image jax/jaxlib/XLA/CUDA/NCCL) | wedges |
| EP64 collective structure | wedges |
| `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0` | wedges (probable) |
| NVLS on vs off | wedges both ways (accidental ablation via the shared-PID gate) |

`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0` is running now.

## #7956 has become the binding constraint: 48-layer ablations mostly cannot finish

Reporting this as an operational finding, because it now determines what experiments are feasible more than any hypothesis does.

### Twelve 8-rack trials over ~14 hours

| run | reached | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `ctrl48b` (control) | steps 33, 17 | **wedged ×2** |
| `procgpu2` (per-GPU) | ~152 | **wedged** |
| `affin1` (`NCCL_IGNORE_CPU_AFFINITY=1`) | 5 | #7956 — task 98 |
| `affin2` (same) | 17 | #7956 — task 104 |
| `n3full` (per-GPU + `LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT`) | 76 | #7956 — task 9 |
| `ngc-smoke` (1 rack, rung 1, NVIDIA image) | 25/25 | clean (validation only) |
| `ngc-8rack` (rung 1, NVIDIA image) | ~115 | **wedged** |
| `ep-8rack` (EP64, 8 racks) | ~1290 | **wedged** |
| `mnnvl0` (`NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0`) | 24 | **wedged** (probable) |
| `pgle0` (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0`) | 37 | **OOM** — see below |
| `nowatch` (watch disabled) | 2 | #7956 — task 61 |

Four wedge verdicts, **four #7956 censorships**, one OOM, one validation run.

Every #7956 event has the same shape: one rank logs `cudaFreeAsync failed ... CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` (or `cuMemAllocAsync`) with no memory pressure, reaches the JAX Shutdown barrier alone, the barrier times out ~5 minutes later, and all 512 ranks abort.

Faulting tasks and times, for correlation against the Xid stream (@ravwojdyla's lead in [comment 5201166967](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5201166967)):

```
03:17:14  affin1   task 98
~05:25    affin2   task 104
06:14:42  n3full   task 9   (global rank 36)
14:11:03  nowatch  task 61
```

**The censorship rate rose through the night.** The first two runs of the session both reached wedge verdicts; four of the last six were censored. If that persists, most multi-hour 48-layer ablations will not produce a verdict, and the practical response is to run short vehicles — rung 1 at 8 racks wedges in ~10 minutes and is far less exposed.

### `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0` is config-blocked at 48 layers

Worth recording so nobody re-runs it. The flag verifiably took effect — the control's PGLE warm-up curve (249.8 → 169.8 → 52.0 → 25.9 → 20.5 s/it over steps 1-17) was **absent**, going straight to 47.5 → 25.6 → 20.4 → 19.7.

But at step 37, task 100:

```
gpu_cudamallocasync_allocator.cc:359] gpu_async_3 cuMemAllocAsync failed to allocate
123724744912 bytes: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY
```

~115 GiB against a 138 GiB limit. Disabling PGLE changes the compiled executable enough to blow up the temp arena. Any mitigation (smaller batch, fewer layers, different mem fraction) moves the config away from the control and confounds the comparison, so **PGLE cannot be cleanly ablated at 48 layers on this shape**.

This is the same trap as the issue body's retired "145 GiB allocation" section — an ablation producing a giant allocation that has nothing to do with the bug. Rung 3 still has no verdict at any scale: censored twice by #7956 at rung 0, OOM at 48 layers.

### A methodological correction on how I have been calling wedges

I have leaned on "100% util at frozen low power" as the wedge discriminator. That is **weaker than I presented it**, and a run tonight showed why.

On `pgle0` at 13:55 I sampled 206-280 W, 100% util, 34-36 °C — which looks exactly like the wedge signature. It was not a wedge: task 100 had faulted at 13:49:41 and the other 511 ranks were spinning in their collectives waiting for a peer that was never coming back. The gang aborted at 14:00:30.

A rank *legitimately waiting* in a collective runs the same NCCL wait kernel as a wedged one. So low, flat power distinguishes **not-computing** from **computing** — not **wedged** from **blocked-on-a-dead-peer** or **transiently-waiting**. What actually makes it a wedge is the conjunction of that reading with sustained no-progress *and* a persistent RAS operation-count gap *and* `failures=0` with every rank alive. Every wedge call in this thread does rest on that conjunction, but I should have been stating it rather than leading with the wattage.

Two further gaps worth flagging:

- **Temperature is a better signal and I was not collecting it.** Those wedged GPUs sit at 34-36 °C while reporting 100% util; sustained compute on these parts runs far hotter. I have no healthy-compute baseline because I never queried it. Added going forward.
- **I cannot currently exclude stale telemetry.** "Frozen power" assumes the reading is live and the value genuinely constant. After an **Xid 43 channel reset**, stale telemetry would look identical. `total_energy_consumption` is not a valid query field on this driver, so I have no monotonic counter to prove liveness. This matters directly for the Xid hypothesis.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## Root cause: NCCL 2.28.9 leaks proxy-op slots on aarch64; a rank whose pool runs dry deadlocks silently

**TL;DR.** The wedge is a host-side deadlock inside NCCL's proxy-op pool, caused by a lost
lock-free update that can only happen on aarch64 (Grace). `ncclProxyGetPostedOps` returns freed op
slots to the shared pool with a *weak* compare-exchange whose retry condition checks the observed
*value* instead of the CAS *result* (`proxy.cc:845-852` in 2.28.9). A weak CAS may fail spuriously
— return false with the value unchanged — and that exact case exits the loop without storing, so
the whole batch of freed slots is orphaned. Slots leak until one rank's 2048-slot partition is
empty; that rank then spins forever in `ncclLocalOpAppend` waiting for a free slot while its own
progress thread sleeps in `pthread_cond_wait` waiting for work, and the other 127 ranks block in
the collective. No error, no timeout, no counter anywhere — the slots just vanish. NVIDIA fixed
exactly this loop in
[v2.29.3-1](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl/commit/25368a7f78bae866f29e46938af94fa586c84484)
(rewritten to retry on the CAS return value), and the [2.29.3 release notes](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2293/release-notes/rel_2-29-3.html)
confirm it verbatim: *"Fixed CAS usage in case of weak failure which was causing a hang on
ARM. The issue affected NCCL when compiled with gcc versions prior to 10."* (The pypi
2.28.9 aarch64 wheel is evidently such a build — the disassembly above shows it.) Our GPU stack pins `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.28.9`.

Causal A/B on the 2-rack minimal repro (#7344 repro branch): stock 2.28.9 wedged **7/7** trials
(6 stock + 1 with GDR disabled) between step 0 and step 347, i.e. within ~30 s of training;
with the one-line lock change to `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7` (verified in-pod: the mapped
`libnccl.so.2` banner reads `NCCL version 2.30.7`), the same program ran **all 20,000 steps to
completion** (`minrepro-nccl2307-20260807-011334`, ~35 min, `state=succeeded`).

### The frozen state, read from a live wedge with lldb

Run `minrepro-gdr0-20260807-004411` (2 racks, 128 GPUs). RAS named rank 84 (task 21, GPU 0, node
`10.186.213.153`) as lagging, 8232 vs 8250. Attaching lldb to that process (via the k8s pod;
trainer is PID 1):

- The launcher thread is spinning at `proxy.cc:499` — `sched_yield` inside `ncclLocalOpAppend`,
  waiting on `pool->freeOps[20] == -1`. Its comm is the global 128-rank communicator, `rank=84`,
  `opCount=8231`.
- That comm's own proxy progress thread is asleep in `pthread_cond_wait` inside
  `ncclProxyGetPostedOps` (`proxy.cc:797`) with `progressState.active == nullptr` and
  `progressState.nextOps == -1` — it believes there is nothing to do.
- The shared pool (same shm mapped at different VAs in the client and service roles — the pointers
  differ, the freeOps fingerprint matches): `nextOps == -1`, `freeOps[20] == -1`, and the
  producer-side cache is empty (`count=0, freeOp=-1, nextOps=-1`).

So all 2048 slots of rank 84's partition are simultaneously absent from the free list, the posted
queue, the producer cache, and the consumer's active list. Producer waits for the consumer,
consumer waits for the producer. Nothing is running, nothing errors, nothing times out — which is
this issue's four-part signature exactly.

### The slots leaked, and the leak is measurable on healthy ranks too

Walking the pool memory for all four local ranks of that process at wedge time:

| rank (partition) | free slots left of 2048 | leaked |
|---|---|---|
| 84 — the lagging rank | **0** | **2048** |
| 85 | 1218 | 830 |
| 86 | 1602 | 446 |
| 87 | 1346 | 702 |

The wedged rank's 2048 is a fully-accounted leak (its producer cache was verified empty); the healthy ranks' numbers are upper bounds on leakage, since slots parked in a producer's private cache are also absent from the free list. The first partition to reach zero wedges the job. The leaked slots form
orphaned chains that converge into shared suffixes (walking partition 20 finds 4 chain heads whose
chains sum to 2240 over 2048 physical slots) — exactly the shape a lost `freeOps` prepend leaves
behind, since each leaked batch's tail points at the free-list head that was current at the moment
of the loss. One orphan chain is precisely 64 ops of a single `opCount`: one whole return batch.

### Why it only happens here

The compiled aarch64 code makes the failure concrete. At the return site, 2.28.9's
`__atomic_compare_exchange_n(..., weak=true, ...)` + `while (swap != oldFree)` compiles to:

```
+824: ldaxr  w0, [x1]      ; load-exclusive freeOps[i]
+828: cmp    w0, w2        ; observed == expected?
+832: b.ne   +840          ; genuine mismatch -> value-based retry
+836: stlxr  w9, w4, [x1]  ; attempt store; w9 = success flag
+840: cmp    w2, w0        ; values are equal here by construction
+844: b.ne   +816          ; never taken after +836
```

`w9` — the store-exclusive success flag — is never tested. If the reservation is lost between
`ldaxr` and `stlxr`, the store silently does not happen and execution proceeds as success. And the
reservation *does* get lost under exactly this workload: a starved producer spins in
`__atomic_exchange_n(&freeOps[i], -1)` — every exchange (even writing −1 over −1) bounces the
cache line and kills the consumer's reservation while leaving the value equal. Backpressure makes
leaks more likely, leaks make backpressure worse. On x86 this is `lock cmpxchg`, which cannot fail
spuriously — the GB200 fleet is our only aarch64 training platform, which is why weeks of ablations
(transport, kernels, containers, allocator, process layout, MNNVL, NVLS, GDR) never moved it.

It also explains the hazard shape: leak events are stochastic contention events, so time-to-wedge
tracks wall-clock × collective rate, not steps; the minimal repro issues collectives ~300× faster than
the hero and wedges in seconds instead of ~40 minutes, and the EP program — the lowest
cross-rack op rate of the three — survived ~5 hours.

Closed along the way: `NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=0` (verified via `via NET/IB/N` lines with no `/GDRDMA`
suffix) still wedged at step 163 — the earlier `received=2, flushed=0` observation was where the
victim pipeline happened to freeze, not the cause. The Xid 13/43 lead is also moot for the wedge:
this deadlock produces no Xid, consistent with the clean host logs on the repro's wedges.

### What this does and does not close

- The minimal repro's wedge is fully explained and causally confirmed:
  same program, one lock-line change: 2.28.9 wedges 7/7 by step 347, 2.30.7 completes 20,000 steps.
- The production stack (`nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.28.9`) has the bug, and the production signature
  (single-rank RAS lag, frozen power, no error, no timeout, wall-clock hazard) matches in every
  detail we have captured. I consider this the root cause of the #7344 wedge on `main`.
- **Not closed:** `t1nccl` (rung 0, 10 racks, 2026-08-05) wedged with 2.30.7 verifiably loaded,
  and `ngc-8rack` wedged on the NGC image that ships 2.30.7. The fixed loop cannot explain those
  two runs. Either a second, rarer mechanism exists at hero scale, or those wedges were a
  different failure with the same surface signature. The forensic method here (find the lagging
  rank via RAS, attach lldb through the pod, census `pool->freeOps` chain lengths per partition)
  takes ~15 minutes on a live wedge and distinguishes "slot-leak deadlock" from anything else —
  the next 2.30.7 wedge should get that treatment before we theorize further.

### Recommendation

Bump `nvidia-nccl-cu13` to ≥2.29.3 (2.30.7 resolves cleanly; the GPU-extra lock diff is one line).
This removes a proven silent-deadlock mechanism from every GB200 job regardless of whether a
second mechanism exists. Runbooks: a wedge from this mechanism is identifiable post-hoc only via
the pool census — power/RAS/py-spy all look identical to other theories — so keep the lldb recipe
with the repro README.

Artifacts on `mcwitt/7344-minimal-repro`: the forensic scripts and method
(`experiments/grug/wedge_forensics/`, commit `6bae32496`), the 2.30.7 pin used for the A/B
(commit `0852e4db3`), and the updated repro README with the superseded GDR-flush section
replaced by this root cause. The full 865-thread lldb dump from the wedged rank is saved
locally (`gdr0-btall.txt`) if anyone wants it attached.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## #8038 verification: the pin removes the proven mechanism; production evidence at 2 and 8 racks is consistent with the fix; the definitive 8-rack positive control is still missing

**What was run here** — the production `moe_hero_fsdp` shape, stock launcher (1 process/node
x 4 GB200, real SlimPajama data), 2 racks, both directions of the lock change, NCCL
provenance read from `/proc/1/maps` on live pods in both runs:

| run | tree | NCCL (mapped) | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hero2r-ctl2289-20260807-034112` | main `839e5e9e1` | 2.28.9+cuda13.0 | **1150 steps / 5 h 58 m clean** (ended by the 6 h timeout) |
| `hero2r-fix2307-20260807-094312` | PR #8038 `25f8cbaf3` | 2.30.7+cuda13.3 | 845 steps / 4 h 26 m clean, killed deliberately once the control null made the arm non-discriminating |

**The control is a null, and an informative one:** stock main on the *broken* NCCL ran ~6 h
clean at 2 racks, against a 20-40 minute onset at 8 racks. Under the naive assumption that
per-rank hazard is scale-independent, the recorded 8-rack onsets (steps 17-183) put the
probability of 1150 clean control steps at roughly 4-5%, so either this was a moderately
lucky draw or — more consistent with the mechanism, whose leak fires at proxy backpressure
episodes that 2-way cross-rack traffic rarely creates — the per-rank leak rate itself
collapses at 2 racks. Either way a 2-rack production A/B has no discriminating power,
which is why the treatment arm was stopped rather than run to completion: without a
demonstrated control wedge under identical conditions, its clean steps are a
compatibility receipt, not causal evidence.

**The causal evidence remains the reproducer**, which preserves the hero's mesh, sharding
and collective structure at ~300x the collective rate and is the only workload on which a
live wedge has been mechanistically dissected: 7/7 wedges on 2.28.9 with the slot-leak
census taken on the live wedge, 20000+5000 steps clean on 2.30.7
([root cause](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5211016784)),
and NVIDIA's 2.29.3 release note naming the bug.

**Production scale, from #8029 (rjpower), same 2.30.7 pin:** the supervised gates ran the
minimal repro 1000 steps clean at 2 racks (NVLS off/on) and 1000 steps clean at 8 racks /
512 GPUs, and three 8-rack production arms ran clean past the entire documented 17-183
wedge window (steps 305 / 205 / 262, ~772 cumulative; one arm `/proc`-verified free of all
recovery instrumentation). Five recorded 8-rack FSDP wedges sit at steps 17-152 and the
wiki:85 incident at 183, all on 2.28.9-era stacks. The wedge has not been reproduced on
the pinned stack at any scale.

**What this does not settle.** Two things keep the file open:

1. The 8-rack **positive control on current code + 2.28.9** has not completed — the
   old-code bisect in #8029 spent its 51-minute budget inside the cold 300B compile and
   never reached step 0. Until a 2.28.9 arm wedges *concurrently* with clean 2.30.7 arms,
   "the cluster/node state changed under us" remains a formal alternative to "the pin
   fixed it". The 2026-08-03..06 wedge cluster against ~772 clean steps since makes that
   alternative strained, but it is not excluded.
2. Two historical wedges on stacks that already shipped 2.30.7: `t1nccl` (10 racks, our
   wheel — provenance probable but not airtight; see the
   [audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5218627084)
   of the cu12/cu13 `libnccl` path collision) and `ngc-8rack` (NVIDIA 26.07 container,
   fully confounded stack). If real, a
   second, rarer mechanism exists above 8 racks. The pool forensics
   (`mcwitt/7344-minimal-repro`, `experiments/grug/wedge_forensics/`) classify any future
   wedge as slot-leak or not in ~15 minutes; that should be the first move on the next
   occurrence.

**Verdict: verified within testable scope.** #8038 causally removes the only #7344
mechanism ever pinned on a live wedge, and every production run on the pinned stack —
2-rack here, 8-rack in #8029 — has run clean through windows where 2.28.9-era stacks
wedged with high probability. What is *not* proven: causality at production scale (the
8-rack 2.28.9 positive control on the current cluster has not completed) and the absence
of a second mechanism at >=8 racks. Merge on the reproducer causality; keep #7344 open
until a warm-cache 2.28.9 control wedges at 8 racks concurrently with clean pinned arms
(or the next live wedge is classified with the forensics).

Note on delivery: resolved 2026-08-07 — #8038 (root override) is closed as superseded by
#8040, whose `nvidia-nccl-cu13>=2.29.3` floors on the levanter/marin GPU extras resolve
every collective-running environment (gpu/tpu/vllm/cpu extras) to the same 2.30.7 wheel.
Residual: a bare `uv sync` with no extras still installs torch's pinned 2.28.9 on Linux,
so ad-hoc torch/NCCL work on a Grace dev pod should verify the mapped `libnccl.so.2`
banner. The verification receipts above are unaffected (the treatment tree `25f8cbaf3`
is preserved on branch `mcwitt/7344-nccl-wedge-fix`).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖

## Audit of the "2.30.7 still wedges" evidence — plus a silent NCCL path collision everyone verifying versions should know about

The two runs behind "the NCCL upgrade was ruled out" were re-audited on three criteria:
was the upgraded library actually invoked, were there confounds, and was the symptom
unambiguously the wedge.

**`t1nccl` (10 racks, our stack, the single-variable arm).** The recorded provenance was
task 0's mapped path (`/uv/cache/archive-v0/<id>/nvidia/nccl/lib/libnccl.so.2`) plus
`importlib.metadata.version("nvidia-nccl-cu13") == 2.30.7`. That chain has a hole: the
mapped **file's identity was never read** (no banner — `NCCL_DEBUG` resolved to WARN — no
size, no sha), and the training environment also installs `nvidia-nccl-cu12==2.28.9` via
`torch==2.11.0+cu128`. Both wheels ship the **identical** install path
`nvidia/nccl/lib/libnccl.so.2`, and uv resolves the conflict silently, last writer wins —
installed in the wrong order, the venv's one libnccl *is* the leaky 2.28.9, while the cu13
wheel metadata still reads 2.30.7. Reproduced locally: sequential install cu13-then-cu12
leaves the 2.28.9 (cu12 build, 400,796,408 bytes) on the path.

The conclusion probably survives anyway: in a single install transaction (which the task's
`uv sync` is) the cu13 wheel won 4/4 repeated local trials, and every pod where a mapped
libnccl's identity was actually verified reads the cu13 build — `hero2r-ctl2289` (banner
`2.28.9+cuda13.0`), `hero2r-fix2307` (`2.30.7+cuda13.3`), and the 2-rack EP64 capture
(size + SHA-256 matched against exactly this collision). Calibrated: ~90-95% that
`t1nccl` really ran 2.30.7 — not the near-certainty "provenance verified" implied, since
one pod of 160 was checked and the identity was inferred rather than read. Confounds were
minimal (identical to the same-day `ctrl10b` control except the one lock line). Symptom
was strong but not the full conjunction: 46 min silent at step 21, all alive, frozen power
229-261 W — no RAS gap or stacks captured.

**`ngc-8rack` (NVIDIA 26.07 container).** Provenance is airtight (hard gate plus the
runtime banner `NCCL version 2.30.7+cuda13.3` from the container library). But it cannot
speak to our stack: jax 0.10.2.dev, an XLA checkout from 2026-07-07 that predates the
CUBIN loader fix (the same image was ruled non-viable for the T2 ablation on those
grounds), CUDA 13.3, cuDNN 9.24, forward-compat driver. And its own capture flags a
desync structure unlike every prior wedge — 8 ranks on 2 nodes across 2 racks instead of
one full rack of 64, with a new AllGather mismatch.

**Net position, refined.** "NCCL ruled out" was never supported at the strength it read:
one leg is fully confounded and structurally atypical, the other rests on a provenance
inference with a real hole (now mostly closed after the fact). What the total record
supports: the slot leak was the dominant mechanism at <=8 racks — 2.30.7 arms are
uniformly clean there (three 8-rack production arms totalling 771 steps in #8029, all
repro runs) against 2.28.9-era onsets of 17-183 — and the only our-stack 2.30.7 wedge is
one 10-rack draw with strong-but-incomplete symptom evidence. The second-mechanism
question stays open above 8 racks; it should be settled by pool forensics on the next
live wedge, not by these two runs.

**The reusable trap.** Do not verify a loaded NCCL by wheel metadata or by the mapped
path shape. `nvidia-nccl-cu12` and `nvidia-nccl-cu13` collide on
`nvidia/nccl/lib/libnccl.so.2` and uv overwrites silently; torch drags the cu12 one into
GPU training environments. The only trustworthy check is the mapped file itself:

```bash
M=$(grep -m1 -oE "/[^ ]*libnccl.so.2[^ ]*" /proc/<trainer-pid>/maps)
strings "$M" | grep -m1 "^NCCL version"
```

Also recorded at https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/93.

comments.body:
🤖 New silent-hang observation on one rack, on the 2.30.7-pinned stack, with the old 1-process-per-node layout.

A 64-GPU benchmark run wedged at step 30 and sat silent for 10.5 hours with every task alive. Setup: `small_scale_abl_launch` d1024 rung, `ep` flavor (fixed all-to-all, 192 experts top-4, latent 512, capacity factor 2.5), seq 4096, batch 1024, 16 nodes x 4 GB200 on `cw-us-east-08a`, code at `origin/main` 070673668 plus benchmark-harness commits that touch no model or levanter code. W&B: [`ar8062-0-f69a45d88`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ar8062-0-f69a45d88).

Timeline (UTC, 2026-08-12): submitted 05:45; steps ran at ~0.66 s through step 30, last logged 06:29:34; no W&B steps and no job logs after that; killed 17:04 to free the rack. `iris job summary` at kill time: 16/16 tasks `running` for 10h21m, task 0 reporting `failures=1` with a truncated import-list diagnostic I could not interpret.

Details that may matter:

- `processes_per_task=1` — the EP small-scale launcher (and `moe_hero_ep/launch.py`, `HERO_PROCESSES_PER_TASK = 1`) still uses the pre-#8040 layout, not the per-GPU-process layout the N3 ablation arm favored. The clean 1,710-step 10-rack record was collected with per-GPU processes.
- Step 30 is a watch step (`INLINE` watch mode, interval 10, per-parameter norms). Steps 10 and 20 completed. One draw, so this is a weak signal.
- The #8062 ladder ran this same launcher and layout for ~26k steps at d1024 ([`mhep-ladder-hist-noinit-20260808c-ep64-d1024`](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ladder-hist-noinit-20260808c-ep64-d1024)) without hanging, so the layout does not hang reliably at this scale.

Evidence limits: the loaded NCCL was not banner-verified (pods are gone; `uv.lock` pins `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.30.7`), and no stacks, power readings, or RAS output were captured — the run was found cold after 10.5 hours.

The same benchmark is relaunched with a watchdog that trips after 20 minutes without a new W&B step, captures the task summary, and kills the job. It can hold the gang instead of killing if a live one-rack specimen is useful for the pool forensics this issue calls for — say so here and I'll flip it.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up to the [Aug 12 one-rack stall report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5269927243): the per-node failure is PGLE-mediated, confirmed in both directions with an instrumented A/B.

Two same-day per-node control jobs (`ppg-d1024-ep-cf133-ctl`/`ctl2`, d1024 rung, capacity factor 1.33, one GB200 rack) died in every gang generation during early dispatch, before step 0. An instrumented rerun (`ctl3`, with `PYTHONUNBUFFERED`/`PYTHONFAULTHANDLER`) captured the origin the earlier attempts lost to stdout buffering: `jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: ALREADY_EXISTS: Another profiling session active`, raised from `jax/_src/profiler.py:521` inside the auto-PGLE trace wrapper at pjit dispatch — two compiled executables contending for one profiling session. This is the same crash that forced the #8062 ladder to run its per-node arms with PGLE disabled.

The discriminator run (`ctl4`, identical but `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=false`) completed 1000 steps cleanly: median step 0.6130 s, 5.01% drops, peak HBM 12.45 GiB ([W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/ppg-d1024-ep-cf133-ctl4)). So on current main, per-node EP fails with PGLE on (session collision at dispatch; the step-30 FDO-recompile wedge reported above when a run survives dispatch) and works with PGLE off. Eight per-GPU rung runs completed cleanly the same day; per-GPU cannot engage PGLE at all.

One correction to the earlier record: the "second per-node stall" I described in the thread context (run `ar8062-0b`, killed pre-step-0 after ~80 minutes) is reclassified as inconclusive — same-day runs later showed 70+ minutes of queue and startup is normal, and no diagnostics distinguish a stall from a slow start there.

#8209 flips the EP hero template to one process per GPU and defaults PGLE off under that layout. The upstream question this thread still owns: whether the step-30 silent wedge (empty PGLE traces on all 16 hosts, then clique re-initialization, then 10.5 h of silence) is the known clique-init deadlock reached via PGLE's mid-run recompile, or a distinct mechanism. The instrumented reproduction recipe is now cheap: per-node, PGLE on, d1024 rung, watch the step-30 + ~16 min window.
